full_judgment:
Feeling aggrieved by a decision of the appellate Court refusing to interfere with the decision of the trial Court by which the latter rejected defendant's application for restoration of a suit for specific performance of contract on setting aside a decree passed ex parte, the defendant being petitioner approached this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure seeking redress praying for setting aside the decisions of the courts below whereupon Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order complained of in the petition moved in Court should not be set aside.

2. The question which falls for decision in this Rule is whether the decisions of the Courts below in refusing to restore the suit on setting aside the decree passed ex parte was well founded on law within the meaning and scope of Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

3. For the purpose of answering to the said question posed, the circumstances giving rise to the issuance of this Rule may be, in brief, put which are as follows:

The opposite party No.1 as plaintiff instituted a Suit being Other Class Suit No.385 of 1984 in the Court of Munsif, Kumarkhali, Kushtia impleading the petitioner and opposite party No. 2 as defendants for a decree of specific performance of contract on the averment that the defendant-petitioner executed a Bainanama in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party and the former having denied to execute and register a deed of conveyance in favour of the latter, the latter filed the suit for specific performance of contract. The defendant petitioner is alleged to have prayed for time for filing written statement by way of a Vokalatnama. On behalf of the defendant No. 2 the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, a prayer for filing written statement has been also alleged to have been filed in the court. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 having not filed written statement, the Sheristadar, of the Court fixed 3-3-1985 for ex parte hearing of the suit. The suit was, ultimately, decreed ex parte on 3-4-1985.

4. The defendant No.1 thereafter, filed an application under the provision of Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit to its file and number on the averments that without serving any summons and notice upon him, the plaintiff fraudulently obtained an ex parte decree against him and by that he sustained irreparable injury. It is also pleaded that he for the first time on 27-7-1986 got the knowledge that the plaintiff was getting deed of conveyance executed and registered with respect to the suit property. There having been a delay in filing the said application the defendant filed an application under the provision of section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of the said delay. The said application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code has been registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 57 of 1986.

5. The plaintiff resisted the said Miscellaneous Case by presenting a written objection taking the stand that the defendant No.1 having been well aware of the institution of the Suit, on 17-1-1986 appeared in the Court and filed an application for time for presenting written statement. The defendant No.1 having not filed any written statement, the suit was decreed ex parte on 3-4-1985. The defendant No.1, thereafter, through his Advocate withdrew the money deposited in the Court by the plaintiff through Challan. The Miscellaneous Case stood barred by limitation, it is further alleged in the written objection.

6. The defendant No. 1 examined himself as OPW 1.

7. The learned trial Judge on examination of the record found that the defendant No. 1 appeared in the court through a Vokalatnama and he signed on the same. The learned trial Judge on a comparison of the signature of the defendant appearing on the deposition in the Miscellaneous case and the Vokalatnama filed on 17-1-85 found that the two signatures were the product of same handwriting. The learned trial Judge, ultimately, came to the conclusion that the presence of the defendant in the Court on 17-1-85 and the withdrawal of the money is a proof that he had been well aware of the proceeding of the suit since 17-1-85 and the Miscellaneous case stood barred by limitation. With the above finding, the learned trial Judge dismissed the Miscellaneous Case.

8. The defendant-petitioner, against the said decision of the learned trial Judge carried an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 26 of 1989 to the learned District Judge, Kushtia. The learned Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat heard the appeal. The learned Subordinate Judge recorded the following findings:

(i) Whether the defendant-petitioner appeared in the court through the learned Advocate Golam Mohammad had not been tested by calling the learned Advocate or his Assistant (Clerk) and also by comparing their signatures;

(ii) There is no evidence showing whether summons or registered notices were ever issued and also the service return of the same;

(iii) It appeared that the Government of Bangladesh out of their own initiative appeared in the suit within forty-seven days of the issuance of summons and thereafter remained absent and in that way paved the path of ex parte disposal;

(iv) It appeared that both the defendants appeared on off date and in both the cases the Sheristadar-in-Charge sitting in the Sheresta allowed the applications on behalf of the presiding judge;

(v) It appeared further that the Local Government pleader without any order and Vokalatnama of the Deputy Commissioner, Kushtia or signature of any Government Officer out of his own-initiative appeared and took time from the Sheristadar-in-Charge for filing written statement and after that he did not appear;

(vi) The suit was decreed ex parte against the petitioner as well as the defendant Government within 73 days of the issuance of summons;

(vii) The defendant though did not enter into any compromise with the plaintiff withdrew the deposited money. The learned Subordinate judge, thereafter, held that the events leading to the ex parte disposal of the suit cannot be said to be natural.

The learned Subordinate Judge, ultimately, held that the analysis and the decision arrived at by the trial Judge though suffered from procedural defects and incompleteness, he did not see any ground for setting aside the decision arrived at by him. With the above findings, the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the appeal.

9. The defendant-petitioner challenged the correctness of the said decision arrived at by the appellate Court before this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

10. Mr Hasan Foez Siddique, the learned Advocate with Mr Md Serajul Islam, the learned Advocate appeared in support of the Rule. The Opposite party No.1 did not appear to oppose the Rule in spite of the service of notice upon him.

11. The grounds upon which the Revision application has been founded are:

(1) From the order-sheet it is not clear that summons of the suit have at all been sent to the defendant-petitioner and there is no endorsement that summons have been served and acknowledgement of the registered post has been returned and there is no proof that the summons have been served nor the process server has been examined to substantiate the claim as to the service of notice to the suit and the courts below committed a serious error of law in not holding that the summons of the suit have not been served upon the defendants.

(2) The learned Munsif was on leave from 16-2-85 to 23-2-1985 and the Sheristadar passed the orders on 16-2-1985 and 23-2-1985 and the posting of the Suit for ex parte hearing was absolutely without jurisdiction and the awarding of an ex parte decree by the learned Munsif on the basis of those orders was a serious error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice.

(3) The lower appellate Court committed a serious error of law in holding that in an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure there is no scope of determination of fraud inasmuch as the court has jurisdiction to set aside an ex parte decree in an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code if fraud is detected, as fraud vitiates everything.

(4) In view of categorical denial by the defendant-petitioner that he did not execute any Vokalatnama for the purpose of appearance before that Court nor did he pray for time for filing written statement nor did he withdraw any money by putting his signature and in view of the assertion that the signatures are forged, the courts below committed a serious error of law in not comparing the handwriting of the defendant-petitioner by Handwriting expert.

(5) The learned Munsif committed a serious error of law in holding that the Miscellaneous Case is barred by limitation inasmuch as the defendant-petitioner brought the Miscellaneous Case for setting aside the ex parte decree within stipulated period of limitation from the date of his knowledge.

12. In order to understand the subject matter in controversy it is desirable to notice the provisions of both rule 6 of Order IX as well as rule 13 of Order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure.

Order IX, rule 6 reads as under:

"(1) Where the plaintiff appears and the defendant does not appear when the suit is called on for hearing, then-

(a) if it is proved that the summons was duly served, the Court may proceed ex parte;

(b) if  is not proved that the summons was duly served, the Court shall direct a second summons to be issued and served on the defendant;

(c) if it is proved that the summons was served on the defendant, but not in sufficient time to enable him to appear and answer on the day fixed in the summons, the Court shall postpone the hearing of the suit to a future day to be fixed by the Court, and shall direct notice of such day to be given to the defendant.

(2) Where it is owing to the plaintiff's default that the summons was not duly served or was not served in sufficient time, the Court shall order the plaintiff to pay the costs occasioned by the postponement."

Order IX, rule 13 runs thus :

"13. (1) In any case in which a decree is passed ex parte against a defendant, he may apply to the Court by which the decree was passed for an order to set it aside; and if he satisfies the Court that the summons was not duly served, or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing, the Court shall make on order setting aside the decree as against him upon such terms as to costs, payment into Court or otherwise as it thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the suit :

Provided that where the decree is of such a nature that it cannot be set aside as against such defendant only it may be set aside as against all or any of the other defendants also.

(2) Provisions of section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908, shall apply to the applications under rule 13(1) of the Order."

<u>13. In the above provisions the term 'Ex parte' occurs. The expression 'Ex parte' has not been defined any where in the Code of Civil Procedure. It is a Latin expression and means "from one party or side." In Tomlin's Law Dictionary 'Ex parte' is stated thus "of the one part; from one party". The accepted meaning is "proceeding by one in the absence of the other." The term 'Ex parte' thus, is applied in law to a proceeding by one party in the absence of and without notice to the other and carries with it the connotation that a Court or a Judge has proceeded in the absence of the other party when it could have had the other party before it or when it was not prevented by law from hearing the other party before it.</u>

14. Order IX, rule 6 of the Code enjoins that when the plaintiff appears and the defendant does not appear when the Suit is called on for hearing then if it is proved that summons was duly served upon the defendant, the court can proceed ex parte. From the above provisions it becomes manifestly clear that before proceeding ex parte the court must be satisfied that there is due service of summons upon the defendant. The court cannot proceed for ex parte without being satisfied that summons had been duly served upon the defendant and if the court proceeds for an ex parte decree, the same will suffer from patent error of law.

15. Order IX, rule 13 mandates that in an application under rule 13 of Order IX the court has to satisfy itself, (a) the summons had not been duly served upon the defendant, or (b) the defendant has been prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing and if either of the conditions are satisfied, the court is bound to set aside the ex parte decree. In the case before me the first part of the Rule is relevant.

16. The expression "duly served" occurring both in rule 6 and 13 of Order IX of the Code would mean the service as required under the provisions of law of the Code. The expression bears the same meaning as in Order 5 and it only means service in such way as to give information of the suit to the defendant and connect him with the knowledge of the suit..

17. Keeping in view of the above provisions of law let me now see whether the summons and also the registered notice has been duly served upon the defendant and also whether he could make out a case for setting aside the ex parte decree passed against him on the ground of non-service of summons upon him.

18. For the purpose of resolving the said question, a perusal of the order-sheet becomes very much necessary. A perusal of the order-sheet establishes the following facts :

(i) The suit was registered on 18-2-1984 without the documents and also the requisite court-fee.

(ii) Basic documents and requisites were filed on 19-2-1984,

(iii) Deficit court-fee was filed on 31-12-1984 and on the same date there was order for issuance of summons upon the defendants fixing 17-1-1985 for ascertaining contest.

(iv) On 17-1-1985 the defendant No. 1 appears to have appeared in the suit by way of a fresh Vokalatnama (নতুন ওকালতনামা) and also appears to have prayed for time for filing written statement. 6-2-1985 was the next date fixed for filing written statement by defendant No. 1. This order has been signed by the Sheristadar.

(v) On 6-2-1985 the defendant No. 1 does not appear to have filed written statement. 23-2-1985 was fixed for the return of the service of summons of defendant No. 2.

(vi) On 16-2-1985 which was off date, Local Government Pleader appears to have appeared in the suit praying for a time for filing written statement. The application for time though filed on behalf of the defendant No. 2, the Deputy Commissioner, the same was neither signed by the defendant No. 2 nor by any other Officer on his behalf empowered to enter appearance in the suit. The Sheristadar of the court allowed the said prayer.

(vii) On 23-2-85 the defendant No. 2 appears to have not presented any written statement and the Sheristadar of the court fixed 3-3-85 for hearing of the suit ex parte.

(viii) On 3-3-85 the suit could not be taken up for ex parte hearing and 34-85 was refixed for ex parte hearing.

(ix) On 3-4-85 the suit was decreed ex parte on recording the evidence of plaintiff as PW 1.

<u>19. On a perusal of the whole order-sheet upto the date 3-4-85 it does not at all appear that summons was at all served. There is nothing on record to show what happened to those summons issued upon the defendants. From the above materials it becomes manifestly clear that summons upon the defendants were not at all served. If it is seen that no summons had been served not to speak of "duly served" the ex parte decree is liable to be shot down. If is worthy to state that the elements of fraud and collusion is manifested in procuring the ex parte decree by the plaintiff.</u>

<u>20. On a reading of the judgment of both the courts below it appears that both the courts below failed to appreciate the moot point which arose for their consideration in the resolution of the controversy. It has been already pointed out that under Order IX, rule 6 of the Code when the plaintiff appears and the defendant does not appear when the suit is called on for hearing then if it is proved that the summons was duly served meaning that service in such way as to give information of the suit to the defendant then only the court is empowered to proceed ex parte. The court must hold due service of summons proved and it is only then that it can award an ex parte decree. The ex parte decree must be set aside where the court finds that the defendant was not duly served with the summons even if the defendant was aware of the institution of the suit against him. The learned trial Judge did not at all care to bear in mind the provisions contained in rules 6 and 13 of Order IX of the Code. The learned trial Judge laid stress on the fact of appearance of defendant No. 1 by a Vokalatnama praying for time for filing written statement and withdrawing the money deposited in the court by the plaintiff and thus committed an error in taking the view that the defendant was aware of the suit since 17-1-85 and the Miscellaneous case was barred by limitation. The learned trial Judge, thus, misdirected himself in his approach on the matter. The learned Artha Rin Adalat being the appellate Court recorded the positive finding that the service of summons upon the defendant had not been proved and also that there was no proof that the summons and the registered notice were ever issued upon the defendants. The lower appellate Court also recorded the finding that there had been procedural defect in the analysis and decision arrived at by the trial Court. In view of the recording of the above positive findings there was no alternative left for the lower appellate Court but to reverse the decision of the trial Court and restore the suit to its file and number on setting aside the ex parte decree thus allowing the Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code. The lower appellate Court failed to take notice that in a proceeding under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code if it is found that summons were not duly served upon the defendant that is sufficient for knocking down the ex parte decree. The Appellate Division in Abdur Rashid and another vs. Abdul Barik and another, 35 DLR (AD) 162 considered the nature and scope of the provision of Order IX rule 13 of the Code in setting aside an ex parte decree. The observations of their Lordships of the Appellate Division are couched in the following language :</u>

<u>"Under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code, if summons is not duly served on the defendant, that is a good ground for setting aside an ex parte decree. On a perusal of the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Code it would be apparent, that due service of summons is an essential condition, which must be satisfied before the Court can proceed to give a judgment and under Order IX, rule 13 if a party satisfies a Court that summons were not duly served upon him, the Court is bound to set aside an ex parte decree. In such a case question of knowledge is not at all relevant and ex parte decree will be set aside even if the defendant had knowledge of institution of suit. No provision of law could be pointed out by the learned Counsel for the respondent, which dispenses with the necessity of proper service of summons."</u>

<u>21. Let me direct my attention to the contention raised by the plaintiff in the courts below that the defendant No. 1 appeared in the suit by executing a Vokalatnama engaging a learned Advocate praying for a time for presenting written statement and also for withdrawing the money deposited by the plaintiff in the court, though, this contention, is not at all material in disposing of a proceeding under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code for setting aside an ex parte decree on the ground of non-service of summons. In this context the allegation made by the defendant-petitioner may be looked into. It is the assertion of the defendant-petitioner that no summons and registered notice were ever served upon him and he did never appear in the suit by engaging any Advocate executing any Vokalatnama empowering the Advocate to do any act on his behalf in the suit. It is also asserted that he did not withdraw the money deposited in the court. In his evidence he gave testimony that in the suit no summons or notice had been served upon him and he did neither appear in the suit nor did engage any lawyer nor did pray for any time for filing written statement. He testified that the signature appearing in the Vokalatnama is not his signature. In the cross-examination he stated that he did not know Advocate Golam Mohammad and he denied the suggestion put forward by the plaintiff that he engaged Golam Mohammad as his lawyer. In view of this unequivocal testimony of the defendant-petitioner no attempt was made from the side of the plaintiff-opposite-party to have his signature appearing in the Vokalatnama and the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code and also the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act compared with the signature appearing on the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-1985 filed in the suit by a Handwriting expert. The trial Court on a comparison of the signature of the defendant-petitioner appearing in the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 and the signature appearing in his deposition dated 24-5-87 found that both the signatures are the product of the same handwriting. On a scrutiny of the signature of the defendant-petitioner appearing in the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 and the signature appearing in his deposition dated 24-5-87 found that both the signatures are the product of the same handwriting. On a scrutiny of the signature of the defendant-petitioner appearing in the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 as well as the application for withdrawing the money deposited in the court it appears that the signature bears the name "Md Abu Zafor Mia" (মোঃ আবু জাফ মিয়া) On examination of the Vokalatnama dated 23-8-86 filed in the Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code and the signature appearing on the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act and the deposition recorded in the Miscellaneous case it appears that the signature bears the name "Md Abu Zafor Sheikh (Mia) মোঃ আবু জাফর মিয়া শেখ (মিয়া) On a close scrutiny of the signatures of the defendant-petitioner appearing on the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 and the application for withdrawing the money dated 8-6-85 it cannot be said that the signature appearing in the said Vokalatnama dated 17-1-85 and the application dated 8-6-85 and the signature appearing on the Vokalatnama and the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code as well as the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act and the deposition dated 14-5-1987 are the products of the same hand writing. The trial Court was not well founded in recording the finding that the signature appearing in the Vokalatnama dated 17-1-1985 and the signature appearing in the deposition dated 24-5-1987 are the product of the same handwriting.</u>

22. Next comes the ground urged on behalf of the defendant-petitioner that the Sheristadar having passed the order dated 16-2-85 and 23-2-85 and fixed the suit for ex part hearing, the passing of the orders and the fixing the suit for ex parte hearing were totally without jurisdiction and the ex parte decree passed on 3-4-85 on the basis of those orders are also without jurisdiction.

23. It transpires from the record that the Sheristadar of the court on 17-1-85 allowed the alleged prayer of the defendant No. 1 for filing written statement. The Sheristadar, also, on 16-2-85, which was an off date, allowed the prayer of the defendant No. 2 for filing written statement. It further appears that though 23-2-85 was fixed for the return of the service of the summons of defendant No. 2 and also for filing of the written statement, the Sheristadar fixed 3-3-85 for ex parte hearing of the suit and on the basis of that order the suit was set down for ex parte hearing and, ultimately, on 3-4-85 the suit was decreed ex parte.

<u>24. The question now comes whether the "Sheristadar" is a "Court" or a "Judge" and whether as a "Court" or a "Judge" he can set down the suit for ex parte hearing. The term "Sheristadar" is neither defined in the Code of Civil Procedure nor defined in the Civil Rules and Orders. In the Civil Rules and Order Volume 1, the works, functions, duties and responsibility of a Sheristadar has been detailed and the work a Sheristadar does are ministerial works and he does not perform judicial functions and duties.</u>

25. In P Ramanatha Aiyar's "The Law Lexicon" 1997 Edition at page 1764, "Sheristadar" is defined as "Keeper of the records'''' or one who keeps a record of accounts or particular transactions. The recorder in a Court of Justice under the company's Government. A revenue accountant of a district who checks the accounts of the regular village curnum or accountant."

26. The term "Court" though appears in almost all sections, Orders and Rules in the Code of Civil Procedure, the same is not defined therein. The "Court" is not defined in the "Definition" embodied in section 2 of the Code. In section 5(2) of the Code "Revenue Court" is defined which means a court having jurisdiction under any law to entertain suits or other proceedings relating to the rent, Revenue or profits of land used for agricultural purposes, but does not include a Civil Court having original jurisdiction under the Code to try such Suit or proceedings as being Suits or proceedings of a civil nature.

27. Section 3 of the Evidence Act defines "Court" as including all Judges and Magistrates, all persons except arbitrators legally authorised to take evidence. This definition has been held to be not exhaustive but framed only for the purpose of Evidence Act and is not to be extended where such an extension is not warranted.

28. It would be relevant, however, to notice the definition of "Court" available elsewhere.

29. In Corpus juris Secundum, Volume 21, Page 1 "Court" is stated thus :

"Broadly speaking a court is a judicial Tribunal engaged in the administration of justice, although the precise meaning of the term in any particular connection will vary with the context in which it is employed.

While the meaning of the term "Court" will vary with the context in which it is used, generally speaking a Court is a body in the government to which the public administration of justice is delegated, being a tribunal officially assembled under authority of law, at the appropriate time and place, for the administration of justice, through which the state enforces its sovereign rights and powers, and consisting in its jurisdiction and functions and not its title or name, although in cases where the character of a Court as created is inconclusive the legislative label or name given to it may be a determining factor in ascertaining its character."

30. Coke on Littleton and Stroud defined the word "Court" as the place where justice is judicially administered.

31. The definition given by Stephen is as hereunder :

"In every Court, there must be at least, three constituent parts—the actor, reus and judex; the actor or plaintiff, who complained of an injury done; the reus, or defendant who is called upon to make satisfaction for it; and the judex, or judicial power, which is to examine the truth of the fact, and to determine the law arising upon that fact, and if any injury appears to have been done, to ascertain, and by fits officers to apply, the remedy."

32. In Halsbury's Laws of England, Fourth Edition Volume 10. Page 701 "Court" is stated thus :

"Originally the term "Court" meant, among other things, the Sovereign''''s palace. It has acquired the meaning of the place where justice is administered and, further, has come to mean the persons who exercise judicial functions under authority derived either directly or indirectly from the Sovereign. All tribunals, however, are not courts, in the sense in which the term is here employed. Courts are tribunals which exercise jurisdiction over persons by reasons of the sanction of the law, and not merely by reason of voluntary submission to their jurisdiction. Thus, arbitrators, committees or clubs and the like, although they may be tribunals exercising judicial functions,are not "Courts" in this sense of that term. On the other hand, a tribunal may be a court in the strict sense of the term even though the chief part of its duties is not judicial."

33. The term "Court" was considered by the Supreme Court of India in Brajnandan Sinha vs Joyoti Narain, SC Appeals 1956 Page 52. Bhagwati, J speaking for the court stated as under :

"It is clear, therefore, that in order to constitute a court in the strict sense of the term an essential condition is that the court should have, apart from having some of the trappings of a judicial tribunal, power to give a decision or a definitive judgment which has finality and authoritativeness which are the essential test of a judicial pronouncement."

34. The term "Court" also came up for consideration before a Division Bench of the High Court Division in IDBP (Bangladesh) vs. Master Industries and also Master Industries IDBP (Bangladesh). 26 DLR 157. DC Bhattacharya J. (as his Lordship then was) observed as follows :

"Although there is no exhaustive definition of a Court in any statute, a long line of judicial decisions of unquestioned authority have pointed out certain essential characteristics which invest a body with the character of a Court and have laid down certain tests which may distinguish it from a body which has some trappings of a Court but is not in fact, a Court.

A Court is according to Coke on Littleton, a place where justice is judicially administered and justice is understood in the forensic world, to be a decision of a binding nature given on a point of dispute in a list between two or more contending parties, by applying the law of the land to the facts of the case, untrammelled by the subjective attitude of the decision making body in exercise of the judicial power of the state and by following a judicial procedure."

<u>35. Thus, to be a Court, the persons or person who constitute it must be entrusted with judicial function in deciding litigated questions in accordance with law. A Court must be a competent authority deriving power from the state to make a judicial decision. A public officer to be a court must be empowered to make a judicial decision. The pronouncement of a definitive judgment is, therefore, considered the essential sine qua non of Court and unless and until a binding and authoritative judgment can be pronounced by a person or body of persons it cannot be predicted that he or they constitute a Court.</u>

<u>36. The word "Judge" is defined in section 2(8) of the Code of Civil Procedure which is quoted thus :</u>

<u>"2(8) Judge means the presiding officer of a civil Court."</u>

<u>A Judge is a Public officer lawfully appointed to determine questions in dispute between the litigants upon merit according to law. A Judge is an officer who presides at a Court. "Judge" is defined in Anderson's Law Dictionary as a "public officer" whose function is to declare the law, to conduct the trial of cases between litigants according to legal force.</u>

<u>37. The Sheristadar is not a Public officer and his function is not to declare law and to conduct the trial of case between litigants and is not invested with any authority to determine any cause or question in a court of judicature created by any Act or Statute. The Sheristadar, as such, did not possess any judicial power to grant any time to the defendants and also to set down the Suit for ex parte hearing and all his orders and acts are absolutely without jurisdiction and the ex parte decree passed on the basis of the orders passed by the Sheristadar are also without jurisdiction. The ground so urged being very much substantial is accepted.</u>

<u>38. Turning now to the next ground which relates to the question of limitation, the learned trial Judge taking the view that since the defendant-petitioner appeared in the suit on 17-1-85 and withdrew the money on 16-8-1985, he was well aware of the proceeding of the suit since 17-1-85 and the Miscellaneous case for restoration of the suit having been filed after a long time, the same stood barred by limitation. The appellate Court did not come to any decision on the question of limitation. It has already been found that no summon was served upon the defendant. Elements of fraud and collusion has been also noticed in the matter of procuring ex parte decree by the plaintiff. The defendant in his application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code made averment that without serving any summons upon him, the plaintiff obtained a fraudulent ex parte decree and he sustained irreparable injury by the said decree and he on 27-7-86 came to know that the plaintiff was getting kabala deed executed and registered with respect to the suit land on the basis of a fraudulent ex parte decree passed in title Suit No. 385 of 1984. The defendant in his evidence also stated that no notice was served upon him and he did never appear in the suit by presenting a Vokalatnama and also engaging a lawyer. The plaintiff, though, in the written objection filed against the Miscellaneous case asserted that summons of the suit had been duly served upon him, the said assertion could not be established by any legal evidence. The lower appellate Court recorded the positive finding that it was not proved that summons was served. In an application for setting aside an ex parte decree on the ground of non-service of summons, Article 164 of the Limitation Act is attracted. Article 164 enjoins that by a defendant for an order to set aside a decree ex parte period of limitation is 30 days when the applicant has knowledge of the decree where the summons was not duly served. It appears from materials on record that the defendant for the first time on 27-7-86 got the knowledge of the ex parte decree and on 23-8-86 filed the Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code which was very much within 30 days of the date of knowledge of the ex parte decree, ie on 27-7-1986. My considered view is that the Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code has been filed within the period of 30 days of the date of knowledge and the same is not barred by limitation.</u>

<u>39. Let me now come to a legal aspect of the case. In the matter of getting an ex parte decree the plaintiff is bound to prove his case to the satisfaction of the Court and his burden is not lightened because the defendant is absent. This is so even when the defendant has lost the right to produce evidence. It is the duty of the court to consider the interest of the absentee defendant. The court in awarding an ex parte decree is to observe minimum legal requirements and the court is to apply its judicial mind as to whether the plaintiff by papers and witnesses proved his case. It is to be borne in mind that the absence of the defendant is no ground for passing an ex parte decree in favour of a plaintiff. In the case in my hand the plaintiff prayed for specific performance of contract on the basis of an unregistered agreement to sale deed (Bainanama) and the said deed is prescribed by one Mohani Mohan and attested by two witnesses, namely, Md Tamijuddin and Md Abdul Khaleque Khan. It appears that plaintiff only examined himself in support of his case and neither the scribe nor any of the attesting witnesses has been examined in support of the .execution of the agreement to sale deed (Bainanama). It was the duty of the plaintiff to prove the agreement to sale deed by examining the scribe and at least one of the said attesting witnesses of the said deed. It, thus, appears that minimum legal requirements were not at all followed in awarding an ex parte decree. The order also does not show that the court applied its judicial mind in awarding an ex parte decree, more so, when the decree is of a Specific Performance of Contract on the basis of an unregistered agreement to sale deed. The order awarding ex parte decree did not satisfy the minimum requirement of Order 20 rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The case of Bangladesh vs. Abdul Wadud and others, 25 DLR (SC) 90, Bangladesh vs. Israil Ali and others. 1981 BLD (AD) 371 and Nurjahan Begum vs. Giri Gopal Sarker being dead his heirs Dulal Chandra Sarker and another, 1979 BSCR 400 may be profitably referred to in this context.</u>

40. The proposition of law emerging out of the above authorities is that in ex parte disposal of the Suit the Court is required to observe minimum legal requirement and the order should show application of the Court's judicial mind as to whether the plaintiff's witnesses and other papers produced proved the plaintiff's case.

41. The duty of a Court is to administer justice in accordance with law. Courts are required not to exercise punitive jurisdiction by depriving defendant ex parte. Our law of Procedure is also designed to facilitate justice and further its end. The laws of procedure are grounded on the principle that a litigant public and a citizen should not be condemned unheard, that decision should not be reached behind his back, that proceeding that affects his properties should not be deprived from participating in them. The Court possesses a discretion to undo injustice caused to the men, the public and the citizens of the State and the Court must exercise that discretion. The hands of the Court are not tied by the ex parte orders. Mandate of law is that interference must be called for in a given case and, if interference is not called for then it is not exercising the discretion which the law says it should. In this context it is significant to point out that in furtherance of the ends of justice court always leans in favour of setting aside an ex parte decree/order rather than maintaining the same because court exists for the advancement of justice and ordinarily would not be understood to deprive a litigant of his right.

42. In view of the discussions made hereinbefore and also the reasons stated I am of the considered view that the judgments of the courts below cannot be allowed to be maintained. The Rule got merit and the same, thus, succeeds.

43. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to cost, the judgments of the courts below are set aside and the Miscellaneous Case No. 57 of 1986 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure arising out of Title Suit No. 385 of 1984 is allowed and the said Title Suit No. 385 of 1984 is restored to its file and number.

Let the records of the courts below be sent down at once.

End.

caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 22 of 1998 (FMAT No. 98 of 1998)
lawyer:
AKM Faiz, with AM Fakhrul Alam and Pervin Hannan, Advocates —For the Appellant. 
Dr Rafiqur Rahman, with Sirajur Rahman, Md Ismail, Jashim Uddin Ahmed, Abdul Hamid, and Zakir Hussain Mazumder, Advocates — For the Respondent Nos. 4 and 7. 
Habibullah, Advocate — For the Respondent Nos. 1 and 3.
parties:
Basati Property Development Limited ------ Appellant
Vs.
Shafkat Hossain and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: By this appeal the plaintiff-appellant questions the correctness of the judgment and order dated February 26, 1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge refusing the prayer for temporary injunction in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract.

2. The only question that survives for determination in this appeal is whether the judgment under challenge refusing plaintiffs prayer for temporary injunction is well-founded on law or not and whether the same warrants any interference by this Court in exercising its appellate jurisdiction.

3. For the purpose of determining the said question posed, facts leading to this appeal may be summarised which are as follows:

Messers Basati Property Development Limited represented by its Managing Director on 18-1-1998 laid a suit being Title Suit No. 15 of 1998 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge in Dhaka for a decree of specific performance of contract with respect to 6 (six) acres of land as described in schedule to the plaint with the averments that a Tripartite agreement had been entered into between the First and Second defendants (First Party Owners of the land), the plaintiff (Second Party Developer) and the Fourth to Seventh defendants (the Third Party Financier who undertook to finance the project). The Tripartite agreement is dated June 19, 1992. The Property of the First and Second defendants (First Party) stood acquired by the then Government in Land Acquisition Case No. 50 of 1964-65. The said acquisition proceeding, ultimately, stood dropped with the help and assistance of Fourth-Seventh defendants. It is further averred in the plaint that the First and Second defendants are not acting in accordance with the conditions contained in the said Tripartite agreement and also making no contacts with the plaintiff company. The First and Second defendants on 5-5-97 most illegally issued a notice canceling the Tripartite agreement and the said notice got no legal basis. The plaintiff on several occasions, in accordance with the conditions contained in the Tripartite agreement requested the First and Second defendants to execute and register deed of conveyance in its favour and they having not executed and registered the deed of conveyance and having also rescinded the contract on 5-5-97 by issuing a notice compelled the plaintiff to institute the suit in the court for a decree of specific performance of contract. In the suit the defendant No. 3 had been impleaded as he was the constituted Attorney by way of Power of Attorney executed in his favour by the First and Second defendants.

4. Almost upon the said averment made in the plaint, the plaintiff filed an application under the provisions of Order 39 rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction restraining the First-Third defendants from transferring the suit property elsewhere.

5. The court on 19-1-98 issued show cause notice upon the First-Third defendants asking them why they would not be restrained by an order of temporary injunction within 7 days of the receipt of the notice. It is pointed out here that the plaint was registered on 18-1-98 and on that date, 18-2-98 was fixed for ascertaining the contest by the defendants and also for the return of the service of summons or notices. On 4-2-98 the plaintiff filed an application for an order of ad-interim injunction or in the alternative for maintenance of status-quo with respect to the suit property pending  the hearing of the temporary injunction matter. No copy of the said application having been served upon the defendants, the application was fixed for hearing on the date after service of the copy upon the defendants. On 8-2-98 the court considered the application of the plaintiff dated 4-2-98 and passed an order upon the defendants asking them to maintain status-quo with respect to any transfer of the suit property till the date fixed i.e., 18-2-98.

6. On 18-2-98 the Third, Fourth and Sixth-Seventh defendants presented written objections against the plaintiffs application for temporary injunction. They also prayed for vacating the order for maintenance of status-quo passed upon them on 8-2-98. The plaintiff by way of another application prayed for extension of the order of status-quo dated 8-2-98.

7. In the written objection filed by the Third defendant it is stated amongst others that the plaintiff got neither cause nor any ground to institute the suit. It is pleaded that the Tripartite agreement having become non-existent, the plaintiff got no locus standi to ask for a decree of specific performance of contract on a non-existent agreement. In the written objection filed by the Sixth and Seventh defendants it is stated that for the misappropriation of money by the Managing Director the Directors of the plaintiff company filed Company Matter No. 101 of 1997 under section 233 of the Company Act of 1994 before the High Court Division. It is further averred that in view of the litigation started amongst the Directors of the company, the Tripartite agreement stood cancelled and the business of the company remains stopped for long period. The case of the Fourth defendant set up in the written objection is almost the same as set up and pleaded by Sixth and Seventh defendants.

8. The learned Subordinate Judge on 18-2-98 heard the temporary injunction matter and fixed 26-2-98 for pronouncement of the judgment.

9. The learned Subordinate Judge by judgment dated 26-2-98 rejected plaintiff''s application for temporary injunction and at the same time vacated the order for maintenance of status-quo dated 8-2-98. In rejecting the application for temporary injunction, the learned Subordinate Judge recorded the finding that the plaintiff company was only concerned with respect to Schedule-Kha property contained in Tripartite agreement and the said Schedule-Kha property over which temporary injunction had been sought suffered from vagueness and indefiniteness and the Schedule property in the plaint and the Tripartite agreement was not at all definite and it could not be at all ascertained on which portion of the property, the plaintiff sought for temporary injunction. The learned Subordinate Judge, thus, was of the view that on the vague and indefinite schedule property there was no ground to consider plaintiff''s prayer for temporary injunction. The learned Subordinate Judge in rejecting the plaintiffs prayer for temporary injunction also considered the cases pending before the High Court Division amongst the parties of the company. The learned Subordinate Judge having taken an overall view of the facts, circumstances of the case rejected plaintiff''s prayer for temporary injunction.

10. Feeling aggrieved by the said order of rejection of the prayer for temporary injunction, Managing Director of the Company as appellant presented this appeal before this Court.

11. Mr AKM Faiz, learned Advocate along with Mr AM Fakhrul Alam and Ms Pervin Hannan, learned Advocates appeared in support of the appeal. The respondents are represented by the learned Advocate Dr Rafiqur Rahman along with the learned Advocates Mr Sirajur Rahman, Mr Md Ismail, Mr Jashim Uddin Ahmed, Mr Zakir Hussain Mazumder and Mr Abdul Hamid.

12. Mr AKM Faiz, learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal, directed his efforts in assailing the judgment under challenge, raising firstly the contention that 18-2-98 was not a date fixed for hearing of the temporary injunction matter and the plaintiff was not afforded any opportunity to conduct the hearing on the matter and the learned Subordinate Judge, thus, committed a gross illegality in hearing the temporary injunction matter on a date not fixed for that purpose and also without affording any opportunity to it.

13. In repelling the said contention Dr Rafiqur Rahman pressed into service submission that on the date of registration of the plaint in the Register, 18-2-98 was very much fixed as a date of the suit and the plaintiff was very much present in the court and duly participated in the hearing of the temporary injunction matter and thus it does not lie in the mouth of the plaintiff that he was not afforded any opportunity in placing its case in the injunction hearing proceeding.

14. The second branch of contention advanced from the side of the plaintiff-appellant is that plaintiff got prima facie case in getting an order of injunction in its favour and the plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss and injury if injunction is not granted in its favour. It is also contended that, the defendants will dispose of the whole suit property to different persons.

15. Controverting the second branch of contention it is submitted from the side of the defendant-respondents that the plaintiff got no legal right to have any decree of specific performance of contract over the suit property inasmuch as in accordance with the terms and conditions contained in the, Tripartite agreement only the intending purchasers of the land from the plaintiff company are entitled to enforce the contract to have the land conveyed to them and the suit at the instance of the second party plaintiff Basati Property is not at all maintainable and as such, the plaintiff-appellant is not at all entitled to have any injunction in its favour.

16. Strenuous argument has been also pressed into service on behalf of the defendant-respondents raising the contention that the Tripartite agreement dated June 19, 1992 stood discharged by the First party defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on May 5, 1997 and the agreement became non-existent and non-existent contract cannot be enforced by a court of law and hence no injunction can be granted on the basis of a non-existent agreement. It is also urged that the suit property is unspecified, indefinite and vague and no injunction can be granted on the unspecified, indefinite and vague property.

17. In the wake of the rival contentions advanced from both the sides, let us now address ourselves to the soundness of those contentions.

18. It appears that the plaint was registered on 18-1-98 and 18-2-98 was fixed for ascertaining the contest by the defendants and for service return of the summons and the registered notices. On 19-1-98 a prayer for temporary injunction was presented by the plaintiff under the provision of Order 39 rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure restraining the First-Third defendants from transferring the suit property elsewhere and till hearing of the temporary injunction matter for an order of ad-interim injunction against the said defendants. The court issued show cause notices upon the said defendants asking them to show cause within 7 days of the receipt of the notices as to why an order of injunction would not be granted against them as prayed by the plaintiff. It transpires that on 19-1-98 the Third defendant entered appearance by a vokalatnama and prayed for time for filing written objection against plaintiff''s prayer for temporary injunction. On 25-1-98 the First and Second defendants also entered appearance in the suit by a vokalatnama and prayed for time for presenting written objection against plaintiff's said prayer for temporary injunction. Court allowed the prayers of the said defendants and directed them to present written objection on the date fixed i.e. on 18-2-98. On 4-2-98 the plaintiff by way of an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure prayed for an order of ad-interim injunction or in the alternative for maintenance of status-quo with respect to the suit property till the hearing of the temporary injunction matter. No copy of the said application had been served upon the defendants and the court fixed for hearing of the said application on the date fixed i.e., 18-2-98. On 8-2-98 the plaintiff by way of an application prayed for hearing of the application dated 4-2-98. Court on that date i.e., on 8-2-98 passed an order against First-Third defendants for maintenance of status quo with respect to transfer of the suit property till the date fixed i.e. 18-2-98. On 18-2-98 the First-Third, Fourth and Sixth-Seventh defendant presented written objections against the plaintiff''s application for temporary injunction. The defendants also presented another application for vacating the order of status-quo passed against them. The plaintiff also filed an application for extending the period of the order of maintenance of status-quo. Thereafter, the temporary injunction matter was taken up for hearing and the same was heard in presence of the plaintiff and the defendants. The Court fixed 26-2-98 for order on the temporary injunction matter. On 26-2-98 the court by its judgment and order rejected the plaintiff''s prayer for temporary injunction and at the same time vacated the order for maintenance of status quo with respect to the transfer of the suit property.

<u>19. From the above it manifests that plaintiff on 18-2-98 filed an application for extending the order of maintenance of status-quo. The defendants also filed another application for vacating the order of maintenance of status-quo. The temporary injunction matter was heard in presence of both the parties. It is, thus, evident that the plaintiff was very much present in the court and participated in the hearing of the temporary injunction matter. It does not appear that the plaintiff raised any objection whatever as to the hearing of the temporary injunction matter on 18-2-98 on the ground that the temporary injunction matter was not set down for hearing on that date. It transpires, further, that on the day of pronouncement of the judgment and order on temporary injunction matter, i.e., on 26-2-98 the plaintiff also does not appear to have raised any objection/plea/voice that no order could be passed on temporary injunction matter without specifically fixing a date for hearing of the temporary injunction matter. The plaintiff is now estopped to put forward the plea when it was not favoured with an order of temporary injunction. The plea so taken by the plaintiff is too much a technical one not at all a substantial one. The first branch of contention advanced on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant does not appear to have any merit and the same, thus, fails.</u>

<u>20. Let us now direct our attention to the question as to the existence of any prima facie case in favour of the plaintiff in getting an order of injunction in its favour. In the case of temporary injunction the applicant must show a fair prima facie case in support of the right claimed. A good prima facie case means a case where the plaintiff has a fair question to raise at the trial. In other words, injunction in favour of the plaintiff may be granted where it is found that the plaintiff has a good prima facie case meaning thereby that a serious question of law is to be tried or investigated in the suit and that in the event of success, if the injunction is not issued, the plaintiff shall suffer irreparable loss and material injury. This is a well-established principle of law which provides correct guideline for the court making an order of injunction. But it is to be borne in mind that the court must be satisfied that there is really a serious question of law to be tried or investigated in the suit.</u>

<u>21. Keeping in view the above principle of law it is to be seen whether the plaintiff has any good prima facie case in getting an order of injunction in its favour.</u>

<u>22. In the preamble of the Tripartite agreement dated June, 19, 1992 it is stated:</u>

<u>যেহেতু উপরোক্ত মেসার্স বসতি প্রপার্টি ডেভেলপমেন্ট লিঃ নিম্ন ‘খ’ তফসিলি বর্নিত সম্পত্তি ডেভেলপমেন্ট করিয়া তাহা ক্রয়েচ্ছু ব্যক্তিগণের নিকট বিক্রয় করিবার জন্য সম্পূর্ণভাবে মধ্যস্থতা করিয়া তদবাবদ উক্ত কোম্পানী লাভবান হইতে চান।</u>

<u>The terms and conditions Nos. 5 and 6 of the said agreement are quoted hereunder:</u>

<u>৫। ক্রয়েচ্ছু ব্যক্তিগণের সহিত প্রথম পক্ষকে চুক্তিবদ্ধ করিবার উদ্দেশ্যে ২য় পক্ষ সর্বোতোভাবে চেষ্টা করিবেন এবং চুক্তির আসন্ন হইলে ক্রয়েচ্ছু ব্যক্তিগণের নাম ধাম আদি, প্রস্তাবিত বিক্রিত ভূমির বর্ণনাসহ প্রথম ৩(তিন) দিনের মধ্যে প্রথম পক্ষ ক্রয়েচ্ছু ব্যক্তিগণের অনুকুলে পছন্দকৃত প্লট বাবদ প্রয়োজনবোধে বায়নানামা দলিল সম্পাদন করিবেন। প্রথম পক্ষে আরব বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংক মতিঝিল শাখার সেভিংস হিসাব নং-০৮৫৭৯০-৩১০ তে টাকা জমা হওয়ার পর ২(দুই) দিনের মধ্যে অত্র চুক্তিনামার সকল শর্ত পূরণ সাপেক্ষে কবলা দলিল সম্পাদন করিয়া দিতে বাধ্য থাকিবেন।</u>

<u>৬। ক্রয়েচ্ছু ব্যক্তিগণ বায়না দলিল লিখাইয়া না লইয়া সংগে সংগে তাহাদের পছন্দকৃত প্লটের বাবদ যথারীতি পারামিশনাদী অন্তে কবলা দলিল প্রথম পক্ষের নিকট হইতে সম্পাদন ও রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া লইতে পারিবেন। শুধুমাত্র নিম্নলিখিত (ক), (খ), (গ) ও(ঘ) শর্তাবলী পূরণ সাপেক্ষে ১ম পক্ষ ক্রয়েচ্ছু ব্যক্তিগণের অনুকুলে কবলা দলিল সম্পাদন ও রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া দিতে বাধ্য থাকিবেন।</u>

<u>From a bare reading of the preamble and the condition set forth in the Tripartite agreement it is manifested that the First party of the agreement, i.e. the First and Second defendants would execute an agreement to sell deed in favour of the intending purchasers of their chosen land and thereafter would execute and register deed of conveyance in favour of the said intending purchasers. The sheet anchor of the plaintiffs claim for a decree of specific performance, of contract is the Tripartite agreement and there is absolutely no condition therein evidencing that the First party i.e. the First and the Second defendants would execute an agreement to sell deed and, thereafter, execute and register deed of conveyance in favour of the Second party, the plaintiff-company. Moreover, no case had been made out in the plaint that there is condition that the First and Second defendants would execute an agreement to sell deed in favour of the plaintiff company for the sale of the suit property and the said contract is liable to be enforced through the medium of court. The plaintiff does not appear to have a right which can be claimed by it for a decree of specific performance of contract. It is, thus, manifestly clear that the plaintiff does not have a fair question to raise at the trial and no serious question of law requires to be investigated or tried in the suit and, as such, no prima facie case appears to have existed in favour of the plaintiff for issuance of an order of injunction.</u>

<u>23. Coming now to another branch of contention advanced from the side of the defendants that the Tripartite agreement stood discharged by the First party, the First and Second defendants and the same being non-existent cannot be enforced by the court of law. It appears that the Tripartite agreement is dated June 19, 1992 and the First and Second defendants are the First party and the plaintiff Basati Property Development Limited is the Second party. The Discharge of contract executed by the First party defendants is dated May 5, 1997 which is in the paper book Part-II. From the said Discharge of contract it appears that the Tripartite agreement executed between the First and Second defendants being the First party and the plaintiff being the Second party stood discharged/cancelled/rescinded by the said defendants for the failure on the part of the Second party plaintiff to comply with the fundamental terms and conditions of the contract causing intentional breach of contract. In the said Discharge of contract it is also stated that the Third party, Fourth-Seventh defendants, also asked the First party defendants to rescind the Tripartite agreement. In the plaint also in paragraph Nos. 11 and 15 it is categorically stated that the First party, the First and Second defendants, issued notices upon the plaintiff cancelling the Tripartite agreement. The suit has been instituted on 18-1-98 and the Tripartite agreement stood discharged on 5-5-1997, about 8 months prior to the institution of the suit. The plaintiff does not appear to have taken any legal steps with respect to the said discharge of the Tripartite agreement. The Tripartite agreement having been non-existent it can easily be suggested that the non-existent contract cannot be enforced in the court of law. From this point of view also, the plaintiff does not appear to have a prima facie case not to speak of good and strong prima facie case.</u>

<u>24. Let us now turn to another aspect of the matter which relates to non-specification, indefiniteness and vagueness of the property over which injunction is sought. Vehement argument has been pressed into service from the side of the defendant-respondent that the suit property suffers from non-specification indefiniteness and vagueness. In the Tripartite agreement there are two schedules, Schedule-Ka and Schedule-Kha. In schedule-Ka there are 11 plots, namely, 697, 698, 699, 700, 701, 702, 703, 704, 737, 739 and 833 covering an area of 10.15 acres of land. In Schedule-Kha property there are 7 plots, namely, 737, 697, 698, 699, 702, 703 and 704 covering an area of 8.42 acres of land out of the foretasted 7 plots covering an area of 8.42 acres, the schedule property in the suit has been made 6.00 acres of land from the above 7 plots and one plot being 700 of the schedule-Ka of the Tripartite agreement. Injunction is also sought for the said 8 plots covering the said area i.e. 6.00 acres of land. Out of the said 7 plots of the Kha-schedule property covering an area of 8.42 acres, injunction is sought with respect to 5.81 acres of land and also on plot No. 700 though not included in the Kha-schedule property but included in the Ka-schedule property. The plaintiff sought injunction on a fraction of the said 7 plots of schedule-Kha property and one plot of schedule-Ka property without any specification and identification whatsoever and, thus, it is evident that injunction has been sought on indefinite, unspecified and the vague land. It is well recognized that an injunction cannot be granted if the subject of the dispute is not specified and definite. In cases of injunction the court must always be cautious in specifying the property in dispute. Since the property in dispute suffers from non-specification, indefiniteness and vagueness, no injunction can be issued therein. On this score also, the plaintiff is disentitled to have any order of injunction in its favour.</u>

<u>25. An injunction is a writ framed according to the circumstances of the case commanding an act which the court records as essential to justice or, restraining an act which it esteems contrary to equity and good conscience. Moreover an injunction is a form of equitable relief and it is to be issued in aid of equity and justice. An injunction, being the strong arm of equity should never be granted except in a clear case of good/strong prima facie case. The plaintiff can invoke the aid of a court of equity to assist him in carrying on an unlawful business when in the absence of any contract/agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant, the former cannot have any legal right to enforce that contract against the latter and specifically when the alleged contract stood discharged long before the institution of the suit.</u>

26. The learned Subordinate Judge took into consideration all aspects of the case and correctly exercised the discretion in rejecting the plaintiff''s application for temporary injunction. It appears that in disposing of the temporary injunction, matter the learned Subordinate Judge has directed a correct approach of the matter and the decisions arrived at by him appears to be well-founded on law. No exception can be taken to the said decisions. It is to be remembered that the granting of any injunction is purely within the discretion of the court. In appeal, the appellate Court will not interfere with the exercise of discretion of the court of first instance except when the discretion has been shown to have been exercised arbitrarily, or capriciously or perversely or where the court had ignored the settled principles of law regulating grant or refusal of interlocutory injunctions. An appeal against exercise of discretion is said to be an appeal on principle. Appellate Court will not reassess the materials and seek to reach a conclusion different from the one reached by the court below if the one reached by that court was reasonably possible on the material. On perusal of the judgment under challenge, it cannot be suggested at all that the learned Subordinate Judge exercised the discretion arbitrarily or perversely ignoring the settled principles of law regulating mussel of the injunction.

27. From all what has been discussed above we are of this considered view that the plaintiff got no prima facie case and the balance of convenience and inconvenience is also against the plaintiff and in favour of the defendants. The appeal being without any substance, the same fails.

28. Before parting with the matter we are inclined to observe that any finding arrived at by us in disposing of the appeal will not affect the merit of the suit and the learned Subordinate Judge will be absolutely free to dispose of the suit in accordance with law.

29. In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The judgment and order dated February 26, 1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is maintained.

The order passed by this Court for the maintenance of status-quo stands vacated.

End.
