full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 19-8-1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Comilla, in Title Appeal No. 5 of 1995 allowing the appeal, dismissing the suit on reversing those dated 30-11-1992 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Chowddagram Comilla in Title Suit No. 10 of 1990 decreeing the suit.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 10 of 1990 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Chowddagram, Comilla for declaration of title in the Schedule 1 land to the plaint measuring an area of 63 decimals appertaining to plot No. 526, Khatian No. 128 of maize Chakla Roshonabad and also for khas possession in the 2nd schedule premises of the plaint after eviction of the defendant there from contending, inter alia, that the suit property belonged to plaintiffs predecessor Azim Miah who died leaving& behind 4(four) sons named Musa, Aslam Amir and Ana Mia. By an amicable partition amongst those 4(four) brothers the suit land was fallen in the saham of Amir Ali. Amir Ali died leaving behind the plaintiff and pro-forma defendant Nos. 10-13 as heirs. Thereafter, by another amicable partition the suit land was allotted to the saham of the plaintiff. While he was in possession in the Schedule-1 land to the plaint he was dispossessed from a part of schedule-1 land that is from the schedule-2 land to the plaint by the middle of 1989 AD. The defendants erected two huts upon the schedule-2 land to the plaint covering an area of 0.0189 acre. It is the further case of the plaintiff that the recent khatian was wrongly recorded in the name of defendants for an area of 0.57 acre and 6 acre was recorded in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiff in khatian No. 86. Taking advantage of that wrong recording of Khatian the defendants had dispossessed him. The plaintiff came to know about the wrong record on 14-12-1989 and, as such, the suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-6 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending inter alia, that the suit was barred by limitation and was bad for defect of parties. It was their case that Azim Mian was a tenant in respect of the suit land and as well as other lands under Selina Banu. Selina Banu died leaving behind only sister Asmat-un-nessa to be her sole heir. Asmat-un-nessa died leaving behind one son Yakub Ali. Yukub Ali died leaving two sons Serajul Islam Chowdhury and Nurul Islam Chowdhury. By amicable partition Serajul Islam and Nurul Islam got the suit land. They used to realize rent from Azim Mian. Azim Miah failed to pay rent and being unable to pay rent surrendered possession of the schedule-1 land to the plaint in favour of Serajul Islam Chowdhury and Nurul Islam Chowdhury. They started possessing the suit land physically. The sons and daughters of Azim Mian defaulted in paying rent for the other lands. Nurul Islam as plaintiff instituted Rent Suit No. 42 of 1945 in the 4th Court of Munsif at Comilla. In the plaint it was written that the possession of the suit land was surrendered in his favour. The plaintiffs father contended the suit but did not claim any title in the suit land and did not deny the plaint's case. While Nurul Islam and Serajul Islam were in possession in the suit land along with other paternal property there took place a registered family partition deed between them dated 27-8-1950 (Exhibit-Kha) and by that partition deed the suit land was allotted to the Saham of Serajul Islam. Serajul Islam Chowdhury while in possession died leaving behind one widow Lutfe Jahan Chowdhury, 4(four) sons Hafizul Islam, Muzibul Islam, Aminul Islam and Dr Mahatabul Islam and 4(four) daughters named Meher Afroz. Thereafter, there took place another amicable family partition between them by a registered deed on 2-9-1968 (Exhibit-Kha(1) and by that deed the suit property was fallen into the saham of defendant Nos. 2-3 and Hafizul Islam, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 4-6. During their possession the SA record No. 128 was prepared in their names but an area of 6 decimal was wrongly recorded in the name of the plaintiff. In fact, the plaintiff had no title and possession in the suit land. The defendants Nos. 2-6 being in possession had constructed shops upon the schedule-2 land to the plaint long ago and had been in possession through barite. The plaintiff had neither title nor possession in the suit land. The plaintiff's elder brother by swearing affidavit had admitted that his father had no title and possession in the suit land.

4. The heirs of Azim Mian namely, the defendant Nos. 7 and 9 submitted written statement on 10-1-1985 and admitted that the defendant's predecessor acquired rayati title in the suit land. Plaintiffs father had neither title not possession in the suit land.

5. The trial Court framed 6 issues in the suit. The plaintiff examined 4 PWs and the defendant examined. 10 DWs. The plaintiffs documents were marked as Exhibit-1, 2 and 2 (Ka). On the other hand, the defendants' documents were marked as Exhibit-Ka, Kha and Ga series.

6. The learned Assistant Judge by the judgment and decree dated 30-11-1992 decreed the suit against which the defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 5 of 1995. That appeal was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Comilla who by the impugned judgment and decree dated 19-8-1995 allowed the appeal, dismissed the suit on reversing those dated 30-11-1992 of the trial Court.

7. Mr TH Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, took me to the impugned judgment and decree and as well as to the judgment of the trial Court and formulated the following points of arguments:

(i) It is not a judgment of reversal

(ii) CS Khatian নিয়ে কোন বিরোধ নেই।

(iii) বিবাদীদের নামে আলাদা খতিয়ান Exhibit ১(খ)হয়েছে যেখানে নালিশী দাগ নেই and that was recorded in the name of Lutfe Jahan Chowdhury.

(iv) The defendant could not prove their title and possession in the suit land. The trial Court lawfully decreed the suit but the court of appeal upon misconception of law and fact had allowed the appeal. The impugned judgment and decree is not sustainable in law.

8. On the other hand, Mr Rafiqul Islam with Mr Md SR Khoshnobish, on appearing for the opposite parties, made the following submissions:

(i) The court of appeal allowed the appeal on considering the evidence on record.

(ii) The impugned judgment and decree is a proper judgment of reversal.

(iii) The defendant by producing Exhibit Kha, Kha(1) and other evidence proved their title and possession in the suit land and the impugned judgment and decree are not liable to be set-aside.

9. From the submission made by the learned Advocates and from the pleadings the following questions came before this Court for decision to determine the real question in controversy :

(i) Whether the defendant's case of surrender of the suit land in favour of the ex-landlord in respect of the schedule-1 land was a lawful surrender in the eye of law?

(ii) Whether plaintiffs father was in possession in the suit land after the alleged surrender, if any, of the suit land?

(iii) Whether the plaintiff by adducing evidence could prove his amicable partition and thereafter his exclusive possession and the case of dispossession as alleged in the plaint?

(iv) Whether the plaintiffs suit was barred by limitation?

10. Admittedly, the plaintiffs' predecessor named Azim Mian was a tenant in the respect of the suit land. It is the plaintiffs case that by two amicable partition the suit land was fallen in his exclusive possession and he was dispossessed from the 2nd Schedule property by the middle of 1989 BS whereas the defendants' case was that the plaintiffs' predecessor surrendered the suit land in favour of the landlord and the defendants' predecessor named Serajul Islam Chowdhury was the successive heir of ex-landlord. Said Serajul Islam got the suit property in his exclusive saham by a registered partition deed dated 27-8-1950 (Exhibit 'Kha'). Said Serajul Islam Chowdhury died leaving 4 sons and other heirs. There took place another registered family partition deed dated 2-9-1968 (Exhibit 'Kha (1)' and by that deed the suit land has fallen in the saham of defendant Nos. 2-3 and as well as in Saham of the predecessor of defendant Nos. 4-6. It is their case that by that partition deed the defendants started possessing the suit land exclusively and the SA record No. 128 was prepared in their names and they paid rent by Exhibit-'Ga' series. There took place no case of dispossession as alleged in the plaint.

11. In the instant case the fact of surrender of physical possession of the suit land in favour of ex-landlord has been admitted by defendant Nos. 7 and 10 who being the heirs of Azim Mian admitted in their examination-in-chief the following:

"DW 7 in- chief added-

নালিশী জমি চিনি-বাদী বা বাদীর বাবা কাহাকে ও নালিশী জমি কখনও চাষাবাদ করিতে দেখে নাই। বাদী আমার চাচাত ভাই।

In cross-examination, the DW 7 admitted the following-আমার মৌরশী বাড়ীর পার্শ্বে নালিশী জমি। আমি ছোট কালে কখনও নালিশী জমি আমাদের পরিবারের কাউকে দখলদার দেখি নাই।”

12. The defendant No. 10 was examined as PW 8 who admitted in his examination-in-chief নালিশী জমি চিনি। বাদী আমার ছোট, বিবাদীগণ প্রতিবেশী গ্রামীণ। আমার বাবা, আমার ছোট ভাই কখনও নালিশী জমি চাষ করে নাই।

This evidence was not denied by the plaintiff at the time of cross-examination. The defendant No. 1 was examined as DW 1 who substantiated the defence case and in his cross-examination he added"- কোর্দা বন্দোবস্তের ২/৩৪ বৎসর পর আজিম মিয়াজী নালিশী জমি সমর্পন করে। সমর্পণটি ছিল মৌখিক সন মাস বলিতে পারিব না। সমর্পন করিয়াছেন তৎকালীন মালিক বরাবর।

13. The PW 5 and PW 6 being the bharatia under the defendants added that they had been in possession in the schedule -2 shops for more than 7-8 years.

14. On the other hand, the plaintiff in his examination-in-chief simply added নালিশী ৫২৬ দাগের ভূমিতে আমার দাদা আজিম মিয়াদ কোর্দা স্বত্বে মালিক দখলদার দাদা মারা গেলে ৪ ছেলে মালিক দখলদার হয়। আছলাম, মুছা, আমির, আলশ মিঞা। ৮-৯ নং বিবাদী হলো আছলামের ওয়ারিশ এবং আমি ও ১০-১৩ নং বিবাদীগন আমির আলীর ওয়ারিশ- বাবা চাচাদের মধ্যে আপোষ বন্টন মতে বাবা মালিক দখলদার ছিলেন। বাবার মৃত্যুর পূর্ব পর্যন্ত দখর করিত। আমরা ভাইগণ যৌথভাবে ৪/৫ বৎসর চাষাবাদেও পর আপোষ বন্টনে আমি একক মালিক দখলদার।

In cross-examination he admitted-

আমার বাবা নালিশী জমি পাইয়াছে তৎপরিবর্তে চাচারা কোন কোন দাগে পাইয়াছে দাগ নং বলিতে পারিব না। আমি ভাইদের সংগে আপোষ বন্টনে নালিশী জমি পাইয়াছি। তাদেরকে কোন দাগের জমি দিয়াছি স্মরণ নাই।

15. The PW 2 simply supported the plaintiff's possession in the suit land but did not adduce any evidence in support of dispossession. The PW 3 being the full brother of the plaintiff simply added that the plaintiff was in possession in the suit land but failed to disclose the date of dispossession. He further added" নালিশী জমিতে ঘর উঠাইতে দেখিয়াছি। বাদীকে খবর দিয়াছি।

In cross-examination he admitted-

বন্টন কালীন সময়ে উপস্থিত ছিলাম না। আমি ঘর উত্তোলন করিতে দেখি নাই। তবে উত্তোলিত ঘর দেখিয়াছিল। আমার ভাই আগে দেখিয়াছে নাকি আমি দেখিয়াছি তাহা আমি বলিতে পারি না। কারন বাদী কখন দেখিয়াছে তা জানি না।”

16. PW 4 claimed himself to be a abrader under the plaintiff who did not mention the date of dispossession.

17. On perusal of the above evidence on record it appears that the plaintiffs own cousin brothers, the defendant No. 7 and 10, did not support the plaintiff's possession rather supported the continuous possession of the defendants in the suit land. It further reveals that there took place two amicable partitions by registered deeds in respect of suit land. One partition deed was dated 27-8-50 (Exhibit "Kha") and another dated 2-9-68 (Exhibit-Kha(i). By those two partition deeds the suit property was partitioned amicably amongst the predecessors of the defendants and ultimately was allotted to the saham of defendant Nos. 2-3 and the predecessors of defendant Nos. 4-6. Following that Exhibit Kha (1) the SA record No. 128 was prepared in the name of defendants and they paid rent vide exhibit-Ga" series.

18. On the other hand, the plaintiff produced the CS Khatian, SA Khatian and 2 receipts. The CS Khatian was proved and was marked as Exhibit-1. The SA Khatian was marked as Exhibit-1(a) and 1(b) and 2 rent receipts dated 16/4/86 and 13/12/89 were marked as Exhibit 2, (a).

<u>19. The evidence of PW 1-PW 4 if be read together with the Exhibits-1,1(a), 2-2(a) those do not prove the plaintiff's continuous possession in the suit land. The PW 1 himself failed to disclose the exact date of dispossession. The PW 1 PW 4 although adduced some evidence in support of plaintiff’s possession but those were very weak type of evidence. The plaintiff was examined as PW-1, PW 3 is his full brother, PW 4 is his broader and an interested witness PW 2 is also not a credible witness. The evidence of PW 2 does not support the plaintiff's possession in the suit land from the time of his paternal grandfather till the date of filing of the suit.</u>

<u>20. On the other hand, the evidence of DW 7 and DW 8 are very much vital. The DW 7 is the defendant No. 7 in the suit and DW 8 is the defendant No. 10. The defendant Nos. 7 and 10 are the cousin brothers of the plaintiff who supported the continuous possession of the defendant for more than the statutory period of limitation. The Exhibit-Kha is the registered partition deed dated 27-8-50 and the Exhibit kha (1) is the registered partition deed dated 2-9-68. From those 2(two) partition deeds it shows that the suit property was in possession of the defendants at least from 27-8-50. The SA record was prepared following the partition deed dated 2-9-68 Exhibit-(1) and the defendants paid rent vide exhibit-"Ga" series which were dated 24-6-1969. 18-9-1973, 16-3-1996, 3-8-1988. The DW 5 and DW 6 supported the defendants' possession and admitted the fact that the shops were constructed upon the suit land for more than 8 (eight) years back. These evidence if be read together have proved beyond doubt that the defendants were in possession all through in the suit land and the plaintiff was never in possession and the plaintiff hopelessly failed to prove his possession and dispossession in the suit land.</u>

<u>21. Now let us consider the case of legality of partial surrender. Partial surrender although is not permitted but a tenant can surrender his possession and abandon his possession at any time during continuation of tenancy. It is the defendant's case that the plaintiffs predecessor being unable to pay rent had surrendered physical possession of the suit land in favour of the defendant's predecessor and thereafter vide exhibit-kha and kha (1) the contesting defendants got the suit land in their actual physical possession. That fact having had proved, the question of partial surrender cannot be fatal in the instant case in view of the fact that the CS recorded tenant's heirs, the defendant Nos. 7 and 10 had admitted the defendants possession in the suit land meaning thereby that there was a surrender. The said surrender being a voluntary surrender the same cannot be said to be illegal surrender. In view of the above, I hold that the predecessor of the plaintiff surrendered the schedule 1 land to the plaintiff in favour of the defendant's predecessor and the plaintiff's predecessor abandoned his title in the suit land. The surrender was a valid surrender. After that surrender the plaintiff's predecessor or the plaintiff was never in possession in the suit land. The plaintiff hopelessly failed to prove his possession and dies possession as alleged in the plaint and the suit was barred by limitation and was barred under section 42 of the SR Act.</u>

22. Moreover, section 86(7) provides the provision of partial surrender which reads thus:

"86 (7) save as provided in sub-section (6) nothing in this section shall affect any arrangement by which a raiyat or under raiyat and his landlord may arrange for a surrender of the whole or a part of the holding."

23. Mr TH Khan referred to the decision of the case law of Osman Gani vs Usha Rani Debi, reported in 6 DLR 648 and submitted that undivided share cannot be surrendered but specific plot of the schedule can be legally surrendered.

24. The facts of that case are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case, in view of the fact that the CS recorded tenants heirs, the defendants Nos. 7 and 10 by adducing evidence supported the defendant's case of surrender and had admitted the possession of the defendant all through in the suit land. In view of the above the decision referred to by Mr Khan is not applicable in the instant case. Mr Khan further cited the cases of Ranjit Kumar vs Shamsuddin Biswas, reported in 1997 BLD 58, 1997 BLD (AD) 47,1997 BLD (AD) 195 and submitted that the appellate Court judgment was not a proper judgment of reversal. He submitted that the judgment is not sustainable in law. On perusal of the trial Court judgment and as well as the judgment impugned in the Rule it appears that the appellate Court upon discussions and consideration of the evidence on record reversed the finding of the trial Court and allowed the appeal. I find that the impugned judgment is a judgment of reversal. I have reason to believe that the plaintiff totally failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land and the suit was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The plaintiff having had failed to mention the date of dispossession the suit was barred by limitation.

25. In view of the above facts and circumstances and the discussions made above I do not find any merit in the Rule.

26. In the result the Rule is discharged however without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 19-8-1995 passed by the learned subordinate Judge, Comilla , in Title Appeal No. 5 of 1995 allowing the appeal, dismissing the suit on reversing those dated 30-11-1992 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Chowddagram, Comilla in Title Suit No. 10 of 1990 are hereby affirmed.

The office is directed to send the lower Court's records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 21-6-92 passed by the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Mymensingh in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 82 of 1989 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 30-3-89 passed by the Assistant Judge, Muktagacha rejecting the petitioner's Miscellaneous Case filed under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The short fact relevant for the purpose of the case is that, opposite party No.1 as plaintiff instituted a suit for partition in the Court of the Munsif, Muktagacha being Partition Suit No. 65 of 1985, claiming partition of the suit properties by metes and bounds and praying for a specific saham for him. It appears that the suit was decreed ex parte on 23-6-1987. In the aforesaid suit the petitioner before me was made defendant No.2. It has been alleged that soon after the petitioner came to learn about the ex parte decree dated 23-6-1987 he obtained necessary information in respect of the suit and the impugned decree and soon thereafter he filed a miscellaneous case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree. It has been stated in the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure that the petitioner is the Superintendent of a school attached to the Women''s Teachers Training College at Mymensingh and he resides at Mymensingh town. This fact was not disputed by the contesting opposite party. It was further contended that for the first time on 30-10-87 the petitioner came to learn about the impugned ex parte decree from one of his relations, who could not give him the particulars of the suit and the date of decree in question. Thereafter the petitioner made necessary enquiries into the matter and learnt definitely on 30-10-87 about the passing of the impugned ex parte decree and soon after he filed this application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree. It was further alleged that the petitioner''s vital interests are involved in the suit and he is highly interested in the subject-matter of the suit and if he had any information or knowledge about the suit, he would have certainly contested it. It was specifically stated in the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure that no summons was served upon the petitioners as required by law and he had no prior knowledge about the suit and the ex parte decree and, as such, the impugned decree is liable to be set aside in the interest of justice.

3. The plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 contested the case by filing written objections denying the material allegations of the petition and contended, inter alia, that summons was duly served upon the defendant-petitioner and the petitioner had full knowledge about the impugned decree. It was further contended that the petitioner was aware of the impugned decree from the very beginning and, as such, he was not entitled to get the decree set aside. It was also contended that notice was duly served upon all the defendants, including the petitioner, but they did not contest the suit as they had no prospect therein. Subsequently this miscellaneous case has been filed for causing unnecessary harassment to the plaintiff. It may be motioned in this connection that neither in the written objection nor in the evidence the contesting defendants took any definite objection to the effect that the petitioner''s application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is barred by limitation.

4. At the trial the defendant-petitioner examined two witnesses and the contesting plaintiff-opposite party examined one witness in support of their respective cases. Mr. Syed AB Mahmudul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the trial Court as well as the Court of appeal below evidently erred in law in not allowing the petitioner''s application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by setting aside the ex parte decree inasmuch as the trial Court never recorded any finding as to the due service of summons upon the defendant-petitioner which alone could give him the jurisdiction to decree the suit ex parte. The learned Advocate further submits that from the order sheet of Partition Suit No. 67 of 1985 it is manifestly clear that no summons was served upon defendant No. 2 and, as such, the learned Courts below erred in law in not setting aside the ex parte decree on an erroneous view of law and on illegal and irrelevant considerations. Mr. Hoque further submits that in the face of the record and the materials before the court it is evident that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 obtained the impugned ex parte decree by fraudulent suppression of summons upon the petitioner and by practicing fraud upon the Court on misrepresentation of material facts and consequently the ex parte decree cannot be allowed to stand.

5. In support of his submission Mr. Hoque has placed before me the order sheet of Partition Suit No. 67 of 1985. It appears from order No. 15 dated 11-8-86 that the summons was not as yet served upon defendant No. 2, who is the petitioner before me and 20-8-86 was fixed for service of summons upon him. It is crystal clear from this order dated 11-8-86 that defendant No. 2 was surreptitiously made defendant No. 3 subsequently in an unscrupulous zeal by defendant No. 3 by interpolation, which is easily discernible from a cursory look at the order sheet, and this fact is further magnified by order No. 16 dated 18-8-86 wherein it was specifically mentioned that the next date of the suit was fixed on 11-9-86 for service return of summons upon defendant No. 2 by usual process as well as by registered post. After that there is no order in the entire order sheet indicating that summons was ever served upon defendant No.2 in the usual course. There is also no clear proof on record to find that summons by registered post was duly served upon defendant No. 2. Although by order No.33 dated 24-5-87 the trial Court in a casual manner found that notice upon defendant No. 2 was served by registered post under the provision of section 19(b) sub-clause (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure but except this stray observation made in the order sheet there is no other material on record to prove that summons was duly served upon defendant No. 2 either by the usual process or by registered post. From this it is manifestly clear that no summons was served upon defendant No. 2 as required by law.

6. Mr. MA Wahhab Miah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, frankly concedes that in the facts of the case, it is difficult for him to assert that summons was duly served upon defendant No. 2. Mr. MA Wahhab Miah, however, lays a great stress on section 164 of the Limitation Act and submits that since defendant No. 2 learnt about the ex parte decree after about one month of the decree he failed to come to the court for setting aside the ex parte decree within 30 days of his knowledge as required by law and, as such, both the Courts below rightly found that the case is barred by limitation. He further submits that since the Appellate Court concurred with the finding of facts arrived at by the trial Court on the question of limitation which is otherwise supported by the evidence on record, there is no scope for interference by this Court exercising power under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. Law for setting aside ex parte decree under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is well-settled. Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that ex parte decree must be set aside on either of the two grounds(1) when summons was not duly served upon the defendants and (2) when the defendants were prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing. In an exercise under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code the primary duty of the Court is to determine whether summons was duly served upon the defendants, when service of summons is denied. If, on consideration of the materials before it, the Court finds that summons was not duly served upon the defendants, it is bound to set aside the ex parte decree without further consideration. In a case when service of summons is admitted or summons is found to have been duly served, the Court will then be called upon to determine the question as to whether the defendants were prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for ex parte disposal.

8. Before setting down a suit for ex parte hearing the court is first required to satisfy itself whether summons was duly served upon the defendants and the order-sheet itself must show that summons was actually served upon the defendants. The order-sheet of the instant suit does not at all indicate that summons was served upon the defendant No. 2 and no satisfaction regarding due service of summons upon defendant No. 2 was recorded by the trial Court before setting down the suit for ex parte disposal on 23-6-87 on the special application of the plaintiff. I have already found that in the case under review no summons was duly served upon the defendant petitioner. Mr. Abdul Wahab Miah, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party, in his characteristic frankness, admits his difficulty to defend the impugned order on the point of service of summons. So, in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, it must be held that summons was not served upon defendant No. 2 and the impugned ex parte decree was passed beyond his knowledge.

9. It has been consistently held by the superior Courts of the country that in a case where it is found that no summons was duly served upon the defendants, the Court is bound to set aside the ex parte decree without any further consideration as due service of summons upon the defendants is a prerequisite for the ex parte disposal of a suit. In the instant case since there was no due service of summons upon defendant No. 2 (petitioner) impugned decree is liable to be set aside on that ground alone and the alleged knowledge about the ex parte decree obtained on fraudulent suppression of summons is of no legal consequence.

10. Now, on the question of limitation, we may refer to Article 164 of the Limitation Act which provides that an applicant is required to challenge an ex parte decree under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure within 30 days from the date of the decree or of his knowledge. From this Mr. A Wahhab Miah strenuously argues that as the petitioner admitted in his cross-examination that he had learnt about the ex parte decree after about one month of the passing of the decree in question and he filed the miscellaneous case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure after about four months and, as such, the learned Courts below were right in holding that the case is barred by limitation. In reply to this submission, Mr. Syed AB Mahmudul Hoque submits that since by fraudulent suppression of summons the plaintiff obtained the ex parte decree by practising fraud upon the Court by resorting to deliberate misrepresentation and manipulations, the question of limitation cannot save the impugned decree, which is a nullity in the eye of law. In support of his contention Mr. Hoque referred to the case of Johara Begum vs. Rafiqul Kader, reported in 15 DLR 91 in which case it has been held that the limitation for filing an application under Article 164 of the Limitation Act is to be counted from the date of the decree or where summons was not duly served when the applicant obtained knowledge of the decree. In this case it has been held that the knowledge is something more than a mere casual knowledge that a decree has been passed against a particular person and in favour of a particular person. Knowledge, in fact, constitutes a bundle of facts giving a distinct and complete perception about the decree under challenge.

11. In this case no definite objection was taken on the point of limitation in the written objections filed by plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 in Miscellaneous Case No. 28/87 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The petitioner as PW 1, of course, stated in his cross-examination that he came to know about the impugned decree after about one month of the decree. PW 2 also stated that he learnt about the ex parte decree 15-20 days after it was so passed. From this it cannot be concluded with any amount of certainty that the defendant-petitioner learnt definitely about the ex parte decree in question in about one month of the passing of the decree. In the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure it has been clearly stated that the petitioner for the first time learnt about the ex parte decree on 30th October, 1987 from one of his relations, who could not give him any particulars of the case and the decree passed against him. Thereafter he inquired about it and obtained necessary information about the suit and the decree and soon thereafter he filed this case. I have already found that no specific objection was taken on the question of limitation in the written objection. Under such circumstances, it must be held that the petitioner's case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not barred by limitation, particularly when fraud is found to have been practised by the plaintiffs upon the Court in obtaining the impugned decree on fraudulent suppression of summons and misrepresentation of material facts. Mr Syed AB Mahmudul Hoque then referred to the case of Abdul Latif Sarder, reported in 32 DLR (AD) 167, wherein it has been held that when fraud is proved there is no question of limitation and it will run from the date when fraud is detected. It has been further held in that case that rule 13 Order 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure itself provides for setting aside an ex parte decree if it is obtained by suppression of the summons. Their Lordships clearly held that it is contrary to the absence of justice to saddle a person with knowledge of an ex parte decree when it is found to have been obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court. I am in respectful agreement with the proposition of law enunciated by their Lordships in the cited case and I am inclined to hold that the petitioner gets instant support of his case from the cited decision.

12. Mr. Syed AB Mahmudul Hoque also refers to the case of Saifur Rahman and others vs. Haider Shah and another reported in 19 DLR (SC) 433 in which their Lordships held that fraud includes "deceit" and "circumspection". Their Lordships further held that decree obtained by fraud is non-existent in the eye of law as fraud vitiates even a solemn transaction. In this case, it is manifestly evident that fraud was practiced upon the Court in obtaining the impugned ex parte decree on fraudulent suppression of summons on the defendant-petitioner. Over jealousy and deceit on the part of the plaintiff in obtaining the ex parte decree being apparent on the face of the record the impugned ex parte decree in not sustainable in law.

<u>13. Since it has been proved beyond doubt that no summons was served upon defendant No. 2 and the plaintiff-opposite parties obtained the ex parte decree behind the back and beyond the knowledge of defendant No. 2 by practising fraud upon the court, the learned Courts below erred in law in rejecting the petitioner''s case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on an erroneous view of law regarding due service of summons as a condition precedent for setting down the suit for an ex parte decree. It is evident that even a minimum care was not taken by the learned Munsif in decreeing the suit ex parte. The learned Court of appeal below also overlooked the vital question of due service of summons upon the defendant as a pre-requisite for ex parte disposal of the suit. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, it must be held that the impugned ex parte decree passed by the learned Munsif is illegal and is a nullity in the eye of law and consequently it cannot stand and the petitioner is entitled to get the relief under Order 9 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

<u>14. In view of the fact that no specific objection was taken in the written objection in Miscellaneous Case No. 29 of 1987 regarding limitation and no evidence was led to prove that defendant No. 2 had definite knowledge about the ex parte decree earlier than what was stated in his application and that he was deliberately late in coming to the Court for vindication of his grievance in a suit for partition, the learned Courts below evidently erred in law in dismissing the Miscellaneous Case saddling the petitioner with the knowledge of the decree in a casual manner and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The principle of law regarding concurrent findings of fact is not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the case.</u>

<u>15. In the facts and circumstance of the case and the evidence on record, I am inclined to hold that the alleged delay of the petitioner in coming to the Court for vindication of his grievances, as found by the learned Court below, cannot stand in the way of his getting the relief, to which he is otherwise entitled to under the law, the essence of law being to advance the cause of justice and not to frustrate it. If fraud is allowed to be perpetrated and perpetuated, the sanctity attached to law will wither away with disastrous consequences to the society. I hold in the circumstances of the case, that Article 164 of the Limitation Act is no bar against the petitioner in getting the relief.</u>

16. In view of the foregoing discussion and the law bearing on the subject, I find that the learned Courts below erred in law in dismissing the petitioner's application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on erroneous view of law and thereby put a premium on the fraud already perpetrated by the plaintiffs in stealing the ex parte decree by fraudulent suppression of summons as well as by misrepresentation of material facts.

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order passed by the learned lower Court of appeal below affirming those passed by the learned Assistant Judge are set aside. Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 1987 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure of the Court of the learned Munsif, now Assistant Judge, Muktagacha is allowed and the ex parte decree dated 23-6-87 passed in Partition Suit No. 67 of 1985 is set aside.

18. Since this is a very old case the learned Assistant Judge is directed to dispose of the suit as expeditiously as possible, preferably within six months from the date of receipt of this order, without granting adjournment to the parties except on compelling reasons.

Send a copy of this order to the learned Assistant Judge for his information and necessary action. Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Bivash Chandra Biswas, Advocate -For the Petitioners
Md Ali, for Kamruzzaman, Advocate -For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Panna Bibi and ors ------ Petitioners
vs.
Rebeka Khatun and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the contesting defendants 1-10 against the order dated 30-8-90 passed in Title Suit 144 of 1975 being a suit for partition by the Subordinate Judge, Jessore rejecting an application for effecting final decree after modifying the preliminary decree considering the transfers of portions of the suit land having taken place after passing of the preliminary decree among the parties in the suit.

2. Opposite party Nos. 1-4 filed the suit for partition of ejmali property described in schedules Ka to Uma of the plaint. The defendants did not file any written statement. On 29-4-77 the present petitioners and opposite party Nos. 5 to 8 (who were defendants 11 to 14) and the plaintiffs filed a compromise petition with a prayer to pass a preliminary decree according to shares as shown in the compromise petition. Accordingly preliminary decree was passed in terms of compromise on 4-5-77. According to preliminary decree the plaintiffs were allotted 0.44 acres land out of 2.22 acres in GS Khatian Nos. 131, 264, 329 and 271. The share of the plaintiffs is 3 annas 4 ganda and 14 til. Plaintiff also were allotted 0.44 acres in Khatian Nos. 259 and 58, the share being 1 anna 11 ganda 7 til. So far the lands in Kha, Ga and Gha schedules are concerned the plaintiffs have not been given any share. Defendant Nos. 1-10 ie the present petitioners were given the lands of schedule Kha, Ga and Gha. The share of the defendants 1-10 was 1 anna 2 ganda 2 kantanti 14 til. Plaintiffs again have been allotted 7-22 acres in Uma schedule. Their share being 9 annas 10 ganda. But after preliminary decree there were certain transfers by registered deeds between the parties, plaintiffs 1-4 sold 57½ acres out of their 0.97 acres of land from plots 75, 1099 and 758/1141 from Uma schedule to defendants 50-52 by registered kabala dated 14-5-79. Plaintiff 1 sold 0.26 acres land from Ka schedule to defendants 3-6 on 29-4-77. The plaintiffs also sold 1.35 acres on the same date to defendants 3-6 from Uma schedule land. Plaintiff 2 sold 0.04 acres from ka schedule and 0.85 from Uma schedule 1 and on 29-4-77 to defendants 3-6. Plaintiff 3 on 29-4-77 sold 0.04 acre from Ka schedule land and 0.42 acres from Uma schedule land to defendants 3-6. Plaintiffs 1-4. sold. 57½ acres land out of their 0.978 acres of land from plot No. 751, 1099 and 758/1141 from Uma schedule land by registered kabala dated 14-5-79 to defendant 50-52. Defendant 51 sold 0.21 acres land from the said plot to defendant 3 on 5-6-85 by registered kabala. He also sold 0.10 acres land from plot No. 1161 to the defendant No. 4 on 10-2-90 by a registered kabala. In the said manner defendants 1-10 claimed to have inherited 0.27 acres and purchased 0.34 acres in Ka schedule land and they inherited 2.54 acres and purchased 2.62 in Uma schedule land. It is worthy to note that some transfers which were made even before the preliminary decree were also not brought to the notice of the trial Court at the time of passing the preliminary decree for incorporating in the petition of compromise and, as such, those lost consideration of the trial Court at the time of passing the preliminary decree. Final decree has not yet been passed or drawn up in this case.

3. The plaintiffs filed an application on 11-2-89 for effecting the final decree in terms of preliminary decree adjusting the shares they had already sold to defendants 3-6 as stated above. On that application an Advocate Commissioner was appointed by order dated 5-3-90 for processing preliminary decree towards the final decree. The Advocate Commissioner filed his report on 18-6-90, but he had refused to adjust the property according to transfers made above. Against the same the present petitioners filed written objection on 30-8-90 and it was fixed for hearing on 2-2-91. At this stage the instant Rule was obtained and further proceeding of the suit has been stayed by this court. Defendants 1-10 filed another application on 19-7-90 for effecting final decree and for allotting a separate saham to them claiming 6.17 acres land which they have acquired by way of inheritance and purchase including those after preliminary decree. The application is Annexure A to the rule petition. Against which the plaintiffs filed written objection alleging that the plaintiffs 1-3 did not sell any land to defendants 1-10. In written objection Annexure B also it has been alleged that the defendants obtained the documents of purchase by forgery and fabrication. The application of the defendants 1-10 was rejected on 10-8-90.

4. The present revisional application has been preferred upon the grievances that the Advocate Commissioner who was approached by the present petitioners to allot the share to them including the lands they had purchased before preliminary decree but the same was refused by the Advocate Commissioner. Then they filed an application before the trial Court to adjust the said purchase deeds in the preliminary decree modifying the same but the same having been refused by the impugned order, the present Rule has been obtained.

5. It is not denied that some transfers were made before the preliminary decree and some have been made after the same as have been stated above.

6. Mr Bivash Chandra Biswas, the " learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner defendants 1-10, submits that the suit in question being a suit for partition of ejamali properties it remains open until the final decree is drawn up and therefore the Advocate Commissioner should have allotted the saham to the petitioner including the land they have purchased before or after the preliminary decree adjusting the allotments and the trial Court also, according to settled principle of law, should have adjusted and modified the preliminary decree by adjusting their claim. In support of his submission, the learned Advocate for the petitioner cites the decision in the case of Phool Chand and another vs Gopal Lal AIR 1967 (SC) 1470 wherein their Lordships have held:

"So far as partition suits are concerned in any event of transfers after the preliminary decree which necessitates a change in shares, the court can and should do so; and if there is a dispute in that behalf the order of the court deciding that dispute and making variation in shares specified in the preliminary decree already passed is a decree in itself which would be liable to appeal."

7. In another decision in the case of Md Latif PLD 1953 (Lahore) 256, in that case it is held that because of inter-transfers after the preliminary decree in a partition suit before final decree the shares can be modified or adjusted since partition suit remains pending till the final decree is passed.

8. Mr Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of Mr Kamruzzaman for the opposite party No. 104, submits that since the plaintiffs denied the transfers made by them before the preliminary decree as stated above, to the defendants 3-6 and also after the preliminary decree to defendants 50-52 by four registered deeds on 29-4-77 and 4-5-79 as stated above and also for the reasons that the aforesaid 3 purchases claimed to have been made by the defendants 3-6 from the plaintiffs said to have been made before the preliminary decree but not incorporated in the petition of compromise and subsequently has not found place in the judgment of the preliminary decree, the same cannot be legally adjusted by modifying the preliminary decree. According to him, very rightly the Advocate Commissioner has refused to allot the shares to the defendants petitioners including their aforesaid purchased lands and the trial Court also committed no illegality refusing to adjust and modify the preliminary decree.

9. I have heard the learned Counsels of both the parties and examined the papers, the petition of revisional applications and counter-affidavit and the records of the courts below meticulously. It is the consistent view of all the superior courts of the subcontinent that parties in a partition suit either plaintiff or defendant are of same status being admitted co-sharers and that a partition suit even after passing of the preliminary decree remains pending until final decree is passed. (See PLD 1954 (SC) 184, 6 DLR (FC) 11, AIR 1940 (PC) 11 and 44 DLR 232). It is also settled law that before final decree is passed and the transfers made the parties can be adjusted in the preliminary decree by adjusting the quantum of share and in some decision it is said that it can be modified at the time of passing of final decree (See AIR (1925) 433, AIR 1965 Mysore) 73, AIR 1940, 11). In the instant case there is one exception as I see. It is that the petitioners as defendants 3-6 claimed that they made 4 purchases on 29-4-77 whereas the preliminary decree was passed on 4-6-77 in terms of compromise petition effected between the parties on 29-4-77. But those purchases were not incorporated in the petition of compromise and those were not placed before the trial Court for consideration while passing the eliminatory decree and the Advocate Commissioner also has not allowed those sales to be adjusted. The share already allotted in the preliminary decree on the face of objection by the plaintiffs that they have not made the aforesaid sales to the said defendants and that those documents are forged, and fabricated and without consideration. The Advocate Commissioner also was correct to refuse adjustments of those purchases made by defendants 50-52 from the plaintiffs 1-4 on 14-5-79 as the same also are denied to be genuine sales by the plaintiffs and also two sales made by defendant 51 to defendant 3 and another to defendant 4 on 5-6-85 and 10-2-85 made after the preliminary decree and also the sales and transfers which were made before the preliminary decree but not incorporated in the compromise petition.

<u>10. After my careful consideration of all the decisions and the facts and circumstances of the instant case. I am of the opinion that in a suit for partition which undoubtedly remains pending till the final decree is passed and drawn up whatever may be the claim and counter-claim between the parties raised on the basis of registered documents should be decided by the trial Court by adjusting and modifying the preliminary decree and accordingly, the commissioner should be directed to work out the preliminary decree to make it final. Therefore, I am not convinced to accept the proposition made from the side of the opposite parties that the claims can be decided and adjusted while making the final decree because unless it is decided in the preliminary decree the Commissioner who is the real machinery to effect the partition will not be in a position to proceed at all to work out and complete his work in terms of preliminary decree. In the aforesaid view of the matter, I am inclined to find that the trial Court committed illegality in passing the impugned order which resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In my opinion, the trial Court shall decide the dispute as to objection of the plaintiffs that they have not made the disputed sales as aforesaid and whether the documents are forged and fabricated so that the claim and counter-claim of the parties, in respect of transfers made, before or after the preliminary decree can be decided allowing the parties to prove their documents and their genuineness by adducing evidence, if any, and the trial Court shall modify the preliminary decree and make allotment to the parties by adjusting the share according to the claims of the parties which can be established and thereafter shall appoint an Advocate Commissioner to work out the preliminary decree for making the decree final.</u>

11. Consequently, the impugned order dated 30-8-90 is set aside and the prayer of the petitioners is allowed to the extent as I have observed above and I am giving directions to the trial Court that it shall re-open the preliminary decree for adjusting the claims of the parties and the commissioner report submitted on 8-6-90 also is cancelled.

12. The Rule is made absolute. The stay order granted earlier is hereby vacated. Since the matter is pending for long time, the trial Court shall take care so that the suit is disposed of quickly.

No order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Tobarak Hossain, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
Rafiqul Haque with Md Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocates—For Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Mufti AM Jalaluddin ----- Petitioner 
Vs. 
Hazera Khatun being dead her heirs Nasiruddin Ahmed & ors ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued on 30-8-95 calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show causes as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 15-2-95 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No.40 of 85, affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-1-85 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 243 of 1982 should not be set aside.

2. The defendant No. 1 of the suit obtained this Rule on filing an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

3. Facts for the disposal of this Rule are that, Hazera Khanam and Mst. Juberia Khanam as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 243 of 82 in the Court of 1st Munsif, Sadar Sylhet for declaration of their absolute and unrestricted right of way over the schedule pathway and for a permanent injunction restraining the defendant No. 1 from interfering with the plaintiffs' absolute and unrestricted right of way over the schedule pathway. Plaintiff stated in the plaint that plaintiffs and defendant belong to same stock. Mufti Abdul Quadir was their remote predecessor-in-interest, who died leaving two sons namely, Mufti Bashiruddin and Mufti Mohiuddin. Then Mufti Bashiruddin died leaving two sons Mufti Mesbahuddin, the defendant No. 2, and Mufti Jainuddin, Mufti Jainuddin died leaving a widow, the plaintiff No. 1, a daughter the plaintiff No. 2 and 4 sons, the pre-defendants Nos. 3-6 as his heirs. Mufti Mohiuddin died leaving only son Mufti AM Jalaluddin, the principal defendant No. 1, plaintiffs and defendants were enjoying ejmali properties. During the last survey and settlement operation, their email properties were recorded in a joint Khatian comprising SS plot Nos. 4604, 4605 and 4608 having a total area of 1.15 decimals of land. Out of these, SS plot No. 4604 was shown under possession of Mufti Mesbahuddin and others including the plaintiffs and pro-defendant Nos. 3-6, the heirs of Mufti Bashiruddin. Whereas SS plot No. 4605 was shown to be under the possession of Mufti AM Jalaluddin alone and SS plot No. 4608 was shown under joint possession in the joint names of the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 1 to 6. But there was no partition among the parties by metes and bounds. For the sake of convenience the plaintiff and proforma-defendant Nos. 2-6 had been owning and possessing the land of SS plot No. 4604 in ejmali including the principal defendant No. 1, whereas, the principal defendant No. 1 alone had been owning and possessing the land of SS plot No. 4605 exclusively. The land of SS plot No. 4608 was being owned and possessed by the plaintiffs and the defendants in ejmali. The plaintiffs and the defendants Nos. 3-6 were residing in the northern most portion of SS Plot No. 4604 and they had been enjoying the land of the SS plot No. 4608 in ejmali with defendant Nos. 1-6 and they had been using the pathway described in the schedule of the suit openly, peaceably, uninterruptedly and unrestrictedly, as of right, without any let or hindrance from any quarter, from the time of their remote predecessor. They claimed that they acquired indefeasible easement right over the suit property and the plaintiffs and the defendants were also owners of the land of the suit pathway. The plaintiffs and defendants had earlier filed Title Suit No. 361 of 66, for another private pathway of their own. The suit pathway was relaid by a local investigateting Commissioner. The local investigating commissioner found the existence of suit pathway. The Suit pathway was being used by the plaintiffs and the defendants for their absolute necessity. The plaintiff No. 1 was a helpless widow while plaintiff No. 2 is her daughter and the pro-defendant Nos. 1-6 are her sons, plaintiff No. 2 mostly resides with her husband, while pro-defendant Nos. 3-6 are residing abroad and taking advantage of the helpless condition of the plaintiffs, the principal defendant No. 1 chalked out a plan to increase and augment quantum of his land lying to the west of the suit pathway, and with this end in view had been creating troubles in the use and enjoyment of the suit pathway smoothly by plaintiffs and the pro-defendants. They had no other alternative pathway accepting the suit pathway to link up with the main road connecting, the Dargah-e-Hazrat Shah Jalal to the west and the Sylhet Airport road to east. The defendant No. 1 was a litigant by nature and he got many designing persons at his beck and call and unless he was restrained by an order of temporary injunction, with ad-interim order from interfering with suit pathway till disposal of the suit, the plaintiffs and the pro-defendants would be confined to their respective houses, and thereby, they would suffer irreparable loss and injury. The suit was amended and a prayer for mandatory injunction for a direction on the principal defendant to dismantle and remove the wall and all other obstructions from the suit pathway within a time specified was made.

4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations in the plaint stating that the plaintiff’s suit was not maintainable, and it had no cause of action. The defendant stated that the suit land along other land belong to Mufti Abdul Quadir. The plaintiffs and defendants were his successors-in-interest. There was an amicable partition amongst themselves. The heirs of Mufti Bashir Uddin got the land of plot No. 4604 exclusively, and the heirs of Mufti Mohiuddin got the plot Nos. 4605 and 4606 in their exclusive saham. The homestead at plot No. 4608 and the path covering plot No. 4607 remained in ejmali. The pathway was encroached by a grand-daughter of Mufti Nazir Uddin, and the plaintiffs and the defendants together brought TS No. 361 of 66. A local investigation was held twice in the said suit and it was found that there was a pathway comprising the plot No. 4607 and No. 4604. The plaintiffs and the pro-defendants were the owners of the said pathway. From the subsequent report it was found that the plaintiffs and the pro-defendants had closed down the pathway covering plot No. 4604 by constructing structures thereon. There was never any pathway over plot No. 4605. The defendant No. 1 had two pucca buildings and a semipucca building on the land of plot No. 4605. Those were let out to bharatias, and for the use of the barratries, the eastern portion of the plot No. 4605 was spared for ingress and outguess to the aforesaid buildings. The road leading to the Darga of Shah Jalal from the Sylhet Shalutikar road runs to the contiguous south of plot Nos. 4604, 4605, 4606. The plaintiffs and the pro-defendants had been using the ejmali path covering plot No. 4607 for their ingress and outguess from their homesteads. The plaintiffs No. 1 and the defendant No. 2 executed a deed of relinquishment in favour of the defendant No. 1 in respect of plot No. 4605, and the plots No. 4605 and 4606 were recorded in the name of defendant No. 1 and the plot No. 4604 was recorded in the name of plaintiffs and pro-defendants. The plaintiffs had no right, title interest in the plot No. 4605 and their claim of right of way of easement was false.

5. On the pleadings of the parties, Assistant Judge framed five issues for determination and recorded 4 PWs and one DW and marked documents as Exhibits of the parties. Thereafter, by the judgment and decree dated 30-1-85, decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs and against defendant No. 1 and ex prate against other defendants. Against the trial Court's judgment and decree, the defendant No. 1 preferred Title Appeal No. 40 of 85, before the District Judge Sylhet, which appeal was transferred to the Third Sub-ordinate Judge, Sylhet, for disposal and who, after hearing the appeal, dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court by the impugned judgment and decree.

6. Mr Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Senior Advocate appearing with Mr Tobarak Hossain for the petitioner; submits that plaint shows that property was a joint property and it was never partitioned by metes and bounds and the plaintiffs and defendants were using the property for their convenience. The plaintiffs have sought for declaration of right of easement in respect of suit land which land belongs to plaintiffs and defendants as well, and therefore, under the definition of section 4 of Easement Act, the plaintiffs cannot seek easement on the land of his own. Claim of easement is to be made on the land of others. He further submits that both the courts erroneously accepted Exhibit 'C' as a deed of partition which is, in fact, a deed of relinquishment. By deed of relinquishment it cannot be said that a partition was made. There is no proof that there was any legal partition. He cited cases reported in AIR 1958 Madhya Pradesh AIR 1938 Bombay 215, AIR 1932 Bom 513, 41 DLR (AD) 88, 42 DLR 167 in support of his submission.

7. Mr Rafiqul Huq, learned Senior Advocate appearing with Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan for the opposite party, submits that in the written statement the defendant No. 1 claimed that he was owning and possessing the plot No. 4605 exclusively on his own right. In the written statement it was mentioned that there was amicable partial partition among the heirs of Mufti Bashiruddin and Mufti Mohiuddin in respect of some of the ejmali properties. The heirs of Mufti Bashiruddin were in exclusive possession of share of land. While the heirs of Mufti Mohiuddin got the land now comprising plots 4605 and 4606 in their saham exclusively on the basis of amicable partition. The land of plot No. 4604 was recorded in the name of pro-defendants and plaintiffs. The land in plot No. 4605 was recorded in the name of defendant No. 1. The defendant No. 1 stated in the written statement that he had 2 puce buildings and semipucca buildings on the land of plot No. 4605, which were let out to tenant and he had allowed the tenant to use the vacant space in the southern portion of plot No. 4605 for ingress and outgoes from the building. He submits that both the courts found that the defendant No. 1 got plot No. 4605, plaintiffs got plot No. 4604 and plots were contiguous and the trial Court believed that the plaintiffs had no malice right in No. 4605, and that plot No. 4605 was partitioned and it was not an email property. He further submits that the trial Court found that the plot No. 4605 was enjoyed by defendant No. 1 exclusively, and it was under his exclusive possession and his claim was established by Exhibit 'C' and further submits that this findings of the courts are concurrent finding of facts, and this court sitting in provisional jurisdiction would not disturb the findings of courts on fact. There was no misreading and misconstruction of evidence by the courts below. Mr Huq lastly submits that in the suit plaintiffs prayed for declaration of their absolute and unrestricted right over the schedule pathway, and the plaintiffs have a prayer for permanent injunction for restraining the defendants from interfering with the plaintiffs' unrestricted right over the schedule property, and he submits that plaintiffs prayer for permanent injunction should be granted which is an alternate prayer of the plaintiffs and the suit could even be decreed for injunction, and the courts below did not commit any wrong in decreeing the suit. He cited decision reported in AIR (1981) Gujarat 93. In support of his submission of maintainability of suit on alternative prayer for injunction even, and decision reported in AIR 1938 Bombay 215, AIR 1932 Bombay 513, and cases of 1999 BLD 25, 1997 BLD (AD) 145 and 199, 1995 BLD (AD) 238 and 14 DLR 44.

8. I have heard the learned Advocates of the parties at length, perused the plaint, written statement and exhibits, evidence of the plaintiffs and defendant, and both the judgments of the courts below. It appears that the plaintiff's suit is for declaration of their absolute right of way over the suit property, and for a decree for permanent injunction. The plaintiffs stated in the plaint that plaintiffs and defendants were of same stock. The suit property belonged to Abdul Kadir, who was a remote predecessor-in-interest of the parties. The plaintiffs and the defendant were joint owners of the property measuring 1.52 acres under a joint khatian comprised of SS plot No. 4604, 4605 and 4608. Plaintiffs and the defendant were in possession of the property for convenience. The property was not partitioned among them by metes and bounds. It is stated that for the convenience of possession the plaintiffs and pro-defendants are owning and possessing SS plot No. 4604 in ejmali excluding principal defendant No. 1. The principal defendant No. 1 alone has been owning and possessing the land of SS plot No. 4605 exclusively, while the land of SS plot No. 4608 is being owned and possessed by the plaintiffs and the defendant in ejmali. Defendant No. 1 stated in his written statement that there was an amicable partial partition among the heirs of Mufti Basiruddin and Mufti Mohiuddin. The heirs of Mufti got the land comprising plot No. 4604 in their saham. The homestead is in plot No. 4608 and the path in plot No. 4607 remained in ejmali. The heirs of Mufti Mohiuddin got plot No. 4605 in their saham exclusively. Plaintiffs and defendants as plaintiffs earlier filed Title Suit No. 361 of 66, for an ejmali path in plot No. 4607, which was encroached upon by a grand-daughter of Mufti Nasiruddin. The suit was subsequently transferred to the Additional Court of Munsif and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 124 of 97. The defendant No. 1 stated that he had two pucca buildings and one semipucca building on the land of plot No. 4605. Same buildings are with frontage to the east. The defendant No. 1 had allowed the tenants of the building to use the vacant space in the eastern portion of plot No. 4605 as passage. In the written statement defendant No. 1 further stated that there was no document of partition and the plaintiff No. 1 and pro-defendant No. 2 executed a deed of relinquishment in respect of plot No. 4605. The plaintiffs cannot claim the right in the suit land as the suit land was never a pathway and the plaintiffs and defendants never used it and they have no right title in plot No. 4605 and their claim of right of way by easement or lost grant or otherwise is false.

9. 'Easement' has been defined under section 4 of the Easement Act which is quoted;

Section 4—An easement is a right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses as such, for the beneficial enjoyment of that land, to do and continue to do something, or to prevent and continue to prevent something being done, in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land not his own.

<u>10. From the averments made in the plaint, it shows that the properties of the plaintiffs, preformed defendants and the defendant No. 1 are the joint properties and they are in possession of the property under a joint Khatian. The property measures 1.15 decimal of land under plot Nos. 4604, 4605 and 4608. According to the plaint, for the sake of convenience, the plaintiffs and pro-defendants Nos. 2-6 have been owning SS Plot No. 4608 in ejmali including defendant No. 1, Defendant No. 1 alone possesses the plot No. 4605 exclusively, and the land SS plot No. 4604 is being owned and possessed by the plaintiffs. Whereas the defendant No. 1 admitted in written statement that earlier a suit was filed by the defendant and plaintiffs and that there was no document of partition and for the sake of obtaining loan from House Building Finance Corporation a document of relinquishment of claim was made by the plaintiffs for the land in favour of the defendant No. 1. It appears that there was no final partition of the property among the plaintiffs and defendants, by metes and bounds. The possession of the plaintiffs and defendants in the property in their respective portion is for convenience of parties. The plaintiffs have claimed easement in the schedule property which belongs to all the parties to the suit, including the plaintiffs. By misreading Exhibit 'C', the deed of relinquishment, the court below took the Exhibit 'C' as a document of partition, and decreed the suit. The court of appeal below also misconstrued the Exhibit C and found same deed to be a 'specific partition' and decreed the suit. The findings of both the courts below on the basis of Exhibit 'C' are erroneous. It is abundantly clear from the plaint that there was no partition of the property among the plaintiffs and the defendants. The Khatian was prepared in joint names and the possession of the plaintiffs and defendants were for convenience in the absence of any partition by metes and bounds. The defendant No. 1 admitted in his written statement that there was no deed of partition and the Exhibit 'C' was executed between plaintiffs and defendant No. 1 for obtaining a loan from the House Building Finance Corporation. The Exhibit 'C' is on record. It is a Photostat copy. It was executed by Md Mezbauddin and Hazera Khatun. This Exhibit 'C' cannot be treated as document of partition, because the property was not owned by Mezbauddin and Hazera only. There are some other owners of the property. Partition is a division made between the several persons of joint land. By the document Exhibit 'C' no portion was divided and all the co-sharers are not party in this document. Thus, it appears that the plaintiffs are also owners of the suit land and they cannot claim right of easement on the property of their own. The learned Senior Advocate Mr Huq has submitted strenuously that the concurrent findings of the courts below are that the property is under the exclusive possession of defendant No. 1 as his own property, and these findings cannot be interfered with by this Court and that it has been proved that there was an amicable partition once and no suit for partition is maintainable, and he cited the case of Halim Khatun vs Hamid Mia reported in 10 BLC 1.</u>

<u>11. I have gone through the case. In this case it has been found that there was no partition by metes and bounds and the possession of the parties is for convenience. The case of Sreementi Aroti Rani Paul vs Sree Sudarshan Kumar Paul and others reported in The Lawyers, January Issue page 23, and the cases reported in 1999 BLD(AD) 25, 1997 BLD (AD) 145, 1995 BLD (AD) 137 are not applicable in this case as I have already found the findings of the Courts below are the result of misreading of evidence and Exhibit 'C'; and are against section 4 of the Easement Act. The last submission of Mr Rafiqul Huq about alternative prayer in the suit is supported by the case reported in AIR 1981 Gujarat 93. I have found from the pleadings and record of the suit that the plaintiffs and defendants are in joint occupation of the property, without partition of the property by metes and bounds. There is no document of partition. The plaintiffs suit for declaration of their right of easement as claimed in the plaint is not maintainable as per the provision of section 4 of the Easement Act. The suit land was not finally allotted to the defendant No. 1. Defendant No. 1 is not the owner of the suit land alone, wherein the plaintiffs are joint owners of the suit land. Thus, they cannot maintain the suit and cannot get decree for easement. Since, it has been found that the property is in joint occupation of the plaintiffs and the defendants, and they are all co-owners of the suit plots, the plaintiffs as co-owners of the property can enjoy the property jointly with other co-sharers. It has been further found from the written statement of the defendant No. 1, that there is a pathway in plot No. 4605, which, of course, defendant No. 1 claimed as his own land for his own benefit and the benefit of his tenants. As I have already found that the possession of the defendant No. 1 in the suit property is not his exclusive possession and the plaintiffs are joint owners of the same. As there exists a pathway in plot No. 4605 and plaintiffs and all other defendants being co-owners of the plot of land are legally entitled to use the pathway. The pathway has been obstructed by the defendant No. 1, as such, he can be restrained by an order of injunction.</u>

<u>12. In the aforesaid discussions, the decrees of the courts below are erroneous and call for interference. The decrees are to be set aside. The plaintiffs are entitled to decree of permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with the use of the pathway in the suit property of the plaintiffs until the property is partitioned by metes and bounds.</u>

13. In the result, the Rule is made absolute in part. The judgment and decree impugned of courts below are set aside. The decree passed by the trial Court declaring the plaintiffs' right of way in respect of the suit pathway is set aside, and the decree of the trial Court restraining the defendants by an order of perpetual injunction from interfering with the plaintiffs' enjoyment of the pathway is affirmed and maintained, and the suit be decreed in part.

Send down the LC at once.

End.

caseno:
Appeal From Original Decree No. 96/91 (Dhaka) 
Appeal From Original Decree No.1 of 1985 (Jessore)
lawyer:
Sk Habibul Alam, Advocate — For the Appellants. 
SM Rezaul Karim with Rezaul Hoque, Advocates — For the Respondents.
parties:
Amirul Islam (Md) and others ------ Appellants
Vs. 
Md Nurul Islam, and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Sirajul Islam J: This first appeal by the defendant is directed against the judgment and decree dated 27-9-1984 passed by Subordinate Judge, Satkhira in Title Suit No. 61 of 1982 decreeing the suit is favour of the plaintiff.

2. The respondent No.1 Md Nurul Islam and others filed Title Suit No. 61 of 1982 in the court of Subordinate Judge, Satkhira against the defendant Md Aminul Islam and others for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for permanent injunction in respect of the suit lands described in the schedule to the plaint. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that the suit land together with other lands originally belonged to one Jonab Ali Sarder, who gave a settlement of the suit land measuring 27.38 acres in favour of his son-in-law Abdul Hamid in the middle of Baishakh, 1355 BS at a salami of Taka 3000.00 and yearly rent of Taka 135.00 12 annas and 6 pies. After this settlement, Abdul Hamid took over possession of the suit land and possessed the same. Abdul Hamid paid rent to the landlord, Janab Ali Sarder, but in course of time there was a default in payment of rent and that landlord Janab Ali instituted a Rent Suit No. 826 of 1956 in the 3rd Court of Munsif at Satkhira against Abdul Hamid for arrear of rent and got the decree. During SA operation the suit land was recorded in the SA Khatian in the name of Abdul Hamid within the knowledge of defendant Nos. 1-5. Abdul Hamid possessed the suit land and during his life time and then died in 1971 during liberation war of Bangladesh leaving behind his wife Jahura Khatun and 2 sons Baki Billah and Moniruzzaman. These heirs of Abdul Hamid possessed the suit land and paid rent to the government. They also submitted a statement of property including the suit land under President''s Order No. 98 of 1972. They thereafter transferred 0.60 decimals of land out of plot No. 294 to defendant No. 15 by a registered kabala. Thereafter Jahura, Baki, Moniruzzaman jointly transferred the suit land measuring 26.77 acres to the plaintiffs by 5 registered kabalas dated 9-3-1982 and 10-3-1982 and made over possession of the same to the plaintiffs. Since purchase, the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land as of their own right and paying rent to the Government. The defendants have no right, title or possession in the suit land but that the defendants threatened the plaintiffs on 28th Jaistha, 1389 BS corresponding to 23-6-82 to remove earth from the suit land thereby disturbing the plaintiffs' peaceful possession therein. Hence, the plaintiffs have filed the suit for declaration as aforesaid.

3. Defendant Nos. 1-5 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material allegations and statements made in the plaint. The defendants' case, in short, is that the suit land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 6 originally belonged to Jonab Ali Sarder. This Jonab Ali Sarder subsequently made a settlement of 27.38. acres of land to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in the first part of Baishakh, 1358 BS at a rental of Taka 131 and 3 annas, At the time of this settlement, these two defendants were minors and that their maternal grand-fathers, Jonab Ali Moral and Mohor Ali Sardar respectively did everything in taking settlement and in paying the rent and salami to the landlord Jonab Ali Sarder. Their maternal grand-fathers paid a salami of Taka 4000.00 on behalf of the defendants to Jonab Ali Sarder and that Jonab Ali Sarder granted dakhila to the defendants. Since settlement, the defendants'' maternal grandfathers used to possess the suit land and look after the same during their lifetime on behalf of the defendants. After the death of their grand-fathers, the defendants 1 and 2 themselves have been possessing the suit land. The PRR Khatian was prepared in the name of defendants in respect of the suit land but subsequently the name of Abdul Hamid was recorded wrongly in the SA Khatian. The defendants filed an objection case against this wrong record under section 19(1) of EBSAT Act and that an order was passed in favour of defendants for correction of wrong SA Khatian but that this order was not complied with. Subsequently, the defendants by filing an application in the office of the ADC got their names recorded in a mutation Khatian and paid rent to the government. The defendants thus have been owning and possessing the suit land. The plaintiffs or Abdul Hamid or his heirs have no right, title or possession in the suit land. The defendants'' uncle or mother never filed any suit in the Sub-Judge Court at Khulna in respect of the suit land as stated by the plaintiff in the plaint. All these are fictitious papers without basis. The plaintiff's kabalas are some paper transactions without consideration and it did not create any title to the suit land in favour of the plaintiff. As such, the plaintiff''s suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge framed 5 issues for decision in the suit and after considering the facts and evidence of the case decided all the issues in favour of the plaintiffs and decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 27-9-84.

5. Being aggrieved by this judgment and decree, the defendants 1-5 have preferred this first appeal in this court.

6. Admittedly, the suit land with other lands originally belonged to one Jonab Ali Sarder. It is also an admitted fact that defendant No. 1 Aminul Islam is the son of this Jonab Ali Sarder and that Abdul Hamid was his son-in-law. The plaintiff''s only case is that Jonab Ali Sarder leased out 27.38 acres of land in favour of his son-in-law Abdul Hamid in the middle of Baisak, 1355 BS at a salami of Taka 3000.00 and at an annual rent of Taka 1.35 and 12 annas 6 pies. The plaintiff's next case is that, Abdul Hamid died leaving behind his wife Jahura, two sons Bakibillah and Moniruzzaman and that the plaintiffs have purchased the suit land from these heirs of Abdul Hamid by five registered kabalas dated 9-3-82 and 10-3-82.

7. Mr. Habibul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-appellants, has submitted that the plaintiffs'' case of Jonab Ali Sarder's granting lease of the suit land in favour of Abdul Hamid has not been proved by any cogent evidence but that the learned Subordinate Judge without considering this aspect of the matter, has come to a conclusion in respect of the alleged lease of Abdul Hamid on the basis of some extraneous papers as referred to by the plaintiffs in respect of some suits and cases which the defendants had categorically denied in their written statement and in their deposition. The learned Advocate submits that this decision arrived at by the learned Subordinate Judge is not based on proper consideration of the facts and evidence of the case and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree are not sustainable in law. Mr Habibul Alam further submits that the plaintiff's whole case is a case of oral settlement made by Jonab Ali in favour of Abdul Hamid. He submits that there is nothing like oral settlement at that time but that settlement could be made by Amolnama or by cheque but that the plaintiff failed to show any Amolnama or cheque in support of any such lease. He further submits that although the plaintiff's, case is a case of oral settlement but the PWs 1 and 2 have said in their deposition that Jonab Ali Sarder granted a cheque but they could not produce any such cheque. The learned Advocate argued that the learned Subordinate Judge did not discuss all the contradictions made by the plaintiffs' witnesses in their deposition and thus the learned Subordinate Judge has committed illegality in coming to the finding in respect of settlement of the suit land in favour of Abdul Hamid as claimed by the plaintiffs.

8. Mr. SM Rezaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondents, on the other hand, has submitted that the plaintiff's case is a case of oral settlement made by Jonab Ali in favour of Abdul Hamid and that the PWs 1-4 have proved the plaintiff''s title and possession by their corroborative evidence.
