Apart from this, the learned Advocate referred to some exhibited documents like Ext. 6, etc. and said that these are the copy of the plaint and written statement filed by Amirul Islam and his mother in Title Suit No. 321 of 1976, 312/80 in which the fact of Jonab Ali''s making settlement in favour of Abdul Hamid has been admitted and that all these taken together can be said that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their case of settlement of the suit land in favour of Abdul Hamid.

9. From the impugned Judgment, it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has stated in his judgment that the PW 2 Ibrahim, PW 3 Ranjit, PW 4 Mohar Ali have made corroborative statement supporting the right, title and possession of Abdul Hamid and his heirs and lastly of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land. The learned Subordinate Judge further stated that the plaintiff as PW 1 had corroborated the averment made in his plaint. But it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has not stated that the PWs have individually stated in respect of the plaintiffs case.

10. By a perusal of the evidence, it appears that the plaintiff has not been examined in the case but that their father one Fazlur Rahman was examined as PW 1 on behalf of all the plaintiffs. This PW 1 said in his deposition that jonab Ali was the original owner of the suit land and that he made a settlement of 32.34 acres of land in favour of his eldest son-in-law Abdul Hamid in the middle of Baishakh, 1355 BS at a salami of Taka 3000.00 and at an annual rent of Taka 135 and 12 annas 6 pie. In the cross-examination this PW 1 has said that Jonab Ali himself wrote a cheque and delivered it to Hamid on the same date of giving settlement to Hamid. There is no statement of granting any cheque in favour of Abdul Hamid in the whole plaint. But PW 1 said that there was a cheque given by Jonab Ali but it appears that the cheque as said by PW 1 has not been filed before the court. The PW 2, Ibrahim also said in his deposition that Jonab Ali wrote a cheque in favour of Hamid. But no such cheque is available in the case. PW 3 Ranjit Kumar Sarder and PW 4 did not say anything about any settlement. The statement as made by PWs 1 and 2 in their deposition in respect of the cheque appears to be not there in the plaint as filed by the plaintiffs. It thus appears that the learned Subordinate Judge did not at all discuss what the PWs have individually stated in their deposition nor did he consider the evidence correctly or properly. It further appears that the learned Subordinate Judge did not read the plaint and the depositions of the PWs at all.

11. It next appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has stated in his judgment that although no dakhila or Amolnama has been filed by the plaintiffs to substantiate the settlement of Hamid but they have filed the certified copy of Rent suit marked as Ext 5 which shows that Jonab Ali filed rent Suit No. 826 of 1956 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Satkhira against Abul Hamid admitting him as a tenant for realization of arrear rent in respect of the suit land and apart from this it appears from Ext. 9 that defendant Md Aminul Islam, son of Jonab Ali filed Misc. Case No. 32 of 1981-82 in the court of Circle Officer (Rev.) Assassin admitting settlement of the suit land in favour of Hamid and from Ext. 7, a written statement filed by father of defendant No. 2 Abdus Sattar in Title Suit No. 312 of 1980 also stated about the settlement of the suit land in favour of Abdul Hamid and that Ext 6 shows that Sahiluddin Sarder, father of defendant No. 2 and Saleha Khatun, mother of defendant No. 1 Aminul Islam filed Title Suit No. 321 of 1976 in the court of Sub-Judge, Khulna against the heirs of Jonab Ali and others. From this the learned Subordinate Judge has drawn the conclusion that all these papers will go to show that Jonab Ali made a settlement of the suit land in favour of Hamid.

<u>12. It appears that all these papers have been stated in the plaint but that the defendants have categorically denied that they have not filed any such suit or written statement as stated in the plaint and that the defendants have also denied all these papers in their deposition. But it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge did not discuss a single word of the denial of the defendants in respect of these pieces of papers which are not relevant papers in this suit nor did he come to any finding in respect of defendants denial. From this manner of conclusion as made by the learned Subordinate Judge, it appears that he has also found that there is no cheque or any Amolnama in support of the plaintiffs' claim of settlement made by Jonab Ali in favour of Hamid but it appears that he has drawn a conclusion on some papers of different cases which apparently appears to be some creation made by the plaintiffs for using it in this suit. The learned Subordinate Judge in the absence of any direct evidence of plaintiffs' claim of settlement appears to have drawn a conclusion by analytical deduction and not by evidence. This conclusion as arrived at by the learned Subordinate Judge being not based on proper discussion nor of correct appreciation of facts and evidence of the case is, in our opinion, not sustainable in law.</u>

13. The learned Subordinate Judge did not consider the fact that the alleged settlement in favour of Abdul Hamid was allegedly made in Baishakh, 1355 BS. But it appears from Ext 5 that only after 4 years of the alleged settlement the father-in-law allegedly filed a suit against his own son-in-law for arrear rent of Taka 219 only. The father-in-law could easily make a compromise with his son-in-law for this small amount of Taka 219 only or could forego the matter without going to court. The question of filing a rent suit for a small amount of alleged rent against his own son-in-law whose family admittedly used to reside in the house of this Jonab Ali Sarder until the sale of the suit land in 1982 to the plaintiffs, did not normally arise. It is also in the evidence that Jonab Ali used to look after Hamid's family and his properties. In that view of the matter also, the question of filing rent suit by Jonab Ali against his such son-in-law does not arise. The judgment or any order of the said rent suit has not also been filed. We therefore cannot understand how the learned Subordinate Judge could make a decision in respect of the root of the plaintiffs'' suit by some analogy on the basis of some extraneous papers not connected with alleged settlement.

14. Mr. Habibul Alam, the learned Advocate, next argued that the possession of the suit land by the plaintiffs or by Abdul Hamid has not been proved by any evidence. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has stated in his judgment that the PWs 2, 3 and 4 have made corroborative statement about the right, title and possession of Abdul Hamid and his heirs and of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land. But it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has not stated what the PWs have individually stated in support of plaintiffs' claim of title and possession. Without discussing the specific statements made by the PWs, it cannot be said that there are corroboration. We, on our part, have perused the evidence of PWs as is there in the record and it appears that the plaintiffs' father, Fazlur Rahman as PW 1 has said in his deposition that after settlement, Abdul Hamid possessed the suit land. But he said in his cross-examination that in the first year of Hamid's settlement, Shahar Ali, Faiz Mistry and others barga-cultivated the suit land under Hamid but at a little later, this PW 1 further said that in the first year one Hamid of Durgapur barga-cultivated for 5/6 years. This is a clear contradictory statement made by PW 1 in respect of possession of the suit land. Again he said that the bargaders deposited the barga crops in the house of Jonab Ali Sarder. Thus it appears that Jonab Ali Sarder was still then in the possession even after the alleged settlement.

15. PW 2 Ibrahim Gazi said in his deposition that Fazlu Mia used to barga-cultivate the land on behalf of Hamid and thereafter he is now cultivating the land as his own. But it appears Fazlu Mia (PW 1 plaintiff's father) did not say that he barga-cultivated the suit land under Hamid. PW 3 Ranjit Kumar Sarder said that Fazlu Mia cultivated the suit land for 9/10 years as bargader of son-in-law of Jonab Ali and before that Jonab Ali himself used to cultivate the suit land through his own man. He further said in his cross-examination that when he first came to know about the suit land, he has seen the people of Jonab Ali to cultivate the suit land PW 4 said in his deposition that Fazlu Mia has been possessing the suit land since last 10/11 years and before him Jonab Ali used to cultivate the suit land. This PW deposed before the court in 1984. If we go back to 10/11 years of 1984 it will come of 1973 and thus from this statement alone, it appears that Jonab Ali used to cultivate the suit land upto 1973. So the question of Hamid's taking settlement from jonab Ali Sarder in 1984 corresponding to 1355 BS does not stand. From the statements as made by all 4 PWs, it appears that there is much contradiction in their statement in respect of possession of the suit land. We find from the evidence that Jonab Ali Sarder was in the scene of the suit land. The learned Subordinate Judge failed to discuss the evidence of the case in its true perspective. We are therefore, of the opinion that the findings arrived at by the learned Subordinate Judge in respect of possession of the suit land is not based on proper consideration or correct analysis of the evidence adduced by the PWs.

<u>16. It next appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has stated in his judgment that the plaintiffs have submitted a statement of property showing the suit land as their own land under President's Order No. 96 of 1972 whereas the defendant No. 1 did not submit any statement including the suit land as has been found by him from the information slip, Ext.11 and 11(I) filed by the plaintiffs. The learned Subordinate Judge observed that had the defendants any right, title, interest or possession in the suit land, they would, have definitely submitted a statement to the government under President's Order No. 96 of 1972 showing the suit land as their own land. It appears that this conclusion of the learned Subordinate Judge is based on a negative approach made by him. An information slip or the submission or non-submission of property statement can never go to any conclusion in respect of title of the suit land. This again appears to be an analytical conclusion made by the learned Subordinate Judge not based on any cogent evidence of the subject in dispute.</u>

17. Admittedly, the suit land originally belonged to Jonab Ali Sarder. The plaintiffs' only case is a case of settlement in favour of Abdul Hamid. We have discussed above all the evidence and facts and circumstances of the case and we find that there is no cheque or Amolnama to show such settlement in favour of Abdul Hamid and that the statements as made by the PWs in support of such a settlement is quite opposite to each other and also contradictory to the averment as made in the plaint about the settlement. The plaintiffs'' claim is that they have purchased the suit land from the heirs of Abdul Hamid by 5 kabalas which are Ext. 1.1 (a)1(b), 1(c) and 1(d) allegedly executed by Jahura, Bakibillah and Moniruzzaman. The learned Subordinate Judge has stated in his judgment that the executants have not come to challenge these documents and so he did not find anything to disbelieve the kabalas, Ext 1 -1(d). But the fact remains that the executants are not the party to this case. So the question of their coming to deny these kabala does not arise. This is again a negative conclusion made by the learned Subordinate Judge without looking to the face of the kabalas. Some sellers having no saleable interest in the suit land are not expected to come to the court to deny their kabalas.

<u>18. It appears that these kabalas are dated 9-3-82 and 10-3-1982. It appears that immediately after the kabalas of 9-3-82 and 10-3-82, the plaintiffs have instituted the suit on 10-6-82. It is not stated what happened to the plaintiffs during this short period of 3 months after their purchase. A simple statement has been made in the plaint that the defendants threatened to cut earth from the suit land on 13-6-82. It is not stated whether actually any earth has been taken away by the defendant from the suit land. An alleged threat of taking earth from the suit land can never be a cause of action to file a suit for declaration of title. Not a single evidence is available to show that the defendants made any threat to take earth from the suit land. We find that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their alleged cause of action for this suit. The plaintiffs filed the suit after 3 months of their alleged purchase. In the facts and circumstances of the case as discussed above, it appears that the plaintiffs have not purchased the land but that they have purchased a litigation only. There is no cause of action at all for filing this suit.</u>

<u>19. It appears that there is an issue framed by the learned Subordinate Judge vides issue No. 2 to see whether the suit is properly valued and duly stamped. But by a perusal of the judgment passed by Subordinate Judge, we do not find any decision in respect of that issue. He has simply stated that after the amendment of the plaint, the plaintiff has paid ad valorem court fee and so the question of maintainability of the suit is redundant. Then he stated that in consideration of the evidence on record, it appears that the suit is properly valued and duly stamped. Thus it appears that there is a decision but that decision is not based on discussion of any facts and evidence in respect of the valuation of the suit land. The suit land is admittedly 82 bighas of land but that the learned Subordinate Judge did not come to any finding as to how much would be the proper value of this 82 bighas of land and whether the plaintiffs have correctly valued the suit land. Thus it appears that the matter of valuation of the suit land is not properly decided.</u>

<u>20. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge did not discuss the evidence of any of the DWs nor did he narrate the case of the defendants. He has, however, stated that the defendants' case is a case of taking settlement of the suit land from Jonab Ali through their maternal grand-fathers but that the learned Subordinate Judge has come to the conclusion that this is a subsequent creation. But it is not stated how it could be a subsequent creation. The learned Subordinate judge did not discuss the defendant’s case or the evidence of the DWs. It is the settled principle of law that the plaintiff is to prove his case without depending on the weakness of the defendant’s case. If the settlement of the defendants is not proved still then the fact remains that the defendants are the sons of Jonab Ali Sarder, the admitted owner of the suit land. The defendants will inherit the suit land as heirs of Jonab Ali Sarder. The PWs have said that Jahura being the daughter of Jonab Ali Sarder has inherited 9 bighas of the land in the suit land. Thus it appears that Jonab Ali's heirs will inherit the suit land. The defendants are also admittedly the heirs of Jonab Ali Sarder. The defendants are not to prove anything. It is the plaintiffs who are to prove their case without any doubt.</u>

21. Considering all the facts, circumstances and the evidence of the case as discussed above and as in the record, we find that the plaintiffs have totally failed to prove their case of settlement in favour of Abdul Hamid from Jonab Ali and that the plaintiffs have also failed to prove their case of title and possession of the suit land. In view of all the above facts and circumstances, we are of the opinion that the learned Subordinate Judge is not justified in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. In such view of the matter, we find that the appeal succeeds.

In the result, the appeal is allowed with costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and the plaintiffs' suit is dismissed with costs.

End.

caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 173 of 1996 with Civil Rule No. 300 (FM) of 1996.
lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Rokanuddin Mahmud. Faisal Mahmud Faizee and Mobina Asaf Rahmann, Advocates — For the Appellants. 
Amirul Islam with Ms. Tania Amir, Shamsul Alam, Advocates — For Respondents.
parties:
Lawrence Loat Ltd and others  ----- Appellants
VS.
AJAX Incorporated and Siltrade International Ltd -----  Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md. Sirajul Islam J: This First Misc. Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 28-10-96 passed by Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Bagerhat in Money Suit No. 3 of 1996 attaching before judgment the vessel of the defendant No. 1 appellant "MV Gold Spring" and directing the defendant to discharge the cargo at Mongla Port in the name of plaintiff-respondent Nos.1 and 2.

2. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 AJAX Incorporated and Siltrade International Ltd as plaintiffs instituted Money Suit No. 3 of 1996 against the defendant No. 1 Lawrence Loat Ltd. and others in Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court Bagerhat for recovery of possession of the cargo of 8800 metrictons cement clinker and for recovery of US$ 4,103,500.00 an amount equivalent to Taka 17,4934,336.50.00 as damage. The case of the plaintiffs is that, the plaintiff-company is a registered company in Pusan, Korea and has been doing the business of international trade, inter alia, buying cement clinker from China and supplying the same to Bangladesh. That the defendant Lawrence Loat Ltd. are the owners of the vessel MV Gold Spring registered under Belige Flag 1772 built as described in the plaint. That the plaintiff had an ongoing renewal business relationship with Meghna Cement Ltd. by a contract No. 001/96 dated 3-7-96 to supply cement clinker upto 28(X)0 metric tons for a full one year period beginning from September, 1996, the first shipment to commence within 30 days after receipt of L/C. Accordingly, the order for first shimpment was placed by Meghna Cement Ltd. to the plaintiffs for supply of 20,000.00 metric tons to effect the delivery of the same in the month of September-October, 1996. It was agreed upon between the parties that initially a L/C would be opened by Meghna Cement for phasing out shipment by instalment of 11,000.00 metric tons each on C & F basis. Accordingly, Meghna Cement Mills Ltd. opened L/C through plaintiff No. 2 in favour of plaintiff No. 1 on 14-7-1996 to supply 11000 metric tons of Cement Clinker at US$ 52.50 per ton.

3. Thereafter on 23-8-1996 the plaintiff No. 1 has entered into a charter party agreement with the defendants by way of signing a fixture note for carriage of cargo by MV Gold Spring from Laushan Rot, China and to discharge the same at buyers (Meghna Cement Mills) Jetty Berth, Mongla Port, Bangladesh with the arrival date on or before 30-9-1996. Accordingly, a Bill of Lading was issued stating that the freight was prepared as arranged and defendant agreed to demand such payment only after delivery of the goods as per C&F terms. Thereafter plaintiffs paid 20,000.00 US dollars as part payment of the freight towards the total cost on 14-10-96. That on 30-9-1996 the last day within which the ship should have arrived at Mongla Port at buyers Jetty, the defendant sent a fax to the plaintiff alleging that the vessel was not fit as two exhaust pipes on the main engine were broken which would take some time to repair. The defendant on 21-10-96 demanded the full payment of freight even before the arrival of the ship. The plaintiff in reply communicated to the defendants that full payment was not possible unless the vessel physically takes berth. That finally the vessel arrived at Mongla Port on 24-10-1996 and informed the plaintiff of its arrival and that it was ready to discharge its cargo. But thereafter the defendants in a cunning device started claiming payment of full freight and insisted upon signing a disclaimer agreement. All this has caused a loss of a big amount of money to the plaintiff as stated in the schedule to the plaint. Hence the plaintiff filed the suit on 28-10-96 for recovery of money and for recovery of possession of the cargo.

4. After filing of the suit, the plaintiff's filed two separate applications, one under Order 38 rule 5. CPC for attachment before judgment of the vessel MV Gold Spring and the other under Order 39 rule 1 CPC for a temporary injunction against the defendants directing them not to remove the vessel from the jurisdiction of the court and for further direction to discharge the entire cargo of clinker as per Bill of Lading. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the learned Advocate for the plaintiff passed an order directing the defendants to show cause as to why they shall not be asked to furnish security and in the meantime has attached the vessel in question MV Gold Spring until further order. The learned Subordinate Judge on the application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 CPC passed another direction in the same order upon the defendants 1-3 to discharge the cargo at Mongla Port in the name of the plaintiffs vide his order dated 28-10-96

5. Being aggrieved by this order dated 28-10-96, the defendant No. 1 Lawrence Loat Ltd. as appellant has filed this First Misc. Appeal No. 173 of 19% in this court.

6. It appears that the impugned order dated 28-10-96 has two parts, one part of the order is under Order 28 rule 5 CPC and the other part of the order is under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 CPC. Since both the parts of the order have been impugned in this appeal, we propose to deal with the matter one after another. We are therefore taking up the first part of the order for discussion.

7. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the defendant appellant, have firstly given a synopsis of the palintiff's case and then started to make their submission challenging firstly, the validity of the first part of the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that the attachment of a vessel is a matter of extraordinary jurisdiction of a court which must be exercised continuously and sparingly. He submits that the plaintiffs must show that there is an attempt to remove the property or the vessel with a definite intention to defeat the decree that may be passed in favour of the plaintiff in the suit and that the show cause as may be issued by the court must be a meaningful and effective show cause clearly specifying the amount of security as per provisions of rule 5 of the Order 38 CPC. The learned Advocate said that there must be a clear prayer also in the application for attachment under Order 38 rule 5 CPC. Then the learned Advocate drew our attention to the application filed by the plaintiff under Order 38 rule 5 CPC and said that there is no definite statement in the application or in the plaint about any attempt made by the defendants to remove the vessel out of the Port Jetty.

8. Mr. Amir-ul-Islam with Ms. Tania Amir, the learned Advocate, has, on the other hand, submitted that the application filed by the plaintiffs under Order 38 rule 5 CPC follows the plaint of the suit and that the application does not require to contain all the statements as made in the plaint. He submits that the plaint has contained all the facts and circumstances of the matter leading to the filing of the suit and that the application for attachment is to be read with the plaint. He further submits that the plaintiff's application has also stated the facts and circumstances of the matter with the prayer for attachment of the vessel.

9. We have gone through the copy of the plaint and the application for attachment under Order 38 rule 5 CPC as produced in this court by the appellant. It appears that the plaint contains the statement as to how the plaintiffs entered into the contract with the buyers for supply of the cement clinkers in question and how the plaintiff entered into the chartered party agreement with the defendant for carrying the cement clinkers from the port of China to the Mongla Port at buyers jetty. There is a statement made in the plaint that on 30-9-1996 the defendant sent a fax to the plaintiff informing them that the vessel had developed a fault in two exhaust pipes and there will be some delay in arrival at the port of destination. Then it has been stated that ultimately on 24-10-96 the vessel arrived at Mongla Port and informed the plaintiffs that it is now ready for discharge of the cargo and requested the plaintiffs to make arrangement for taking delivery of the same. We do not find anything wrong with the defendants as far as this statement is concerned. Then it has been stated the defendants were insisting on getting payment of the freight and on signing disclaimer agreement and upon these matters there were some correspondence between them and thus the plaintiffs suffered loss due to such circumstances. This is strictly a matter to be decided in the main suit by evidence. But we do not find any clear statement in the plaint as to when and how the ship made any attempt to leave the port at any point of time.

10. The same statement has been made in the application under Order 38 rule 5 CPC. By a reading of the copy of the application we do not find any specific statement of any attempt made by the defendant to remove the vessel from the port except a statement made in paragraph 28 in the application to the effect "that the plaintiff is now threatened that the defendants would remove the vessel in order to avoid the claim or decree that may be passed in favour of the plaintiff." But it is not stated as to when, how and where and by whom the plaintiff was threatened that the defendants would remove the vessel. It appears that it is simply a general and a vague allegation made in the application and also in the plaint so far as the threatening is concerned. The ship arrived in the Mongla Port on 24-10-96 and duly informed the plaintiffs about its arrival and readiness to discharge the cargo and requested the plaintiff to make payment of the freight. The suit was filed on 28-10-96 only after 3 days. Then where was the time for the ship to run away from the port. The cargo was booked for the Buyer, Meghna Cement Ltd. The Buyer was to receive the goods. But he is not coming to the scene as a party to say anything in respect of ship's movement.

11. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Advocate, referred to a number of decisions in support of his contention that the application must contain clear and specific averments with concrete allegations in respect of any attempt or act done by the vessel for its removal. He has referred to the case of Md. Shamsul Huda vs. Mozammel Huq and others reported in 27 DLR 256. It has been laid down therein that :

"The power which has been conferred on the court under the provision of Order XXXVIII Rule 5 CPC is an extraordinary power whereby a party in the suit may be prevented from use and enjoyment of his own properties, before any decree has at all been passed against him, and when there is no certainty that a decree will at all be passed against him. This power, must, therefore, be used with utmost caution and should be sparingly exercised. It is clear that before issuing an order under the said provisions of the Code, the court must be satisfied that the defendant has been trying to frustrate the effect of the decree that may be passed against him by disposing of his property or removing it from the jurisdiction of the court. That is to say, the court must be satisfied not only that the defendant is about to dispose of his property or remove it from its jurisdiction but also that this disposal or removal is with the object of obstructing or delaying the execution of any decree that may be passed against him. This satisfaction. however, is to be judicial satisfaction and it must be based on some materials, which are to be found in the affidavit filed by the party or otherwise. It is true that an order of attachment under this provision is to be passed on the basis of an application made by the plaintiff and an order of conditional attachment may be passed even ex parte. It is, of couse, to be borne in mind that it is difficult to produce any conclusive evidence before the court to prove the intention of a party which is secretly conceived and sought to be surreptitiously executed but even then, there must be some concrete allegations before the court about the actions of the defendant and some materials in support thereof. Otherwise, this provision of law is likely to be turned into an instrument of oppression and great harassment."

12. The learned Advocate referred to another decision in the case of Messrs United Venture Navigation Co Ltd vs. Samudrajatra Shipping Line Ltd reported in 28 DLR 231 wherein it has been held that :

"The court shall have to be satisfied not only that the defendant is trying to dispose of certain property or remove certain property from the jurisdiction of the Court but also that he has been doing so with an intention to obstruct or delay the execution of the decree which may be passed against him."

13. It has been further observed therein that even if the apprehension of the plaintiffs is well-based such kind of difficulty is not a sufficient ground for taking recourse to the provision of Order 38 rules 5 and 6 when the said provision makes it quite clear that it should be invoked only when the removal of the certain property is sought to be made with an intent to obstruct or delay the execution of a prospective decree which may be passed against the defendants."

14. In the case of Unimarine SA Panama through Local Agent Bengal Shipping Line Ltd and another vs. Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR (AD) 112, it has been observed by their Lordships as under :

"The court is to insist upon the proof of the allegation in the petition for attachment before judgment by affidavit or other mode of proof and the opposite party must be served with notice and given an opportunity to show cause."

15. The party imputing the motive on the defendant must be ready with the evidence to satisfy the court, if called upon to do so. Vague or general allegations without any materials are insufficient to invoke the power of the court under this provision.

<u>16. From the principles as laid down in the above cited decisions it appears that for the purpose of invoking the power under Order 38 rule 5 CPC for attachment before judgment there must be some concrete allegations in the application made before the court with sufficient materials of evidence to satisfy the court that the defendants have been doing an act for removing certain property or the vessel in question from the jurisdiction of the court with an intention to delay or obstruct the execution of the decree that may be passed against the defendants. In the instant case we have already stated above that the plaint or the applications under Order 38 rule 5 CPC filed before the court did not contain any concrete allegation with sufficient materials to satisfy the court that the defendants have been doing any act of removal of the vessel from court's jurisdiction with intent to obstruct or defeat the decree that may be passed in favour of the plaintiff. The statement of allegation of threat or removal of the vessel as made in para 28 of the application, in our opinion, are some 'vague' and 'general' allegations without giving any material in support thereof.</u>

17. In this respect Mr. Amir-ul-Islam, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent, drew our attention to Annexure-14 and 18 filed with their affidavit-in-opposition in the Rule and said that the defendant by these two letters dated 21-10-96 and 22-10-96 respectively informed the plaintiff that the payment of their freight is already 17 days over-due and unless they receive the freight immediately they will have to consider advising the vessel to anchor outside the Port limit. The learned Advocate wanted to say that this is the threat made by the defendants to the plaintiff. But the fact remains that these are some correspondence made by the defendants to the plaintiff requesting them to make payment of their over-due freight charge and more so, these correspondence were made prior to the arrival of the vessel and of filing of the suit when there was no thinking of any suit in the mind of the defendants. Moreover, it appears from the plaint itself that the vessel has duly arrived in Mongla Port on 24-10-96 after these letters were issued and was ready for release of the goods. Thus it appears that these letters did not contain any threat to remove the vessel and no act has been done to remove the vessel thereafter. Therefore, these letters do not make a case of threat or act of the defendants to remove the vessel from the port. In the facts and circumstances, we do not find any ground for attaching the vessel.

18. The next question arises as to whether the foreign ship can be attached before judgment under Order 38 rule 5 CPC as ordered by the learned Subordinate Judge. We have already stated above that the plaint or the application for attachment did not contain sufficient material or ingredients for granting an ad-interim order of attachment. We have further found above that there is no sufficient or specific allegations made in the application for the purpose of satisfying the court to pass such an ad-interim order of attachment before judgment. We also found above that only a 'vague' and 'general' allegation of threat without any action of removal of the vessel has been made in the application.

19. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Advocate, submits that the court ordinarily should not attach a foreign vessel in normal course of business. In support of this contention the learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of United Venture Navigation Co Ltd vs. Samudrajatra Shipping Line Ltd reported in 28 DLR 231 as cited above for other matter. It has been observed therein that:

"It is extremely doubtful if the provisions of Order 38 have any application in the case of a defendant who does not usually reside, or whose property is not normally situated, within the jurisdiction of the Court concerned. The terms of rule 1 and rule 5 of the Order are sufficiently clear to indicate that the defendant or the defendant's property, as is contemplated in the said rules, is such as does usually live or lie within the jurisdiction of the Court. The obligation of the defendant to attend the Court or produce the property in question in Court, as and whenever directed by the Court is inconsistent with the case of a defendant, who is a foreign national and lives abroad, or whose property does not usually lie within the jurisdiction of the Court. The rule contemplated such property as may be "produced in court whenever the defendant may be asked to do so. The presence of and production of a certain property by such a defendant within the jurisdiction of the court being dependant upon the will of another sovereign state whose national the defendant is, the provisions of this Order appear to be hardly applicable."

20. In this respect a reference may be made to the case of Unimarine SA Panama vs. Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR (AD) 112 as already discussed above on other ground wherein it has been observed by their Lordships as under:

"A foreign ship which is calling at international ports on her usual voyage, it comes within the jurisdiction of the court shall not ordinarily be treated as a moveable property within the jurisdiction of the court liable to attachment before judgment, unless there are other facts and compelling reasons calling for an action under this rule, apart from other question of jurisdiction."

21. From the observations as made by their Lordships in the above cited two cases, it will appear that in normal course of business a foreign ship should not be attached unless there are compelling facts and circumstances for such an action.

22. Mr. Amir-ul-Islam, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents, submits that the statement of facts as made in the plaint and in the application for attachment filed by the plaintiff taken together will show that there are sufficient facts and compelling reasons for the purpose of invoking this provision to justify an order for ad-interim attachment.

23. But we have already discussed and found above that there is no clear or specific allegation of any attempt of the defendants to remove the vessel nor any act done by them to that effect in the plaint or in the application supported by sufficient materials for satisfying the court. Therefore, we are unable to accept this contention as put forward by Mr. Amirul Islam in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

24. Mr. Amirul Islam futher submits that if the ship in question is allowed to leave the Mongla Port, there will be no remedy left for plaintiff to get relief of his probable decree as may be passed in favour of the plaintiff and this is again a ground for making an order of ad-interim attachment of the ship in question. But we are unable to accept this proposition of the learned Advocate in view of the following observations as made by their Lordships in the case of Messrs United Venture Navigation Co Ltd vs. Shamudrajatra Shipping Line Ltd reported in 28 DLR 231 as referred to above which runs of follows :

"It has been submitted that if the ship which is alleged to be belonging to the defendants is allowed to leave the port of Chittagong the plaintiffs would have no other assets to fall upon for the recovery of the money which may be decreed in their favour. We do not think that the plaintiffs will be without any remedy in respect of any transactions involving foreign companies. This kind of difficulty is likely to arise in many cases. But even then the Private international law recognises remedies which may be taken recourse to in an appropriate case in order to enforce the judgment which may be passed in the suit. But even if the apprehension of the plaintiffs is well based, such kind of difficulty, in our opinion, is not sufficient ground for taking recourse to the provision of Order 38 rules 5 and 6 when the said provision makes it quite clear that it should be invoked only when the removal of the certain property is sought to be made with an intent to obstruct or delay the execution of prospective decree which may be passed against the defendants."

In the facts and circumstances of the instant case and in view of the principles as laid down in the decisions cited above and in view of the fact that there is no concrete allegation with supporting materials as found above we find that there are no compelling facts and circumstances for the purpose of attaching the defendant's ship in question before judgment and accordingly, we find that the learned Subordinate Judge is not justified in passing the ad interim order of attachment before judgment which is the first part of the impugned order.

25. Coming back to the second part of the impugned order it appears that by this part of the order the learned Subordinate Judge has directed the defendant Nos. 1-3 to discharge the cargo at Mongla Port in the name of the plaintiffs without delay. From the nature of the order it appears to be an ad-interim mandatory order of injunction.

<u>26. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant, seriously challenged this part of the order stating that the Order 39 rules 1 and 2 CPC has specifically provided that the court shall in all cases, before granting an injunction, direct notice of the application for the same to be given to the opposite party, but that here in this case the learned Subordinate Judge did not issue any notice for the defendants to show cause and thus the impugned order, to that extent, has been passed without giving the defendants any opportunity to show cause which is a right given by law to the defendants. It appears from rule 3 of Order 39 that there is a mandatory provision set out in this rule for issuing show cause to the defendant before granting an injunction. But here in this case, the learned Subordinate Judge did not pass any order to issue show cause notice upon defendant. So this part of the order apparently appears to be an order not in conformity with the provision of Order 39 rules 1 and 2 in respect of issuance of a temporary injunction.</u>

<u>27. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate submits that it was an ad-interim order and as such, the show cause notice was not a must before issuing the order. But there is a mandatory provisions in rule 3 of Order 39 CPC that before granting any injunction the court shall direct notice of the application to be given to the opposite party. Therefore, an ad-interim injunction can only be granted simultaneously with the issuance of show cause notice in a case where the property in question is in imminent danger of being wasted or alienated by any party. There was no danger of any alienation of the property in this case. The ad-interim order of injunction passed by the learned Subordinate Judge without being followed by any show cause notice has been passed against the provision of law.</u>

28. By a reading of the application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 CPC filed in court by the plaintiff, it appears that the plaintiffs have prayed for a temporary injunction for restraining the defendants from removing the vessel from the jurisdiction of the court and to issue a show cause notice as to why temporary injunction should not be granted. Thus it appears that there was a prayer in the application itself for issuing show cause notice. But it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge did not look to this prayer. It has been again prayed in the same prayer portion by the plaintiffs that the defendants be directed to bring the vessel MV Gold Spring to the buyer's Jetty Meghna Cement and to discharge the entire cargo as per Bill of Lading dated 14-9-96. These three kinds of prayer at a time in an application for temporary injunction are not the contemplation of Order 39 rules 1 and 2 CPC. From the portion of the plaint, it appears that the plaintiff has prayed for a decree for recovery of possession of cargo 8800 metric tons of cement clinker and for realisation of US Dollar as mentioned therein. So, the impugned order as passed by the learned Subordinate Judge directing the defendants to discharge the entire cargo in the name of the plaintiff is in effect a decree for recovery of possession of the whole charge 8800 metric tons of cement clinker. Thus it appears that this order has given full relief to the plaintiff before trial of the suit without evidence to see as to who was owner of the goods.

29. In view of the above facts and circumstances of the case, we find that the impugned order of ad-interim mandatory injunction passed by the learned Subordinate Judge has been passed contrary to the provisions of law and also to the factual position of the matter and, as such, we are of the opinion that this part of the impugned order is also not sustainable in law.

30. A reference may be made to a case of Md. Shid Ali vs. Province of East Pakistan and ors reported in 22 DLR 694 wherein it has been observed that "an order of a mandatory injunction in ad-interim form is issued by a court only when there is an imminent grave danger to life or property and only for the purpose of restoring or maintaining a status quo and not granted to establish a new state of things differing from the state which existed at the date when the suit was instituted". In the instant case when the suit was instituted it was a question of removal or not removal of the ship and that the cement clinker were there within the ship and the relief sought for in the suit was for recovery of the same which was a matter for decision in the suit after trial. So the order of ad-interim mandatory injunction as passed by the learned Subordinate Judge has clearly established a new state of thing different from the thing which was in existence at the time of filing of the suit. In this view of the matter also we find that the second part of the impugned order relating to mandatory injunction is not sustainable in law.

31. We have already stated above that the first part of the order is not in confirmity with the provision of law and that there was no compelling facts and circumstances for the purpose of attaching the ship. Accordingly, we find that the learned Subordinate Judge is not justified in passing the impugned order.

32. We may, however, make an observation here that since admittedly the freight has not been paid to the ship owner and that the ship arrived at Mongla Port as per statement made in para 23 of the plaint itself, hence we do not find any difficulty for the parties to sort out their problem of paying the freight charge and of getting the cargo discharged from the ship in accordance with law. We may further direct the learned Subordinate Judge to dispose of the suit as expeditiously as possible.

33. For all the reasons stated above, this appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Bagerhat in Money Suit No. 3 of 1996 dated 28-10-96 are hereby set aside.

In view of the disposal of the appeal, the connected Rule being Civil Rule No. 300 (FM) of 1996 becoming infructuous is hereby discharged.

End.

Md Munsurul Hoque Chowdhury, AJ Mohammad Ali and Ashoke Kumar Paul, Advocates—For the Opposite Parties.

full_judgment:
Destiny of Civil Revision Case hinges on answer to following probes:

i. Whether decision recorded by Court of first instance and maintained by Court of Appeal in not restoring Title Suit to its file and number on allowing Miscellaneous Case laid under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure (for short the Code) is well grounded and well founded

And

ii. Whether adjudication rendered by the Courts below warrants any interference by this Court in exercise of Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged in section 115 of the Code.

2. In broaching and riposting to questions posed, factual matrix, evidences adduced from both sides, materials on record and fact and circumstances may conveniently be taken into account. Legal aspect touching the controversy is, also, required to be ruminated.

3. A detailed recounting of factual scenario is not essential and only those which shed light in resolving war of words are being taken heed of.

4. (a) Rita Bimala Purification, predecessor-in-interest of first-fourth-opposite parties as plaintiffs on 7-4-1981 instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 434 of 1981 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka for a decree of partition in respect of A and B property described in schedule to plaint imp leading Kiron Purification and others as defendants. Suit was transferred to some other Courts and lastly, to Joint District Judge and Arbitration Court and there Suit was numbered as Title Suit No. 25 of 2002. Plaintiff Rita Bimala Purification died on 3-1-1999 and on her death present first-fourth opposite parties have been substituted as Plaintiff Nos. 1(Ka)-1 (gaha).

(b) Rahimullah Chowdhury, predecessor -in-interest of present petitioners and Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, predecessor-in-interest of twenty-seven-thirty-four opposite parties had been eighteenth and nineteenth defendants in the Suit. Eighteenth and nineteenth defendants on 26-1-1982 presented a joint written statements traversing material allegations put forth in plaint.

(c) Eighteenth defendant drew his last on 28-12-1985 and his heirs had been substituted as defendant Nos. 18(ka)-18(gaha) who are petitioners. Order No. 50 dated 8-8-1989 indicates that summons upon substituted defendant Nos. 18(ka)-18(gaha) had been served. Nineteenth defendant, also, breathed his last and heirs had been substituted as defendant Nos. 19(ka)-19(Ja) and order dated 7-10-1992 demonstrates that summons upon substituted defendants 19(kha)-19(Ja) had been served.

(d) Good number of dates had been set down for peremptory hearing but peremptory hearing could not be held. Fifth defendant and sixth defendant submitted written statement and contested the suit. Ultimately on 25-8=1999 Suit was taken up for peremptory hearing and on that date evidence of plaintiff 1(ka) had been recorded in part.

(e) On 29-11-1999 Suit was decreed exparte on contest against fifth defendant and ex parte against other defendants including defendant No. 1(ka)-1(gaha) and defendants Nos. 19(ka)-19(Ja). Preliminary Decree was drawn and signed on 30-11-1999. On the prayer of decree-holder plaintiffs-opposite parties, an Advocate Commissioner was appointed for effecting partition on holding local investigation and survey on the property. Leaned Advocate Commissioner on 28-5-2000 submitted Report. Sixteenth defendant on executing Vokalatnama entered appearance in the Suit and sought time for laying an objection. Fifth defendant, also, bestowed a petition seeking time for filing written objection.

(f) Fifth defendant having been dead his heirs had been substituted as defendant Nos. 5(ka)-5(ga).

(g) Sixth defendant on entering appearance prayed for a saham in respect of his share.

(h) Preliminary Decree had been made final and final decree had been drawn on 16-8-2004. A separate saham had been granted to substituted defendants Nos. 5(ka)-5(ga) and, also to substituted defendants Nos. 7(ka)-7(kha). Decree Execution Case No. 2 of 2005 had been laid by decree holder plaintiffs-opposite parties for getting possession of partitioned land. Plaintiffs-opposite parties got possession of decreed property on 24-5-2005 and defendant Nos. 5(ka)-5(ga) and 7(ka)-7(kha) got possession of their saham property on 26-5-2005.

5. Defendants-petitioners, thereafter, laid a petition under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code for restoration of suit to its file and number on setting aside ex parte preliminary decree dated 29-11-1999 canvassing basic contentions:

(i) No summons had been served upon substituted heirs of eighteenth defendant and decree-holder plaintiff in collusion with process server managed fraudulent service of summons and signature of service on summons has been illegible and defendants-petitioners did not authorize anybody to receive summons.

(ii) Suit had been transferred from one Court of Subordinate Judge to other Court of Subordinate Judge and no notice of transfer had been served upon defendants-petitioners.

(iii) Defendants-petitioners for the first time on 24-5-2005 became aware of exported preliminary decree when Advocate Commissioner landed on the land to execute order recorded in Title Execution Case No. 2 of 2005. Petition under Order IX, rule 13 had been numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 2005.

6. Plaintiffs-opposite parties and other, defendants-opposite parties put up resistance to Miscellaneous Case on presentation of three sets of written objections taking stand which are as hereunder:

a. Eighteenth and nineteenth defendants filed joint written statement on 26-1-1982. Eighteenth defendant having been dead his heirs stood substituted as defendant Nos. 18(ka)-18(ghha). Summons upon substituted defendant No. 18(ka) 18(gaha) had been served as evidenced from order No. 58 dated 8-8-1989. Plaintiffs-opposite parties obtained ex parte Preliminary Decree on 19-11-1999 and Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code had been filed on 4-6-2005 i.e. after a period of five years six months and five days.

7. Learned Advocate Commissioner grated saham to substituted heirs of fifth defendant on 28-5-2003. Heirs of seventh defendant had been, also, granted saham by Advocate Commissioner and report to that effect had been submitted. Decree holder plaintiffs-opposite parties, thereafter, filed Title Execution Case No. 2 of 2005 and got possession of their saham property on 24-5-2005. Defendants-petitioners had been all well aware of all proceedings of Suit and Execution case.

8. Defendants-petitioners examined one witness in support of case put forth in Miscellaneous Case. Defendant Third petitioner stood on witness box as PW 1. Plaintiffs-opposite parties placed on witness box five (5) witnesses to lend assurance to the case projected by them.

9. Learned Joint District Judge by Judgment dated 17-1-2006 dismissed the Miscellaneous Case.

10. Defendants-petitioners having felt resentful of above verdict of dismissal of Miscellaneous Case carried an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 26 of 2006 before learned District Judge Dhaka. Learned District Judge by Judgment dated 5-9-2006 dismissed the Miscellaneous Appeal and maintained Judgment recorded by learned Joint District Judge.

11. Feeling still dissatisfied, defendants-petitioners invoked this Court's civil provisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code on presentation of a Revision Petition. In revision petition essential statements leading to Revision Petition have been incorporated.

12. Plaintiffs-opposite parties by way of counter-affidavit controverter statements embodied in revision petition.

13. Grounds formulated and contentions pressed into service from the side of defendants-petitioners are catalogued hereunder:

(i) Suit was filed in the Court of first Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on 7-4-1981 and, thereafter, it was transferred to Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and then to Fourth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and no notices of any transfer before 29-11-1999 had ever been served upon defendants-petitioners and both the Courts below committed a serious error of law holding that petitioners had knowledge of the suit and by that error a failure of justice has been occasioned.

(ii) In Annexure-B to Civil Revision Petition there is no mention of name of anybody to receive summons for and on behalf of defendants-petitioners and none of attesting witnesses took the stand to prove service of summons upon defendants-petitioners and both Courts below misread report of summons and testimony of OPW 5 and arrived at a wrong decision in the case.

(iii) There is nothing on record to show that before 25-5-2005 defendants-petitioners had any knowledge of institution of Suit and plaintiffs-opposite parties having failed to show otherwise, Courts below committed serious error of law and facts in holding the case to be barred by limitation.

14. Contentions so raised have been hit back from side of plaintiffs-opposite parties in surging forward counter-contentions which are as follows:

(i) Summons upon the defendants-petitioners had been duly served and there had not been any fraudulent suppression of summons and defendants-petitioners had been well aware of proceeding of Suit leading to drawing up Preliminary Decree as well as the Final Decree and as well as getting saham on partitioned property and Miscellaneous Case is hopelessly barred by limitation.

(ii) There is no mandate of law that notice of transfer was required to be served upon defendants-petitioners and Court of its own motion, without serving any notice, can transfer any suit or appeal or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal. High Court Division or District Court may at any stage of proceeding transfer any Suit, Appeal or other Proceeding to any Court subordinate to it. Section 24 of the Code is pressed in aid of the said contention. Md Insan Ali vs Mir Abdus Salam 40 DLR (AD) 193, Abdur Rashid and another vs Abdul Barth and another 35 DLR AD 162, MA Wahab and another vs Abul Kalam and another 44 DLR AD 13 had been referred to from the Bar.

15. On Judicial decision it can profitably be observed that a Judicial decision is only an authority for what it actually decides. It cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to follow from it. Every Judgment must be read keeping in view particular facts proved or assumed to be proved. Generality of expression which may be found is not intended to be exposition of whole law but must be read as governed or qualified by particular facts of the case in which such expression occurs. It is not desirable nor permissible to pick out a word or sentence from a Judgment of Superior Court divorced from the context of the question under consideration and treat it to be a complete law declared by Court.

16. In the backdrop of resume of facts, evidences, materials on record and fact and circumstances of case and rival contentions pressed into service from both sides, questions posed now may be approached and answered.

17. Suit for partition was laid on 7-4-1981 Eighteenth defendant Rahimullah Chowdhury, predecessor of defendants-petitioners and nineteenth defendant Hamidul Huq Chowdhury entered appearance in Suit and presented written statement on 26-1-1982. Eighteenth defendant died on 28-12-1985 and his heirs defendants-petitioners stood substituted as defendant 18(1 ka)-18(1 gaha). Order No. 58 dated 8-8-1989 demonstrates that service of summons upon substituted heirs defendant Nos. 18(1 ka)-18 (1 gaha) i.e. defendants-petitioners, had been caused. Relevant portion of the said order is in the following terms বিবাদী ১৮(এ)-১৮(ডি) নামীয় সমনজারীঅন্তে ফেরৎ আসিয়াছে।

Annexure B to Civil Revision Petition manifests that summons upon defendant 18(ka)- 18(gaha) had been served by Process Server Md. Khabiruddin on 9-4-1989 in presence of Mokabila witnesses and defendants having not found service had been caused upon authorised agent/employee = ভারপ্রাপ্ত কার্যকারক কর্মচারী accepted summons on putting signatures on upper portion of summons. Relevant portion of Report of Process Server is extracted hereunder: সমনের লিখিত বিবাদীগণের সাকিনে যাইয়া বিবাদীগণকে হাজির পাই নাই। তৎপক্ষে তাহাদের ভারপ্রাপ্ত কার্যকারক কর্মচারীকে প্রাপ্ত হইয়া ১৮(এ)-১৮(ডি) নং নামীয় নকল সমন গ্রহণ করিয়াছেন। Process-server Md Khabiruddin made a declaration/verification that he caused service of summons in the manner stated in the return. Verification /declaration is in the following way: আমি মোঃ খবিরউদ্দিন আদালতের জনৈক জারীকারক পেয়াদা প্রকাশ করিতেছি যে, ১৯৮৯ মামলার তারিখে উক্ত মোকদ্দমার একখানি সমন/নোটিশ জারি করিবার জন্য পাইয়াছি এবং উহা আমি উপরের লিখিত মতে জারি করিয়াছি। Khabiruddin process server who caused service of summons having been dead service of summons upon defendant Nos. 18(ka) -18(gaha) had been proved by OPW 5 Md Helaluddin Khan, a process server. He standing on witness box proved hand writing of Khabiruddin and recitals in service return. OPW 5 provided version that Abdul Barik and Abdul Kader had been present when service of summons had been caused upon heirs of eighteenth defendant and summons had been accepted on putting signatures on the body of summons.

18. Order V, rule 19A enshrines that a declaration made and subscribed by serving officer shall be received as evidence of the facts as to the service or attempted service of summons. Service of summons had been verified by serving Officer i.e. process server and learned Judge having been satisfied with verification in respect of service of summons declared that service had been duly served and declaration had been entered by learned Judge in order No. 58 dated 8-8-1989: Law and procedure in respect of service of summons transpired to have been observed and followed in respect of due service of summons upon defendant Nos. 18(ka)-18(gaha). Section 114(e) of the Evidence Act enjoins that Court may presume that Judicial and official acts have been regularly performed. Service of summons is judicial/official act. A presumption as to due service of summons upon defendant Nos. 18(ka)-18(gaha) has been attached.

19. Ground surged forward and contention brought home from side of defendants-petitioners is that in service return there is no mention of anybody's name who received summons for and on behalf of defendants-petitioners. A close examination of service return Annexure-B to Civil. Revision Petition reveals that in the forehead of service return it is written "signature illegible" স্বাক্ষর অস্পষ্ট 9-4-1989. Name of the person receiving summons appears in the forehead of service return. It cannot be, thus, said that there had not been any mention of any name in the body of service return who received summons. Ground and contention so raised do not hold water.

20. Order IX, rule 13 of the Code enjoins that in any case in which a decree is passed exporter against a defendant, he may apply to the Court by which the decree was passed for an order to set it aside; and if he satisfies the Court that the summons was not duly served, or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing, Court shall make an order setting aside the decree as against him upon such terms as to costs payment into court or otherwise, as it thinks fit and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the Suit.

21. Only ground undertaken by defendants petitioners is non-service of summons upon them. Ex parte decree could be set aside if defendants-petitioners could satisfy the Court that summon upon them were not served. The other ground that defendants-petitioners were prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing is not at all relevant in resolving legal controversy.

22. Article 164 of The Limitation Act enjoins that limitation on the part of a defendant for an order to set aside the decree/ order passed ex parte is 30 days from the date of decree or where summons was not duly served, where applicant has knowledge of decree/order. Under Article 164 of the Limitation Act, time, thus, runs from date of the decree or where summons was not served from the date when applicant got knowledge of decree. The object of service of summons is that defendant may be informed of institution of suit in due time.

23. Stand taken by defendants-petitioners is that for no service of summons upon them they were not aware of ex parte decree awarded against them and they for the first time became aware of ex parte decree on 24-5-2005 when Advocate Commissioner landed on the property to execute order passed in Title Execution Case No. 2 of 2005. Assertion of plaintiffs opposite parties is, that summons upon defendants-petitioners had been duly served and they were well aware of proceeding of suit and ex parte decrees, both Preliminary and Final, against them and allowed the suit to be decreed against them. plaintiffs-opposite parties in counter-affidavit annexed certified copies of testimonies of PW 1 Tarek Mahtab Rahim as well as of OPW 1 Shanti Mary Cruez, OPW 2 Alam and OPW 3 Atikullah. Certified copies of testimonies have been annexed as Annexure-1. P W 1 stated in his evidence that he became aware of ex parte decree on 24-5-2005 when decree was going to be executed on his property. Evidence is produced below: একতরফা ডিক্রির কথা ২৪-৫-২০০৫ ইং তারিখ বিবাদীর জ্ঞাত হন। উক্ত তারিখে আমার জমিতে ডিক্রি একতরফা ডিক্রি বিষয়ে জ্ঞাত হই। Evidence offered by PW 1 in respect of date of first knowledge of ex parte Preliminary Decree dated 29-11-1999 could not be at all corroborated by any other witnesses. Knowledge on the part of defendants-petitioners as to ex parte Preliminary Decree was required to be proved by convincing and clinching corroborative evidence from the lips of other witnesses when endeavour had been mounted to set at naught decree after a period of five(5) years six(6) months and five(5) days of the decree. But no corroborative evidence came forth from defendants-petitioners in proof of alleged first date of knowledge of passing of Preliminary decree. No evidence emerged from the mouth of P W 1 that who had gone to execute decree on his property. P W 1 did not furnish any searching slip in respect of the ex parte preliminary decree recorded against them. "Knowledge" must be "definite knowledge". "Knowledge" is something more than mere "knowledge" that a decree has been passed against him in a particular Court in respect of a particular property and not merely the knowledge that decree had been passed by some Court against. him. Defendants-petitioners could not substantiate first knowledge of the ex parte Preliminary decree awarded against them. OPW 1 in his evidence provided account: Heirs of nineteenth defendant took step in the Suit from 1992-1997. Preliminary decree had been passed on 29-11-1999. Commissioner surveyed property on 5-5-2000 and persons who stayed on partitioned property as tenants under eighteenth and nineteenth defendants had been present there and they informed defendants. Preliminary decree had been made Final on 24-4-2004. Decree Execution Case No. 2 of 2005 was filed on 9-1-2005. On 5-3-2005, Advocate Commissioner could not place them in possession of allotted (saham property and heirs of eighteenth defendants put up obstruction and with assistance of police they took possession on property on 24-5-2005. OPW 2 blurted out in his evidence: Rahimullah Chowdhury predecessor-in-interest of defendants-petitioners allowed them to stay on suit property. In the month of May, 2000 survey on suit property had been performed and they approached the house of Rahimullah Chowdhury and communicated message that survey and measurement were being carried out from Court and they replied that survey and measurement be carried out. Evidence is extracted hereunder word for word:

রহিমুল্লা সাহেবকে চিনিতাম। তার জায়গায় আমাদের থাকতে দেয়। ২০০০ সনের মে মাসে নালিশি জমি মাপঝোপ হয়। আমি তখন ফিতা ধরেছি। আমরা রহিমুল্লার বাসায় গিয়ে তাদের জানাই কোর্ট হতে মাপঝোপ করছে। তখন তারা জানায় মাপঝোপ করুক।

OPW 3 offered evidence: He used to stay in the house of Rahimullah Chowdhury (eighteenth defendant). They used to stay on suit property on construction of hut. In the month of May 2000 people from Court had gone to suit property to have the property surveyed and before and after survey operation he informed survey matter/incident to the house of Rahimullah Shaheb. Version is produced below in verbatim:

রহিমুল্লা চৌধুরী সাহেবের বাসায় থাকতাম। আমার খালু আহম্মদ উল্লাহ রহিমুল্লার বাসায় থাকত। সেই সুবাদে নাল জমিতে ঘর করে থাকতাম। ২০০০ সনের মে মাসে কোর্ট হতে মাপঝোপের জন্য যায়। মাপের আগে ও পরে রহিমুল্লা সাহেবের বাসায় গিয়ে জানাই।

Plaintiffs-opposite parties through lip evidence of OPW 1, OPW 2 and OPW 3 could successfully prove that defendants-petitioners had been well aware of suit proceeding, Decrees, both Preliminary and Final. Execution case and, also, of their possession on suit properties i.e. properties allotted to then through process of Court since the year 2000.

24. From statement contained in Civil Revision and counter-affidavit and papers and documents annexed, the following true-to-life matters preeminently emerged:

i. Eighteenth and nineteenth defendants Rahimullah Chowdhury and Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, two cousin brothers (Mamato and Fufato Bhai = (মামাতো ফুফাতো ভাই) jointly entered appearance in the Suit and jointly filed written statement.

ii. Eighteenth defendant having been dead his heirs stood substituted and summons upon substituted defendants 18(ka)-18(jha), defendants-petitioners had been served on 9-4-1989 as evidenced from service return, Annexure-B to Civil Revision Petition and order No. 58 dated 8-8-1989. Nineteenth defendant having been dead his heirs had been substituted as defendants Nos. 19(1 ka)-19(1 ghaha) and appeared in Suit upto the year 1997 which shall be evidenced from order Nos. 91, 101, 102 and 107 recorded in Suit.

iii. Fifth and sixth defendants filed written statements. Heirs of deceased fifth and seventh defendants had been graced with allotment of Saham's in their favour.

It cannot be at all suggested that in the event of so many proceedings leading ultimately to execution of decree, defendants-petitioners would not know anything and would be in quite darkness about so many proceedings. Defendants-petitioners are not rustic and they are literate persons carrying on business in Dhaka city.

25. True it is that the suit was transferred from first Court of Subordinate Judge to different Courts of Subordinate Judge and ultimately to Court of Joint District Judge and Arbitration Court. All transfers had been made suomotu by learned District Judge. Law of Transfer is engrafted in section 24 of the Code. Relevant provision of section 24 of the Code runs thus:

24. (1) On the application of any of the parties and after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desire to be heard, or of its own motion without such notice, the High Court Division or District Court may at any stage—

(a) transfer any suit, appeal or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same, or

(b) withdraw any suit, appeal or other proceeding pending in any Court subordinate to it, and

(i) try or dispose of the same; or

(ii) transfer the same for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same; or

(iii) retransfer the same for trial or disposal to the Court from which it was withdrawn.

26. A reading of section 24 demonstrates that if District Court of its own motion transfers any suit, appeal and other civil proceeding to any other Court subordinate to it, notice of transfer is not required to be issued upon parties to proceeding. It is posited that non-issuance of notice upon parties in the matter of transfer, whether on application of any parties or soot of a Civil proceeding by. District Court to any other Court subordinate to it does not come under the purview of Order IX, rule 13 of the Code. Under Order IX, rule 13 an ex parte decree can be set aside only on ground of non service of summons upon defendants and non issuance of notice of transfer of a suit possibly can be a ground for setting aside decree in a properly instituted suit for setting aside decree and definitely not, under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code and scope and purview of Order IX, rule 13 of the Code is very much limited.

27. This drives me to Judicial authorities referred to from the Bar.

28. In Abdur Rashid and another vs Abdul Bank and another (Supra) Learned Munsif allowed a Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code and restored the Suit to its original file and number with a finding that notice of the suit was not served upon defendants. A Civil Revision carried before High Court Division met with success. High Court Division set aside Judgment passed by learned Munsif. Against the Judgment of High Court Division, Appellate Division was approached in a Civil Appeal arising out of a Leave Petition. Civil Appeal was allowed. It has been held by Appellate Division: Under Order XI, rule 13 of the Code if summons is not duly served on defendant that is a good ground for setting aside an ex parte decree. Under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code if a party satisfied a Court that summons were not duly served upon him, the Court is bound to set aside an ex parte decree. In such a case question of knowledge is not at all relevant and ex parte decree will be set aside even if the defendant had knowledge of institution of a. Suit. In the said case, learned Munsif as the Judge of first instance on consideration of evidences and materials on record found that notice of Suit was not served upon defendants. In the case in hand, learned, Joint District Judge as Judge of first instance on consideration of evidences and materials on record, positively held that summons upon defendants-petitioners had been duly served and defendants-petitioners had been well aware of proceeding of suit and Suit stood barred by limitation. Decision rendered by learned Joint District Judge has been maintained by learned Appellate Judge who held that summons upon defendants-petitioners had been duly served. Fact and circumstances of the case-referred to is quite distinguishable in the facts and circumstances of the case in hand and the case cannot be of any assistance to the defendants-petitioners.

29. In MA Wahab and another vs Abul Kalam and another (Supra), Suit in question was transferred from one Court to another Court by virtue of a notification and transfer was given effect on an off-date. In the instant case transfers were not made on off dates. The said Judicial authority cannot also ensure any benefit to defendants-petitioners.

30. In Md Insan Ali vs Mir Abdus Salam (Supra). Plaintiff-Appellant in Civil Appeal obtained an ex park decree in a suit and got delivery on possession of land in suit in execution of decree. Trial Court passed ex prate decree having been satisfied that summons was duly served upon defendant. Thereafter, on the basis of a Petition under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, decree was set aside by Court decreeing the Suit On the finding that summons was not duly served. Order allowing Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code was challenged in a Civil Revision Case. Rule issued therein was discharged. Plaintiffs as appellants then, approached before the appellate Division. Appellate Division held that claim put forth in application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code that summons was not served was not backed by evidences as against process server's report and evidence of plaintiff and claim is not sufficient for the trial Court to alter its previous finding that summons was duly served and trial. Court illegally set aside the ex parte decree. Appellate Division, thus, dismissed petition under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code. The above Judicial authority has been pressed in aid of contention advanced from side of plaintiffs opposite parties and the same lends support to the case projected by plaintiffs opposite parties.

<u>31. Trial Court as Court of firs instance on consideration of evidences, oral and documentary, specially Annexure, (service return) to Civil Revision Petition and evidence of OPW 5 in respect of service of summons upon defendants-petitioners and taking stock of various orders recorded in Suit including Order No. 58 dated 8-8-1989 and drawing up of Preliminary Decree and Final Decree and, also, that defendants Nos. 5(ka)-5(kha) and defendants 7(ka)-7(ga) got saham in respect of their claimed portion and, also, that defendant Nos. 19(ka)-19(Ja) took step in the suit upto the year 1997 and, also, that Miscellaneous Case had been filed after a period of five (5) years, six (6) months and five (5) days, held that defendants-petitioners having been aware of every affair of the Suit, out of greed, laid the suit on false statements after a long period and the Suit is seriously barred by limitation. Trial Court further found that it was not at all possible that defendants-petitioners had not been aware of the Suit and awarding of Preliminary Decree. Trial Court in coming to the above decisions scanned evidences carefully. Court of appeal as last and final Court of fact, also, took into account pleadings of parties, evidences adduced from both sides, specially evidence of OPW 5 process server and various orders recorded in the Suit came to positive decision that defendants-petitioners were well aware of original Suit and they were substituted on, the death of their predecessor and summons had been duly served upon them. Court of appeal, also, found that Miscellaneous Case was rightly dismissed on a detailed discussion and it found no justification nor any ground to interfere with decision rendered by learned Joint District Judge.</u>

<u>32. Findings reached by Courts below had been preeminently concluded by concurrent findings of fact. Concurrent findings of facts does not at all warrant any interference by this Court in the exercise of its Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure unless it is demonstratively shown that decisions, are based on gross misreading of evidences and those went against weight of evidence and materials on record or it has been founded upon misconception or misapplication or misapprehension of law or any misinterpretation of any material document or otherwise it is perverse being contrary to law and evidences on record. Exploration of decisions recorded by Courts below does not at all appear that there had been misreading of evidence or those went against weight of evidence and materials on record or it has been founded on any misconception, misapplication and misapprehension of law or misinterpretation of any material document or otherwise it is perverse being contrary to law and evidence on record and those suffer from patent wrongness, legal dodderiness and waywardness and, also fragrant error of law. Decisions rendered, reasons counted in recording reasons and conclusion reached by Courts below appear to be well founded and firm grounded and discreet. No exception can be taken to those. No interference, therefore, is called for.</u>

33. Doom of Civil Revision case is ordained in the following epithet:

(i) Decisions recorded by Courts below in not restoring Suit to file and number on allowing Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is well grounded and firm founded.

And

(ii) Adjudication rendered by Courts below does not warrant any interference by this Court in, exercise of Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged under section 115 of the Code.

34. Viewed from the above discourse and, also, having been gauged with evidences, materials on record and fact and circumstances of the case, the inevitable conclusion that can be drawn is that this Rule arising out of Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is bereft of any substance. It does not survive. It fails. Rule stands discharged.

35. Regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case I direct the parties to bear their respective costs.

Stay granted by this Court stands vacated.

End.
