full_judgment:
Civil Revision Case in hand appeared in the list on 13-3-2007. Revision Case could not be taken up for hearing on that date i.e. on 13-3-2007. Revision Case was taken up for hearing on 13-3-2007 and on that date learned Counsel for petitioners had been present in Court to press Revision Case but learned Counsel for opposite party had not been present in Court to put up opposition to Revision Case. Search had been conducted by this Court through its staff to locate learned Counsel for opposite party in Supreme Court premises. Learned Counsel for opposite party could not be found. In the interest of justice and fairplay an opportunity was accorded to learned Counsel for opposite party to place case before this Court. This Court, accordingly, suo motu adjourned hearing of Revision case. This Court passed order to place the Revision Case in the list for hearing in the name of learned Counsel for petitioner as well as opposite party.

2. Learned Counsel for opposite party today, also, is found absent, though, Revision Case appeared in the list with names of learned Counsels for petitioner and as well as opposite party.

3. Since Rule arose out of a petition under section 25 of The Small Causes Court Act of 1887 (for short The Act of 1887), power to be exercised by the High Court Division is supervisory which may, also, be exercised suo motu. Section 25 of The Act provides a safeguard to meet ends of justice in a given case brought to notice of High Court Division. High Court Division is clothed with supervisory power of superintendence and control over order/judgment/decree recorded by Small Causes Court. The High Court Division can interfere with any order Judgment, decree, action, etc if it is satisfied that the same is not according to law. In the exercise of Revisional power High Court Division is not obliged to hear parties in disposing of Civil Revision Case and a Judgment can be pronounced in the absence of any party or both parties when he/she/they had an opportunity to appear but failed to appear to represent respective case of parties. For the view adopted by me I am fortified with Judicial authorities of our Jurisdiction, such as, Darshatullah vs Manik Mondal 1984 BLD (AD) 234 = 36 DLR (AD) 88, Sharafuddin vs Fazlul Huq 49 DLR (AD) 151 and Lakshmi Bazar Shahi Masjid Committee vs St Francis Xavier's Girls' High Court 5 BLC 58 (wherein I, AK Badrul Huq, J is Author Judge). Of course, in those Judicial pronouncements, cases had been decided not under section 25 of The Act of 1887. but under section 115 of The Code of Civil Procedure and Judicial pronouncements in Revision cases under section 115 of the Code is equally applicable in Revision cases under section 25 of The Act. In this Rule opposite party, though, is absent. Petitioner is present. In exercise of supervisory power envisaged under section 25 of The Act of 1887 I propose to dispose of Civil Revision Case.

4. Feeling aggrieved by Judicial verdict pronounced by learned Small Causes Court Judge dismissing a Small Causes Court Suit No. 3 of 2004, plaintiff as petitioner invoked this Court's Civil Revisional Jurisdiction on laying a petition under section 25 of The Small Causes Court Act, 1887 whereupon a Rule was issued calling upon sole-opposite party to show cause as to why Judgment and Decree dated February 20, 2006 passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar and Small Causes Court, Comilla dismissing Small Causes Court Suit No. 3 of 2004 should not be set aside and as to why other order or further order or orders would not be passed.

5. Petitioner of Civil Revision Petition as plaintiff laid a suit being Small Causes Court Suit No. 6 of 2001 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge and, also, Small Causes Court Judge, Comilla for a decree of possession of shop room /premises described in schedule to plaint on eviction of defendant opposite party there-from.

6. Averments made in plaint is as here-under:

a. Begum Sufia Akhter, wife of Mvi Ali Ahmed Majumder by way of a deed of conveyance dated 16-3-1957 from Nirupoma Dey and others became owner and possessor of suit property. During State Acquisition Survey operation suit property along with another property stood recorded in the name of Sufia Akhter. Sufia Akhter constructed two separate buildings with good number of rooms and rented rooms on monthly basis to different persons and through monthly tenants remained owner of tenanted shop rooms/premises.

b. Sufia Akhter gifted property and buildings standing thereon along with another property in favour of her two sons Abu Md Shah Newaz and Abu Md Rahe Newaz by a registered deed of gift dated 27-4-1991 and handed over possession of gifted property in favour of doonees, her two sons.

c. Two sons of Sufia Akhter Abu Md Shah Newaz and Abu Md Rahe Newaz being owners and possessors of suit property and building standing thereon along with another item of property executed and registered a deed of exchange or ewaz themselves on 29-6-1997. In accordance with recital in the deed of exchange Abu Md Shah Newaz got suit property and building named Khaza Mansion standing on suit property and his other brother Abu Md Rahe Newaz got other property and building named Sufia Mansion standing thereon and both of them in the exercise of their right, interest and possession were in exclusive possession of exchanged properties and buildings standing thereon. Abu Md Shah Newaz inducted different persons on suit property and building named Khaja Mansion as monthly tenants and remained owner of property. Abu Md Shah Newaz subsequently constructed another building and rented the same on monthly basis to different persons, Schedule property and building standing thereon stood recorded correctly in the name of Abu Md Shah Newaz in present Khatian No. 578.

d. Abu Md Shah Newaz having being owner and possessor of Khaja Mansion buildings transferred the same by way of a duly executed and registered sale deed dated 26-11-2000 in favour of plaintiffs and plaintiffs since purchase remained absolute owners of said purchased property on mutating their names and separating jamas and recording their names in concerned khatian and on paying rents regularly and opening a holding in their names with Pourashava.

e. Sole-defendant took rent in respect of suit property and shop room on a monthly rent of Taka 2,000 from vendor of plaintiffs with condition of payment of monthly rent within 7th day of following month and sole-defendant was only a temporary monthly tenant. defendant having been a tenant, plaintiffs before their purchase had conversation with him. Plaintiffs since their purchase asked defendant-opposite party to satisfy monthly rent in respect of schedule shop, and, also; to receive receipts as evidences of payments of rent but defendant-opposite party did not pay any heed to the request offered by plaintiff towards him. Plaintiffs on 17-3-2001 issued an Attornment Notice upon defendant and made a request to him to realise arrear rent and current rent in respect of rented shop. Attorney Notice had been duly served upon defendant on 20-3-2001. In spite of receipt of Attorney Notice defendant did not pay any rent to plaintiffs. Defendant, thus, became a habitual defaulter, plaintiff, thereafter, issued a registered notice on 7-5-2001 under section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act. The notice having not been received by defendant stood returned back. On 14-5-2001 defendant in spite of notice did not hand over vacant possession of schedule shop room in favour of plaintiffs. Plaintiffs, thus, had been constrained to institute suit in Small Causes Court.

7. Defendant-opposite party contested suit on presentation of written statement. Core contentions pressed into service in written statement are catalogued hereunder :

13. In approaching and resolving points formulated provisions of law engrafted in section 25 of The Act demand meditation. A legal survey of pleadings, evidences, materials on record and fact and circumstances of the case are, also, required to be taken heed of.

14. Section 25 of The Small Causes Court Act enshrines that High Court, for the purposes of satisfying itself that a decree or order made in any case decided by any Court of Small Causes was according to law may call for the case and pass such order with respect thereto as it thinks fit.

15. A decision of Court of Small Causes cannot be said to be according to law where it is based on an erroneous view of law and where presumptions required to be drawn had not been drawn in accordance with law and when substantial injustice directly resulted from a misapprehension of law or from a material error resulting in an error occasioning a failure of justice. The real test is, whether any substantial injustice had been done by decisions complained of. It is well nigh to remember that High Court Division in the exercise of power under section 25 of The Small Causes Act will interfere only when a substantial injustice has been caused to a party by the order/Judgment/ decree under protest in Revision Petition. It is conveniently posited that power conferred upon High Court Division for interference under section 25 of The Act of 1887 is more extensive than power exercised by High Court Division under section 115 of The Code of Civil Procedure.

ওরফে লাবলু হইতে বিগত ১৪০৭ বাংলার ১২ই অগ্রাহায়ন ৷ ঐক্যে ২৬-১১-২০০০ ইং তারিখের সম্পাদিত ও রেজিষ্ট্রারীকৃত পন প্ৰবৃত্তি মূলক সাফ কবলা দলিল মূলে খরিদ করিয়া তাহা বিভিন্ন ভাড়াটিয়ার মারফত দখলকরা বিদ্যমান আছি । আপনি নোটিশ গ্রহিতা আমাদের ভায়া ডাঃ আবু মোহাম্মদ শাহেনেওয়াজ ওরফে লাবলু হইতে নিম্ন তফছিলের বর্নিত দোকান কোঠা মাসিক মং ২০০০/- টাকা হারে ইংরেজী মাসের নিয়মে প্রতি মাসের ভাড়া পরবর্তী ৭ তারিখের মধ্যে আদায় করার অঙ্গীকারে অস্থায়ী স্বত্ব বিহীন মাসিক ভাড়াটিয়া স্বরুপে ভাড়া নিয়া তাহাতে দখলকার বিদ্যমান আছেন৷ আপনি নোটিশ গ্রহিতা একজন ভাড়াটিয়া হওয়ায় আমরা নোটিশ দাতাগণ আমাদের খরিদের পূর্বে আপনার সাথে আমাদের খরিদের বিষয়ে আলাপ আলোচনা করিয়াছি ৷ আমাদের খরিদের পরও উক্ত বিষয়ে আপনার সাথে বিভিন্ন তারিখে বিস্তারিত আলাপ আলোচনা করিয়া আমাদিগকে ভাড়াটিয়া দোকান কোঠার ভাড়া রীতিমত আদায় করতঃ ভাড়াটিয়া রশিদ গ্রহন করার জন্য আপনাকে বারংবার অনুরোধ করিয়াছি৷ কিন্তু আপনি নোটিশ গ্রহিতা আমাদের অনুরোধ সত্বেও আমরা নোটিশ দাতাগনকে Attom করতঃ নিম্ন তপছিলেৱ বর্ণিত ভাড়াটিয়া কোঠার ভাড়া আদায় করেন নাই ৷ তদাবস্থায় আমরা নোটিশ দাতাগন আপনি নোটিশ গ্রহিতাকে বিগত ১৮-০৩-২০০১ ইং তারিখে রেজিষ্ট্রারী ডাক যোগে একটি Attornmcnt Notice প্রেরণ করতেঃ নোটিশ প্রাপ্তির ৭ দিনের মধ্যে আমরা নোটিশ দাতাগনকে Attorn করতঃ আপনার দখলিয় নিম্ন তপছিলের বর্ণিত ভাড়াটিয়া দোকান কোঠার বকেয়া ভাড়াসহ হাল মাসের ভাড়া আমারা নোটিশ দাতাগনকে আদায়ত্রুমে ভাড়াটিয়া রশিদ গ্রহন করার জন্য অনুরোধ করি। উক্ত Attornment Notice আপনার উপর বিগত ২০-৩-২০০১ ইং তারিখে যথারীতি জারী হয়। উক্ত Attornment Notice যথারীতি জারী হওয়া স্বত্বেও আপনি নোটিশ গ্রহিতা আমরা নোটিশ৷ দাতাগনকে Attom করতঃ কোন ভাড়া আদায় করেন নাই। আপনি নোটিশ গ্রহিতা একজন Habitual defaulter বটেন I আপনি নোঢিশ গ্রহিতা নিম্ন তপছিলের বর্ণিত দোকান কোঠার অস্থায়ী স্বত্ব বিহীন মাসিক ভাড়াটিয়ার স্বত্ব অত্র নোটিশ দ্বারা বর্তমান ২০০১ ইং সনের মে মাস অস্তে Determine করা হইল ৷ আপনি নোটিশ গ্রহিতা বর্তমান ২০০১ ইং সনের যে মাস অন্তে নিম্ন তপছিলের দোকান কোঠার দখল আমরা নোটিশ দাতাগণের বরাবরে বুঝাইয়া দিয়া অন্যত্র চলিয়া যাইবেন ৷ তদন্যথায় আপনি নোটিশ গ্রহতাকে নিম্ন তফছিলের বর্ণিত দোকান কোঠা ইেতে উচ্ছেদ করার জন্য উপযুক্ত আদালতের আশ্রয় গ্রহন করা হইবে এবং তদাবস্থায় আপনি নোটিশ গ্রহিতা সমস্ত ক্ষতি খরচের জন্য দায়ী হইবেন৷ ইতি ১৪০৮ বাংলার ২৪ বৈশাখ, ঐক্যে ৭-৫-২০০১ ইং।

Defendnat-opposite party in spite of Attornment Notice did not admit new owners, plaintiffs-petitioners as landlords and, in spite of Notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act did not pay rent to plaintiffs-petitioners and, thus, became habitual defaulter making him liable to be evicted from suit shop/ premises.

19. Plaintiffs-petitioners instituted suit in hand on 28-6-2001. Defendant-opposite party laid written statement on 18-4-2002. In written statement he asserted that he became aware of an Iwaz deed dated 29-6-1997 in between two brothers Abu Md Rahe Newaz and Abu Md Shah Newaz and that Abu Md Shah Newaz got in his saham schedule Bharatia premises. Statement is in the following language:

প্রাক বর্ণিত মতে এই বিবাধী আবু মোহাম্মদ রাহে নেওয়াজ (ভেলু) এর অধিনে ভাড়াঢিয়া স্বত্বে নিম্ন তপছিলোক্ত ৮টি দোকান কোঠায় ভাড়াঢিয়া সাব্যস্থ থাকাবস্থায় আবু মোহাম্মদ রাহে নেওয়াজ (ভেলু) ও তদ্বীয় ভ্রাতা ডাঃ আবু মোহাম্মদ শাহনেওয়াজ (লাভলু) এর মধ্যে ২৯-৬-৯৭ ইং তারিখে এক এওয়াজ নামা দলিল হওয়ার বিষয় বিবাদী পশ্চাৎ জানিতে পারে৷ ডাঃ আবু মোহাম্মদ শাহনেওয়াজ ওরফে লাভলু নিম্ন তপছিলোক্ত ভাড়াটিয়া প্রেমিসেস নিজ ছাহামে প্রাপ্ত হওয়ার বিষয় বিবাদী পশ্চাৎ অবগত হয় ৷

Further averment made by defendant-opposite party in written statement is that he admitted Anwarul Huq as owner of suit premises and Anwarul Huq admitted defendant-opposite party as tenant and received rent from him and defendant had been paying rent to Anwarul Huq since 1-1-1998. Relevant portion of statement is in following language:

বিবাদী মোঃ আনোয়ারুল হককে মালিক স্বীকার করিয়া দোকানের ভাড়া ১-১-৯৮ ইং তারিখ হইতে মোঃ আনোয়ারুল হককে আদায় করিতেছে।

Defendant-opposite party accepted Anwarul Huq as owner of suit shop/premises on the strength of an agreement for sale. But mere agreement for sale did not confer any title on Anwarul Huq Section 54 of Transfer of Property Act can be pressed into service in this regard which enjoins that a contract for sale of immovable property is a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between parties and it does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on such property. Anwarul Huq could not become owner of suit shop/premises on the strength of alleged agreement for sale entered between him and Abu Md Shah Newaz and there could not be any legal justification to pay rent to Anwarul Huq and payment of rent to Anwarul Huq by defendant-opposite party as owner of suit shop /premises is no payment of rent in eye of law.

20. It is lip evidence of defendant-opposite party as DW 1 that western portion of property (suit property) fell in saham of Lablu (Abu Md Shah Newaz) and out of two brothers Abu Md Shah Newaz Lablu got suit Market by way of amicable settlement and Abu Md Shah Newaz got possession over entire market and Shah Newaz, realised rent from other tenants except him and that he was well aware of deed of partition (Deed of Exchange) and he was a witness to deed of partition (Exchange Deed). Relevant portions of version provided by defendant-opposite party No. 1 as DW 1 are extracted below:

এওয়াজ মুখে পঃভাগ রাবলুর ভাগে পড়ে।

২. ভাইয়ের মধ্যে আপোষে শহনেওয়াজ লাবলু না/মার্কেট পায়।

পুরো মার্কেটের দখল শাহনেওয়াজ পায় সত্য। আমার থেকে ছাড়া শাহনেওয়াজ মার্কেটের বাকী ভাড়াটিয়াদের থেকে ভাড়া আদায় করা সত্য।

২. ভাইয়ের মধ্যে বন্টন নামা বিষয়ে জানতাম। বন্টননামায় আমি সাক্ষী ছিলাম।

21. From statements made in written statement dated 18-4-2002 and testimony furnished by defendant-opposite party point had been crystallised that defendant-opposite party became aware in respect of Iwaz deed dated 29-6-1997 between two brothers, Abu Md Shah Newaz and Abu Md Rahe Newaz and that Abu Md Shah Newaz got schedule (suit) shop/premises by way of deed of exchange. Defendant-opposite party in spite of clear knowledge of deed of exchange, and, also, of getting of suit shop/premises in saham of Abu Md Shah Newaz and, also, of the deed of conveyance executed and registered on 26-11-2000 by Abu Md Shah Newaz in favour of plaintiffs-petitioners and, also, in spite of receipt of Attornment Notice, Exhibit 11 and Notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act did neither attorn nor admit plaintiffs-petitioners as owner and landlord of suit shop-premises and did not pay rent to them and, thus, became habitual defaulter rendering him liable to be evicted from suit shop/premises.

22. It has been stated earlier that Anwarul Huq on the basis of an agreement for sale from Abu Md Shah Newaz instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 24 of 2001 impleading Abu Md Shah Newaz and plaintiffs-petitioners as First and Second-Fourth defendants. The said suit was dismissed in terms of solenama. In Petition of Compromise it has been positively stated that plaintiff (Anwarul Huq) on the strength of agreement for sale could not put forth any claim of ownership and title on suit shop/premises. Exhibit Ga, Gal and Gat are evidences of dismissal matter of suit. Decree of dismissal was recorded on 25-10-2003. It is the evidence of defendant-opposite party that suit for specific performance of contract ended in compromise. Evidence is in the following terms:

লাবলু আনোয়ারের কাছে কবালা না দেওয়ায় ২৪/২০০১ করালা পাওয়ায় মামলা হয়। সেই মামলা পরে তাহারা আপোষ নিষ্পত্তি করে।

Defendant-opposite party having admitted himself as tenant under Anwarul Huq was very much bound by the sole-decree recorded in Title Suit No. 24 of 2001. Defendant-opposite parties even in the face of dismissal of suit filed by his alleged Landlord Anwarul Huq by way of solenama following sole-decree did not care to admit plaintiffs-petitioners as owners/land-lords on suit shop/premises and did not care to pay rent from being saved to be adjudged as defaulters.

23. Annexure A to Civil Revision Petition is a petition dated 10-2-2004 submitted in Miscellaneous Rent Case No. 28 of 2002 by defendant-opposite party seeking permission to Rent Controller for depositing rent in the name of plaintiffs-petitioners in place of Anwarul Huq. But defendant opposite party became a defaulter long before bestowing the petition before Rent Controller and Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla for depositing rent in the name of plaintiffs-petitioners. This petition laid by defendant-petitioner for depositing rent before rent before rent Controller and according permission to defendant-opposite-party for depositing rent and deposit of rent by Challans, Annexures B, B1 and B2 could not and cannot save defendant opposite-party from being a defaulter/defendant is default, whether habitual or not. defendant-opposite party could deposit rent with Rent Controller immediately after dismissal of Title Suit laid by Anwarul Huq for Specific Performance of Contract and it was too late in the day to deposit rent with Rent Controller and defendant-opposite party could not save himself from being a defaulter.

<u>24. Payment of rents to Anwarul Huq is no legal payment of rent in asmuchas Anwarul Huq could not be owner/landlord of the suit shop/premises on the strength of an Agreement for sale in asmuchas an Agreement for sale did not confer any title and ownership upon Anwarul Huq. Small Cause Court fell into a serious error in holding that defendant Zobair Alam Sarker by way of agreement had been paying rents regularly and he could not be treated as defaulter for non-payment of rent and by this error the merit of decision of the case has been seriously affected.</u>

25. From the above discussion, the irresistible conclusion which can be drawn is that defendant opposite party has established himself as a defaulter in payment of rent to owner/ landlord who are no other than plaintiffs-petitioners and plaintiffs-petitioners could prove through legal evidence that defendant-opposite party is a defaulter. Result that follows is that defendant opposite party is to be evicted from suit shop/premises.

26. Small Cause Court Judge misdirected himself in total approach of the legal debate involved in the suit. Plaintiffs-petitioners as transferees/purchasers of suit shop /premises from the rightful owner-transferor Abu Md Shah Newaz were and are entitled to rent from the date of transfer of ownership in the property and relationship of landlord and tenant had been established between plaintiffs-petitioners and defendant opposite party from the date of transfer of ownership of suit shop/ premises. Plaintiffs-petitioners served Attornment Notice upon defendant-opposite party and the said Notice had been received by the latter as evidenced from acknowledgment receipt. But defendant-opposite party did not care to pay rent to plaintiffs-petitioners in compliance with Attornment Notice. Finding reached by Small Causes Court Judge to the effect that relationship of landlord and tenant had not been established between plaintiffs and defendant suffers from gross illegality and legal infirmity.

<u>27. Small Causes Court Judge, also, committed a substantial error in rendering decision that payment of rent by defendant with Rent Controller had been established inasmuch as plaintiffs-petitioners became entitled to rent from defendant-opposite party from the date of acquisition of ownership on suit shop/premises on the baluster of deed of transfer from owner-vendor Abu Md Shah Newaz and, thereafter, on service of Attornment Notice upon defendant-opposite party and defendant-opposite party became defaulter long before his laying of petition before Rent Controller for according permission to deposit rent with it and by deposit of rent (Annexure A, B and B1 respectively) to Rent Controller defendant-petitioner could not and cannot at all derive any benefit of provision engrafted in section 19 of Premises Rent Control Act of 1991. Payment of rent by defendant-petitioner only on 6-3-2006 and 6-4-2006 with Rent Controller is no lawful payment of rent and defendant-opposite party cannot save himself from being evicted from suit shop/premises and he has rendered himself liable to be evicted from suit shop/ premises.</u>

28. Small Causes Court Judge, also, has been in grave error in holding that dispute having been cropped up in respect of title between parties, the suit as framed is not maintainable. No dispute arose in respect of title over suit shop/premises. Ownership and title over suit shop /premises on the part of plaintiffs-petitioners is undisputed and invincible and defendant-opposite party, also, admitted absolute ownership of plaintiffs-petitioners and, also, took plaintiffs-petitioners as landords by petition laid before Rent Controller Annexure 'A' to Civil Revision Petition. Finding reached by Small Cause Court Judge on this point perilously borders on perversity.

29. Small Causes Court Judge also fell into a substantial error in his decision that bonafide requirement on the part of plaintiffs has not been proved. Case of bonafide requirement of suit shop /premises had neither been pleaded in the plaint nor any evidence had been led by plaintiffs-petitioners. Finding on Bonafide requirement is a demonstration of non-application of mind on the part of Small Causes Court Judge.

<u>30. In the discourse made hereinbefore, the inevitable conclusion that flows is that decision rendered by Small Causes Court Judge are contrary to law and those suffer from gross illegality and legal infirmity and those demand over-throw. Rule arising out of a Civil Revision Petition under section 25 of the Small Causes Court Act of 1887 carries substance and it succeeds. Rule is made absolute. Judgment and decree recorded in Small Causes Court Suit No. 6 of 2001 stands quashed/set aside. Suit is decreed. Plaintiffs-petitioners shall get vacant possession of suit shop/premises as described in schedule to the plaint. Small Causes Court and Senior Assistant Judge, Comilla shall place plaintiffs-petitioners in possession of suit shop /premises as described in schedule to plaint on evicting defendant-opposite party therefrom within Two (2) months of the receipt of this Judgment.</u>

31. No costs.

Lower Courts Records are sent down at once.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 5-12-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3868 of 2004).
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Matin J: These two appeals are directed against the common judgment and order dated 28-1-2002 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal Nos.108 and 203 of 1995 dismissing the appeals and affirming the judgments and decrees dated 16-2-1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur in Title Suit Nos.25 and 16 of 1992 dismissing the suits.

2. The facts in short are that the appellants in CA No. 8 of 2005 i.e. Mohiuddin Khan and another as plaintiff filed the above Title Suit No.16 of 1992 on 6-2-1992 against the heirs of Shihamul Haque since deceased and others stating, inter alia, that they by kabala Nos.1586, 1588, 1589 and 1600 dated 1-2-1974, 15-2-1974, 11-2-1974 and 14-2-1974 respectively purchased 0.54 acres of land appertaining to CS Plot No.248 of CS khatian No.235 corresponding to SA khatian No.406 of Mouza Chandana PS Joydebpur, District-Gazipur described in schedule 'A' of the plaint from Chaturi Tanti and got delivery of possession and by Mutation Case No.170/74-75 their names were mutated in SA Khatian No.406 in place of said Chaturi Tanti and they paid ground rents and got dakhilas. Against the above order of mutation, Shihamul Haque preferred Misc. Appeal Case No.13 of 1981 claiming title on the basis of deed of exchange (settlement) dated 16-6-1980 and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka, by order dated 12-1-1982, without at all giving any finding as to possession of the suit land, cancelled the mutation. The appellants then filed Appeal No.8 of 1982 and the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka who heard the appeal, having found that the appellants and others were in possession of the case land, set aside the above order dated 12-1-1982 and restored the mutation in the name of appellants and others. Then Shihamul Haque preferred Appeal No.96 of 1984 before the Board of Land Administration and after hearing the same was dismissed. Shihamul Haque then filed Writ Petition No.159 of 1989 and the High Court Division, after hearing declared that the above orders passed by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka and the Board of Land Administration are without any lawful authority with the observation that the question of title and ownership and validity of the deeds in question could be gone into and decided only by a civil court. the appellants out of the proceedings of the above Misc. Appeal Case No.13 of 1981 and also from the contents of the annexures of the above Writ Petition No.159 of 1989 for the first time came to know about the alleged deed of agreement for exchange dated 30-10-1963, the alleged powers of attorneys dated 7-6-1965, the deed of exchange dated 16-6-1980 in terms of Exchange Case No.35/69-70, Title Suit Nos.27 of 1971 and 150 of 1972, Civil Revision Nos.315 and 1387 of 1977 and also of the withdrawals of the same on 29-1-1980 and 21-1-1980 which were referred in the above proceeding. The appellants are bonafide purchasers of the suit land for valuable consideration without any notice of agreement of exchange and other facts as stated above. Ordinance No.1 of 1964 (EP Disturbed Persons Rehabilitation Ordinance, 1964) having died by the efflux of time on 31-12-1964 as held in 17 DLR 451, the above proceeding of Exchange Case No.35/69-70 stated on 24-7-1969 for forfeiting the land of the appellants for the purpose of granting so-called settlement is without jurisdiction. The possession of the property in question was always with the appellants and was never taken over by Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka or Sub-Divisional Officer and the same was never enlisted in the Census List of 1966-1967.

3. The contesting defendant Nos.1 (a) to 1(d), the heirs of Shihamul Haque contested the above suit by filing written statement denying the claim of the appellants and stating, inter alia, that Shihamul Haque, his father Enamul Haq and his mother Tahera Sogra Begum, were the inhabitants of Bardwan District in India and after they settled in the then East Pakistan in 1950 migrating from India, Chaturi Tanti along with Shibulal, Bhutu, Surjagaya and Nathuri Tanti proposed to exchange their lands including suit land of the above mouza Chandana with the land of Shamsul Hoque, Enamul Hoque and Tahera Sogra Begum at Bardwan and then a deed of agreement was duly executed which was registered on 30-10-1963 and pursuant to the above agreement the parties handed over the possession of their respective lands to each other acknowledging delivery of possession. Embargo being created upon the Hindus to transfer their properties by registered deed of conveyances on promulgation of defence of Pakistan Rules several powers of attorney were given to each other by both sides on the basis of which exchange deeds were executed in Bardawan in India and by one of such deed of exchange dated 9-8-1968 executed in India Tahera Sogra Begum exchanged 1.36 acres of her lands at Bardwan with 0.89 acres land of Chaturi and Nathuni Tanti of mouza Chandana which includes the suit land. Bhatu Tanti, Chaturi Tanti and 3 others made joint declaration before the Notary Public in Calcutta on 15-7-1968 and 12-8-1968 confirming the above exchange of their lands of mouza Chandana including the suit land. The facts of the execution and registration of the above agreement, to exchange in the year 1963, the irrevocable power of attorney and the exchange deeds were duly certified by the Magistrate, First Class, Alipur West Bengal, India on 17-7-1968 and 10-9-1968. Shihamul Haque applied to the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka praying for permission to execute and register the deed of exchange under the authority of general power of attorney executed in his favour whereupon the above Exchange Case No. 35/69-70 was stated. Shibulal Tanti, Chaturi Tanti and others filed an objection in the above exchange case contending, infer alia, they did not enter into any such agreement nor did they exchange their properties and that the exchange deed is fraudulent and powers of attorney are collusive and were vitiated by coercion, threat and intimidation. Shibulal Tanti also filed Title Suit No. 27 of 1971 in the 1st Court of Sub-Judge, Dhaka against Shihamul Haque and others challenging the deed of agreement for exchange, powers of attorney as well the deed of exchange but the suit was dismissed for non-prosecution and subsequently he prayed for restoration of the suit which was rejected by order dated 8-6-1972 and thereafter Shibulal Tanti filed Title Suit No. 150 of 1972 in the same Court against Shihamul Haque and others seeking same declarations as made in the previous suit and then prayed for amendment which was rejected as the suit filed earlier was dismissed. Against this order of rejection Tanti filed Civil Revision No. 315 of 1977 and also filed Civil Revision No. 1372 of 1977 on more or less similar grounds. Then both the above Rules were discharged on the basis of prayers of Tanti to the effect that they do not want to press the Rules, after the disposal of the above suits/revisions Shihamul Haque applied to Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka to proceed with the above Exchange Case No. 35 of 1969-70 who then after making necessary enquiry and after completing all the formalities executed and registered the deed of exchange (Settlement) on 16-6-1980 transferring 7.12 acres of land of mouza Chandana in favour of Shihamul Haque thereafter on the basis of the above exchanged Shihamul Haque started Mutation Appeal Case No.  13 of 1981 in the office of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka praying for cancelling the earlier mutation in the name of the appellant and got the mutation cancelled. The subsequent order as stated earlier where passed by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka in Appeal Case No. 8 of 1982, the Board of Land Administration in Appeal No. 86 of 1984 and the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 159 of 1980 made the Rule absolute with the observation that the question of title and validity of the deed of exchange could be decided only by the civil court. The defendants have been possessing the suit land along with other lands by cultivating and growing crops therein through bargadars namely Kamal's mother and her son-in-law.

4. The appellants in CA No.  9 of 2005 i.e. Sree Monmohan Shaha and another as plaintiff on 25-2-1992 filed the above Title Suit No.  25 of 1992 against the heirs of Shihamul Haque and others claiming similar relief on more or less similar averments made in the above Title Suit No. 16 of 1992, variation being that the area of the suit land was 0.98 acres as described in Schedule A, B and C of the plaint, the appellant No. 1 purchased from Shibulal Tanti 0.02 acres of land of Plot No. 1952 of Khatian No. 68, 0.35 acres of land of Plot No. 1905 of Khatian No. 290, 0.05 acres of land of Plot No. 1916 of Khatian No. 429 i.e. total 0.06 acres, all within the said mouza Chandana by registered kabalas dated 24-1-1979 and appellant No. 2 also purchased 0.06 acres of land of the aforesaid Plot No. 1916 and some other land from aforesaid Plot No. 1952 by registered kabala dated 6-1-1979 from the aforesaid Shibulal Tanti and they were put into possession of the suit land immediately. They had filed the Separation and Mutation Case No. 1384 of 1978-79 in the office of CO (Rev) Joydebpur and their names were mutated in SA Khatian Nos.  68,290 and 429 under the order of CO (Rev) dated 19-6-1979 and they have been paying ground rent for the suit lands since 6-9-1979. The plaint of the above suit also contained averments regarding filing of Misc. Appeal Case No. 13 of 1981 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka, Appeal No. 8 of 1982 before Additional Commissioner, Appeal No. 96 of 1984 before Board of Land Administration and Writ Petition No. 159 of 1989 before the High Court Division and in the above suit the defendant Nos. 1(a)-1(d), the heirs of Shihamul Haque also filed written statement making averments similar to in their written statement filed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1992. The trial court by judgment and decree dated 16-2-1995 dismissed both Title Suit Nos. 16 and 25 of 1992. The appellants preferred First Appeal Nos. 108 and 203 of 1995 and the High Court Division after hearing dismissed both the appeals holding, inter alia, that Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka was competent and legally authorized to execute and register the deed of exchange (settlement) and it is not necessary that the property should be declared either as enemy property or vested property for its vesting upon the government for regularizing the pending genuine exchange cases including the instant one. The plaintiff-appellants having not filed the suits within three years from the date of knowledge of the settlement deed as required under Article 91 of the Limitation act, the suits are hopelessly barred by limitation. The plaintiff-appellants, during the pendency of the suits/civil revisions which were admittedly filed by their vendors made the purchases without the permission of the court and so the above purchases of the plaintiffs are hit by the principles of lis pendens as provided under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. The plaintiff appellants having not paid proper court fees as required for the several reliefs as sought, the suits are also hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and section 7 of the Court Fees Act. After withdrawal of the suit or dismissal of a suit for non-prosecution for default no fresh suit can be filed by the same parties or any party claiming through them on the same subject of dispute without the permission of the court and as the earlier suits including the civil revisions being dismissed for non-prosecution, the present suits being filed without obtaining permissions, are not, maintainable.

5. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants in Civil Petition No.1759 of 2002 submitted that the appellant having prayed for declaration of title of the disputed land which became clouded in view of the judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 2-12-1991 passed in Writ Petition No.159 of 1989 setting aside the order of mutation in favour of the appellants, the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the suit filed by the appellants in the year 1992 was barred by limitation. The appellants not being party to the deed of exchange (settlement) dated 16-6-1980 it was not necessary for them to seek declaration that the said deed is invalid and the appellants having purchased the disputed land in 1974 as bonafide purchasers for value without notice the deed of settlement cannot affect the title of the appellants. No issue was joined by the parties as regards the enemy status of the disputed property and the High Court Division, having found the disputed property not being an enemy property, erred in law in holding that the Government under Act XLV of 1974 acquired the authority to execute the deed of settlement. The High Court Division upon an erroneous view of the provisions of section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act wrongly held that the purchase of the appellants was barred by the principles of lis pendens. The High Court Division was wrong in not noticing that the instant suit is on a different cause of action arising out of order dated 2-12-1991 of the High Court Division clouding the title of the appellant. The suits filed by the original owners of the disputed cause of action airing from the creation of documents relating to exchange of the disputed property and so the provisions of Order XXIII, rule 1(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure regarding withdrawal/dismissal are not applicable and the High Court Division was wrong in not properly considering the evidence of both the parties on the question of possession of the disputed land.

6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant in Civil Petition No.1758 of 2002, adopted the above submissions.

7. Leave was granted to consider the above submissions in both cases.

8. Heard Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel appearing for the appellants in CA No. 8 of 2005 and Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel appearing for the appellants in CA No. 9 of 2005 and Mr. TH Khan and Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-4 in both cases and perused the petition and the impugned judgment and order to the High Court Division and other papers on record.

9. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel submits that the appellants having prayed for declaration of title to the disputed land which became clouded by the judgment of the High Court Division passed on 2-12-1991 in the writ petition setting aside the order of mutation in favour of the appellants, the High Court Division was wrong in holding the suit filed by the appellants in 1992 to be barred by limitation.

10. Mr. TH Khan, the learned Counsel on the other hand submitted that the plaintiff appellants had the knowledge of the settlement and therefore the courts below were right in holding that the suit is barred by limitation because the suits were not filed within 3 years from the date of knowledge of settlement.

11. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel submits that the appellants were not a party to the deed of settlement and therefore it was not necessary for the appellants to have a declaration of invalidity of the said documents and when the plaintiff purchased the land in 1974 a deed of settlement long after i.e. in 1980 cannot have any affect on the plaintiffs title.

12. He further submits that the settlement being void ab initio as the Government had no title on the land deed not be avoided by the plaintiff and therefore the question of limitation did not arise.

13. It appears that the cause of action of the suit arose on 2-12-1991 when the High Court Division set aside the mutation of the appellants in respect of the suit land and the suits were filed in 1992 and therefore the suits were well within time.

14. The learned Counsel submits that the suit land was never enemy property or vested property and never vested in the Government and therefore the settlement of a land by the Government which did not belong to the Government is void abnitio and it need not be avoided by filing a suit and therefore the plain-tiff were not obliged to challenge the settlement dated 16-6-1980 as they purchased the land in question from the original owner by registered sale deeds in 1974.

15. In such view of the matter the courts below erred in law in holding that the suits are barred by law.

16. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the Counsel appearing for the appellants submits that the High Court Division found that the disputed land is not enemy property and the PW 1 admitted in his deposition that it is not enemy property or forfeited property and therefore the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the Government acquired the suit land under Act XLV of 1974 and had the authority to grant the settlement.

17. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel submits that in the case of Chitta Ranjan Sutar vs Secretary, Judicial Department reported in 17 DLR 451 both sections 4 and 6 of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 were declared ultra vires and Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 became a dead law in 1964 and this position was reiterated in the case of Abdul Majid Bepari vs Kashem Ali Maloo reported in 27 DLR 1 and therefore the GOs issued under a dead law namely ordinance No.1 of 1964 were ineffectual and moreover the alleged forfeiture was not done under Ordinance No.1 of 1964.

18. It appears that sections 4, 6 and 6A of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 were declared ultra vires the Constitution and therefore the position is as if sections 4, 6 and 6A of the Ordinance, No. 1 of 1964 had never been passed at all.

19. Mr. Willoughby was quoted in the case of 27 DLR to explain the position of an unconstitutional law, which runs as under:

"An unconstitutional act is not a law, it confers no right, it imposes no duties, if offers no protection, it creates; no office; it is in legal contemplation, as inoperative as though it has never been passed."

20. It appears that the deed of settlement Annexure-J in the paper book was issued under the authority of Act XLV of 1974 and not under Ordinance No.1 of 1964. Moreover DW 1 in her deposition categorically admitted বিনিময় মোঃ ৩৫/৬৯-৭০ তে ২০-১১-১৯৭০ ইং তারিখে জেলা প্রশাসক এর দেয়া নোটিশে উল্লেখিত, সম্পত্তি বাজেয়াপ্তকৃত সম্পত্তি নয়।

<u>21. Thus it appears "that the Government had no authority to forfeit the land under section 6A of the Ordinance No.1 of 1964 and in fact it did not forfeit under Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 and there is nothing on record that the property was enemy property or vested property and therefore the Government had no authority to grant settlement of the land in question in favour of the defendants and the High Court Division was wrong in holding otherwise.</u>

<u>22. The High Court Division found that the suits are hit by doctrine of lis pendens and also under Order XXIII, rule 1(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

23. Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act runs as under:

"52 During the (pendency) in any Court (in Bangladesh) of (any) suit or proceeding (which is not collusive and) in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be therein, except under the authority of the Court and on such terms as it may impose."

<u>24. It appears that the suit filed by the original owners in 1971 was on different cause of action and cause of action of the present suits is all-together different. The earlier suits were for declaration that the deed of agreement for exchange, powers of attorney as well as the said exchange deed effected in West Bengal are illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff in that Suit No. 27 of 1971 and Suit No.150 of 1972 was filed praying for the same reliefs as were prayed in Title Suit No. 27 of 1971. But the present suits are for declaration of title and possession and a further decree for declaration that the settlement deed in favour of the defendant is void and not binding upon the plaintiff. Therefore the cause of action of the present suits being all-together different the principle of section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act as quoted above has no manner of application inasmuch as in the earlier suits right to immovable property was not directly and specifically in question whereas in the present suit right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question.</u>

25. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel has referred to the case of Shanmughasundaram Filial vs. Parvathi Alumni reported in AIR 1945 Madras 454 where it was held that for the doctrine of lis pendens to apply, the right to specific immovable property must be directly in issue.

Order XXIII, rule 1(3) runs as under:

"Where the plaintiff withdraw from a suit, or abandons part of a claim, without the permission referred to in sub-rule (2), he shall be liable for such costs as the Court may award and shall be precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of such subject-matter or such part of the claim."

<u>26. As we have already held that the subject matter of the present suits and the earlier suits are not same and therefore Order XXIII, rule 1(3) has no manner of application in the present case.</u>

27. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that the suit on a different cause of action even though related to the same property is not barred.

28. In support of his contention the learned Counsel has referred to the case of the Order of the Holy Cross vs Lonnappan Thattil reported in AIR 1990 Kerala 215.

29. Mr. Mahmudul Islam has also referred to the case of Amir Hossain Khairati being dead his heirs: Altaf Hossain vs. Abdul Aziz Beoari reported in 47 DLR (AD) 106 and submitted that since the suits were dismissed for non-prosecution Order XXIII, rule 1(3) has no manner or application. In that case, this court held as under:

"From the averments made in the plaint it appears that Title Suit No.7 of 1983 was dismissed for non-prosecution and that suit was not withdrawn by the plaintiffs. As such, the provision of Order XXIII, rule 1(3) is not applicable as the order of non-prosecution of the earlier suit does not amount to withdrawal. Hence the plaintiff is not precluded to file a fresh suit by making out a new cause of action on fresh averments made in the subsequent suit."

30. Therefore the finding of the High Court Division that the suits are barred under Order XXIII rule 1(3) is also not tenable in law.

31. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that both the courts below failed to appreciate the evidence on record on the question of possession of the suit land. He has taken us through the deposition of PWs and DWs and particularly PW 2 who was nephew of Chaturi the vendor of the plaintiff who supported the plaintiffs possession.

32. He also referred to evidence of PW 3 who testified that the plaintiff constructed houses on the suit land.

33. Mr Islam has referred also to the deposition of DW 2 who admitted in his cross-examination that he did not know the suit land.

34. He also referred to the deposition to DW 4 who also admitted that he did not know the suit land and submitted that the finding of the High Court Division on possession is contrary to the evidence on record.

35. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan learned Counsel adopted the argument of Mr. Mahmudul Islam on other points but on the question of possession he referred to written statement of the respondents submitted in the suit in para 45 where the respondents admitted that they were dispossessed by the appellants from the homestead land and exchange lands during pendency of the exchange case.

36. In para 55 in the written statement the respondents admitted that they were dispossessed in August 1972.

37. Mr. Bhuiyan has taken us to the evidence of PWs and DWs and also referred to PW 1 who testified that having purchased the suit land he is possessing the same by constructing houses thereon. In his cross-examination the plaintiff asserted that when he purchased the suit land from his vendors no suit was pending.

38. He has also referred to the evidence of PW 3 who asserted that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land having houses thereon and cultivable lands.

39. He has also referred to the evidence of PW 5 who asserted the plaintiffs possession with house thereon and DWs 2 and 3 who admitted that they did not know the suit land.

<u>40. We have perused the evidence ourselves and found that the plaintiffs sufficiently proved their possession in the suit land and the defendants are admittedly out of possession and therefore the finding of the High Court Division and the trial court on this point are not tenable in law.</u>

<u>41. Mr. TH Khan, the learned counsel appearing for the respondents on the other hand submitted that they entered into an agreement for exchange as early as on 30-10-1963 with the vendors of the appellants, obtained power of attorney in 1965, but ultimately the land was forfeited in favour of the Government as per provision of section 6A of the East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance; 1964 and the Government as the owner of the land granted the deed of settlement for 7.12 acres of land. The respondents handed over their lands in favour of the vendors of the appellants but because of the legal bar could not get the exchange deeds registered and therefore the courts below rightly dismissed the suits.</u>

42. He has referred to Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 and submitted that as per explanation to section 4 of the Ordinance the word to transfer shall include the exchange  and any agreement for such exchange and since the transfer was done in violation of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 as per section 6A of the Ordinance the land stood forfeited to the then Government.

43. Mr. Khan has also referred to 43 DLR (AD) 137 and submitted that the GOs referred to in the judgment on the basis of which settlement has been given in favour of the respondents by the Government are all valid GOs having force of law.

<u>44. It appears from the judgment in the case of Chitta Ranjan Sutar that both sections 4, 6 and 6A were declared ultra vires the Constitution and therefore the position is that sections 4, 6 and 6A never existed before. Moreover the Ordinance No.1 of 1964 died natural death by a efflux of time and the exchange proceeding case No.35 of 1969-70 having been started on 24-7-1969 to forfeit the land and for settlement has been done without any lawful authority.</u>

45. Moreover the property in question was never enlisted in the census list of 1966-67 and admittedly the land in question was not forfeited land as per the deposition of DW 1 and the deed of settlement in question refers to Act XLV of 1974 and it does refer to Ordinance No.1 of 1964. The case referred to by Mr. TH Khan reported in 43 DLR (AD) 137 relates to vested property and has no manner of application in this case.

<u>46. In view of our discussions as above it appears that the plaintiffs proved their case and they were entitled to a decree as prayed for and the findings of the courts below on the maintainability of the suits are not tenable in law.</u>

47. Mr. TH Khan, the learned Counsel submits that the plaintiff of both the suits are merely claiming pat of the land covered by the deed of settlement and therefore they are not entitled to decree as prayed for.

<u>48. Be that as it may since the judgments of the courts below suffer from gross illegality these are liable to be set aside and the plaintiffs are entitled to a decree in respect of the title to the suit land and a further decree that the deed of settlement, Annexure-J to the paper book on the basis of Exchange Case No.35 of 1969-70 is not binding upon the appellants of both the suits.</u>

49. In the result both the appeals are allowed and the impugned judgment and decree are set aside.

Both the suits are decreed. In Title Suit No.16 of 1992 the plaintiffs do get a decree declaring that the plaintiffs had right, title, interest and possession in the suit land described in Schedule 'A' of the plaint and a decree for declaration that the settlement deed described in schedule 'B' is not binding on the plaintiffs. Title Suit No. 25 of 1992 be decreed declaring that the plaintiffs have right, title, interest and possession in the suit land described in schedule 'A', 'B' and 'C' of the plaint and a decree for declaration that the settlement deed described in schedule % B' is not binding on the plaintiffs.

End.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Chowdhury Md Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellants. 
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate, Instructed by Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record __ For the Respondents.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 26-5-2003 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No.100 of 1995.)
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: The facts out of which this appeal arose are as under:

2. In a suit or partition the plaintiffs who are the appellants claimed that `Ka' schedule land measuring 4 acres originally belong to Imam Bux in Raiyati right, who died leaving behind a widow Pathani Bibi, a son Sayed All and two daughters Elemjan Bibi and Halimon Bibi. Subsequently Pathani Bibi died leaving behind her aforesaid son and daughters. There was an amicable partition of the inherited property among Elemjan, Halimon and Sayed Ali. Syed Ali got 'Ga' schedule land measuring 2.07 acres out of `Ka' schedule and Elemjan and Halimon got 'Kha' schedule land measuring 1.94 acres out of `Ka' schedule. Schedule 'Gila' land was the self acquired property of the said Sayed Ali. Abdul Majid filed a partition suit being Title Suit No. 175 of 1968, in which Abdul Majid admitted about the amicable partition. Syed Ali died leaving behind a widow, Kulsum, 3 sons Wazuddin, Abdul Majid (predecessor of the defendants) and Ofazuddin and a daughter. Banesa Bibi. The aforesaid Ofazuddin died leaving behind his mother Kulsum, two brothers Wazuddin and Abdul Majid and sister Banesa. The heirs of the Sayed Ali dispossessed Elemjan and Halimon Bibi from 'Kha' schedule land against which Elemjan Bibi and Halimon Bibi filed  Title Suit No. 1225 of 1922 in the Court of 3rd Munsif, Dhaka, in which, they got decree for khas possession. Suit plot Nos. 27 and 29 were sold in auction for arrear of rent in Money Execution Case Nos. 110 and 111 of 1952. Siratunnessa and Atikullah, wife and son respectively of Abdul Majid purchased those on auction.

3. It is further claimed that the defendant Nos. 2, 5 to 9 filed Title Suit No. 14 of 1982 against the plaintiffs, Soleman and Osman for ejectment from the suit land claiming them as licencees, which was dismissed for default. Kulsum Bibi acquired 1/8th share from her husband and 1/24th share from son Ofazuddin, who transferred some land from plot No. 23 and thereafter gifted 0.18½ acre to the plaintiff Nos. 1 to 4. Banesa Bibi, inherited 1/8th share from her father and 1/24th share from brother Ofazuddin, who by a registered deed of Hiba-bil-ewaj dated 11th June 1976 transferred 0.32-3/4 acre to plaintiff Nos. 2 to 4. Wazuddin got 1/8th share from 'Kha' schedule as heir of Elemjan Bibi and 1/8th share from his father,1/12th share from his brother in 'Ga' schedule land and in this way he got 1/3rd share in 'Ka' schedule land, who died leaving a widow the plaintiff No. 1, 3 sons, the plaintiff Nos. 2 to 4 and 2 daughters the plaintiff Nos. 5 and 6. The plaintiffs are entitled to 1/2 share in `Kha' schedule, 1/3 rd share in 'Ga' and 'Gha' schedule by inheritance and also 1/4 share by Hiba-bil-ewaj from Kulsum Bibi and Banesa Bibi from 'Ca' schedule land.

4. Defendant Nos. 2-9 contested the suit claiming that Sayed Ali died leaving 2 sons, Wazuddin and Abdul Majid. His another son Ofazuddin died before his father and as such he has not inherited any share in the suit land. The auction sale in respect of the suit land has not been aside. Kulsum Bibi transferred 0.48 acre of land from plot No. 23 to Jamal Kha and others and they are possessing the same and as such she had no right to make any gift in favour of the plaintiffs. Wazuddin, by a registered deed of Hiba-bil-ewaj dated 21st June, 1962 transferred 0.55 acre of land from plot Nos. 29, 30, 31, and 0.14 acre of land from plot No. 115 to his brother Abdul Majid who is possessing the said land. Abdul Majid died leaving the defendant Nos. 1 to 10. Moreover, defendant No. 2 Atikullah and Siratunnessa have also auctioned purchased part of the suit land. Defendant Nos. 2 to 9 have been possessing 1.12 acres of land from northern side of the tank of the plot No. 29 and 0.16 acre of land north western side of plot No. 31 by inheritance. Except 0.07 acre of land, the plaintiffs have no title and possession in any part of the suit land.

5. Defendant No. 21 Razia Khatun also contested the suit and denied the claim of the plaintiffs and claimed that she has been possessing 0.28 acre of land in schedule 'Kha'.

6. Learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit in preliminary form allotting a saham of 1.29 acres of land in favour of the plaintiffs. On appeal from the said judgment and order, the High Court Division allowed the appeal in part and allotted a saham of 0.35 acre of land to the plaintiffs.

7. Leave was granted to consider as to whether the High Court Division is justified in modifying the decree and allotting a saham of 0.35 acre in place of 1.29 acres to the plaintiffs relying upon the defendants claim of auction sale, ext `Ka' and the deed of gift, exhibit 'ga' executed by the plaintiffs predecessor.

8. There is no dispute that both the parties are heirs of Imam Bux and the plaintiffs are claiming title as heirs of Wazuddin, son of Syed Ali and on the other hand, the defendants are claiming title and heirs of Abdul Majid, son of Sayed Ali. Admittedly Imam Bux died leaving widow Pathani Bibi, son Sayed Ali, daughters Elemjan and Halimon. Pathani Bibi subsequently died leaving her son and daughter. Therefore, admittedly Syed Ali inherited 8 annas share and Elemjan and Halimon inherited 4 annas share each in the suit land. There is also no dispute that Sayed Ali, Elemjan and Halimon amicably partitioned schedule 'Ka' land and as per partition, Elemjan and Halimon got 'Kha' schedule land and Sayed Ali got 'Ga' schedule land. Admittedly Elemjan and Halimon were dispossessed by the heirs of Sayed Ali and in Title Suit No. 1225 of 1922 they got possession though Court, which is evident from exhibit-3 series. The learned Subordinate Judge observed that though in Money Execution Case Nos. 110 and 111 of 1952 the defendant No. 2 Atikullah and his mother Siratunnessa purchased 0.20 acre in plot No. 76, 0.89 in plot No. 27 and 0.64 acres in plot No. 29 in auction, the parties had amicably compromised the matter and in pursuance of such compromise, sale in respect of only 0.07 acre of land in plot No. 27 in Money Execution Case No. 111 of 1952 and 0.20 acre of land in plot No. 76 of Khatian No. 40 relating to 'Gha' schedule land in Money Execution Case No. 110 of 1952 were confirmed, and that the auction sale in respect of other land was set aside.

9. The High Court Division interfered with the judgment of the trial Court on the reasonings that in Title Suit No. 175 of 1968 Atikullah was defendant No. 2 and thus the interest of Abdul Majid and Atikullah was conflicting, that whatever statements Abdul Majid made in that suit regarding setting aside of the auction sale would not be binding upon the defendant Atikullah , that no decision was given in that suit since the suit was dismissed for default and that since Wazuddin gifted 0.55 acre of land in favour of Abdul Majid, the land covered by auction sale and Exhibit 'Ga' should be left out of hotchpotch.

10. Therefore, the disputes between the parties are (1) whether the auction sale was compromised by the parties and (2) whether Wazauddin gifted land to his brother by Exhibit 'Ca' if the plaintiffs claim for setting aside the auction sale is believed, Elemjan had 1.03 acres of land in schedule 'Kha', and in that case the trial Court was justified in giving saham to plaintiffs out of those land. Mr Mahbubey Alam, appearing for the plaintiffs contended that the High Court Division failed to notice that apart from the admission of Abdul Majid, the plaintiffs led both oral and documentary evidence in support of their claim, but the defendants failed to substantiate their claim that in pursuance of auction sale, they got possession of the land through Court other than 0.20 acre in plot No. 76 Exhibit 'Kha'. Mr Mahmudul Islam, on the other hand, contended that the High Court Division rightly found that Atikullah and his mother purchased the land in auction by Exhibit 'Ka' and therefore, the High Court Division is justified in not  bringing the land sold in auction in hotchpotch.

<u>11. In paragraph 7 of the plaint; the plaintiffs specifically stated that Money Execution Case Nos. 110 and 111 of 1952 were disposed of on compromise and sale of 0.07 acre in plot No. 29 towards west was confirmed and the rest 0.57 acre was set aside, and the sale in respect of land in plot No. 27 was set aside. The defendants simply stated in paragraph 6(Kha) of their written statement that the sale was not set aside rather confirmed. This statement is not in our view is sufficient to meet the positive claim of the plaintiffs on the point of setting aside the auction sale. According to the law of pleadings, the defendant is bound to deal specifically each allegations of fact, the truth of which is not admitted. The written statement must not only deal with specifically, the defendant must also answer the point of substance. If his denial of fact is not specific but evasive, the said fact shall be taken to be admitted. In such event, the admission itself being proof, no other proof is necessary.</u>

12. The plaintiffs produced exhibit-4, Register of Rent Execution Case No. 110 of 1952, which showed that the case was dismissed on 4th August 1956 with observation "in term of Rafanama". The pleadings, the oral evidence of Mohiuddin (PW 1) the plaintiff No. 2, who deposed in support of setting aside the sale and the documentary evidence sufficiently, support the plaintiff's claim of setting aside the auction sale, except 0.07 acres in plot No. 29. Defendants though claimed that Atikullah and his mother purchased in auction 0.20 acre of land in plot No. 76, 0.89 acre of land in plot No. 27 and 0.64 acres in plot No. 29 by exhibit 'Ka' series, on 10th September, 1952, they produced exhibit 'Kha' showing delivery of possession of only 0.20 acre in plot No. 76 in Money Execution Case No. 111 of 1952. Mr Mahmudul Islam failed to meet our query as to why the defendants did not produce documentary evidence showing delivery of possession in pursuance of their claim other than exhibit 'Kha' Exhibits 4 and 'Kha' supported the plaintiffs claim that as per compromise the defendants got 0.07 acre of land in plot No. 29 and 0.20 acre of land in plot No. 76, although no documentary evidence in respect of 0.07 acre could be filed but in view of the plaintiffs admission, we presumed that the defendants got only 0.27 acre by way of auction purchase.

13. What is more, in Title Suit No. 14 of 1982, exhibit-2 (Ka), the defendants prayed for recovery of possession in respect of plot Nos. 2 and 29 from the plaintiffs claiming them as licenses since 12th November, 1961. The plaintiffs filed a written statement claiming title in those plots on the basis of deeds dated 21st January, 1960 and 17th April, 1970. The suit was dismissed for default in presence of the plaintiffs under Order IX, rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This admission of possession in those plots since. 1961 supported the plaintiffs' claim of setting aside the sale. The High Court Division has totally ignored these admitted facts. In view of the above, we find that the learned Subordinate Judge is justified that the auction sale was set aside and Banesa, daughter of Syed Ali gifted 0.323/4 acre of land to the plaintiffs Nos. 2-4 by exhibit-5.

<u>14. Now turning to Hiba-bil-ewaj, exhibit ga, by which, the defendants claimed that Wazuddin gifted 0.55 acre on 21st June, 1962 in favour of Abdul Majid. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge disbelieved the defendants claim on the reasonings that in this deed Wazuddin and Kulsum were shown as donors but Wazuddin alone executed the deed. Further, the defendants did file the original deed and they also did not prove the said deed by examining scribe and witnesses and that in presence of Wazuddin's sons, daughters and wife, it was not a believable story that he would donate land without any cause. The High Court Division, on the other hand, was of the view that though Kulsum Bibi did not execute the deed, the defendants would get the share of Wazuddin and that by this deed the defendants could not get more than 0.53 acre out of 0.69 acre of land.</u>

15. Mr Mahbubey Adam contends that the High Court Division erred in law in believing the Hiba deed in failing to notice that Abdul Majid did not say anything regarding this deed in Title Suit No. 175 of 1968 (exhibit-2) instituted by him against Wazuddin and others seeking partition of the ejmaii property. This suit was dismissed for default on 6th September, 1979 exhibit-2 (Ga). Abdul Majid, thereupon, filed a petition under Order IX, rule 9, which was also dismissed for default on 24th February, 1982 exhibit -3 (Ka). The land, said to have been gifted, is in respect of plot Nos. 29,30 and 31. These plots are included in schedule-A to the plaint in Title Suit No. 175 of 1968. We noticed that there is no statement in this plaint regarding this deed of gift. We failed to understand why Abdul Majid did not claim land on the basis of exihibit-Ga had his brother really gifted land to him? Furthermore, the defendants did not examine the scribe and witnesses of the said deed. According to Mr Alam, the defendants collusively created this deed and this examination cannot be totally ignored from the facts noticed above. According to Mr Mahmudul Islam, this Hiba-bi-ewaz having exhibited without any objection by the plaintiffs, the trial Court was wrong in disbelieving it. Mr Mahmudul Islam has referred the case of Jainal Abedin vs Mizanur Rahman and other, 44 DLR (AD) 162. Mr Islam further contended that view of section 47 of the Transfer of property Act, even if it is assumed that no possession was given in pursuance of the deed of gift the plaintiffs cannot deny the alienation of the land by their predecessor since the defendants are admittedly co-sharers, an undivided share may be transferred by way of gift to another co-sharer.

16. The defendants examined two witnesses in support of the gift, of them, Ashmat (DW 2) claimed that at the time of execution of Hiba he was present but in cross examination, he stated that at the time of delivery of possession he was not present. He positively stated that Wazuddin and others i.e. Wazuddin and Kulsum executed the deed but as a matter of fact, Kulsum did not execute the deed. He is not a witness in the deed. Shah Alam (DW 3) though claimed that the defendants are in possession of the suit land on the strength of deed of gift but in course of cross-examination he admitted that he was not present at the time of execution of the deed. These witnesses are close neighbours, though not witnesses of the deed, supported the gift without disclosing the basis of their claim and from the nature of evidence they deposed do not inspire us to believe them as reliable witnesses.

<u>17. We do not dispute the statement of law argued in the case cited by Mr. Mahmudul Islam. The submission that this document having been marked as exhibit without objection became admissible in evidence is a general rule and the same principle is not applicable in all cases. This rule dis-entitling a party to object to the admissibility of secondary evidence in appeal, when no objection was taken in the Court of first instance cannot have universal application. The rule contained in section 65 which excludes secondary evidence is not so rigid as to be enforced even if no objection is taken at the trial by the party against whom the secondary evidence is offered. As there is no mention of secondary evidence being given of the execution of a document in section 56, a certified copy is only evidence of the existence, condition and contents of a document and not of its execution. A certified copy is a copy signed and certified as true by the officer to whose custody the original is entrusted, and it is admitted upon the credit of such officer without comparing with original. Unless a party can be found to have been stopped from objecting to the admissibility of the evidence, evidence, not otherwise admissible, or which would have been liable to rejection if objection were taken to it, cannot be said to be good evidence, if admitted by the consent of parties.</u>

<u>18. Suppose a deed is forged and the beneficiary of the deed destroyed it in order to avoid future complication and filed a certified copy which was admitted in evidence without object on. Now the question is whether the Court at all believes it as genuine after it has been detected as forged at the appellate stage? Section 65 is exhaustive of the grounds on which secondary evidence may be admitted. It has been argued by the judicial committee in Krishna Kishori Chaodhrani vs Kishori Lal Roy, 14 IA 71 (PC) that secondary evidence of contents of a document cannot be admitted without the non-production of the original being first accounted for in such manner as to bring the case within one or more of the clauses to section 65.</u>

19. What we suspect is the basis the defendants claim, inasmuch as, if Exhibit 'Ga' along with exhibits 2, 'Ka' Kha' and 'Cha' series are taken into consideration, a reasonable inference may be drawn that the defendants are claiming the suit land by setting up different pleas at different stages to deprive the right of the plaintiffs. In view of the above we find force in the contention of Mr. Mahbubey Alan that this exhibit-'Ga' is collusive Document and the learned Subordinate judge has rightly disbelieved the defendants claim and rightly allotted a saham of 1.20 acre of land in favour of the plaintiffs. The High Court Division failed to notice that if there was existence of such deed of gift, Abdul Majid ought to have claimed saham on the basis of exihibit-Ga Title suit No. 175 of 1968. Furthermore, in Title suit No. 14 of 1982 the defendants admitted the plaintiffs possession since 12th November 1961, which fact negated the defendants claim of transfer of land by Wazuddin by way of gift, inasmuch as, if the plaintiffs were helpless in November, 1961, how their predecessor had gifted 0.55 acres out of the ejmali property including one plot of the deed of gift to Abdul Majid on 21st June, 1962 is not clear to us? It is not understandable that though Wazuddin and Kulsum were shown as, donors, why Kulsum did not execute the deed? The defendants did not give any explanation in that regard. The story of missing the original deed during the war of liberation is also doubtful one, inasmuch as the defendants filed other title deeds including exhibits-Cha series, which are relating to the same land.

<u>20. The High Court Division while believing the deed of gift did not advert to the findings arrived at by the learned Subordinate Judge. We are convinced that the story of auction purchase, giving licence of two plots to the plaintiffs and then the execution of the deed of Hiba bil ewaj have been set up by the defendants during the period between 9th July, 1955 and 21st June, 1962 with a view to deprive the plaintiffs from their inherited and acquired property.</u>

<u>21. Section 47 of the Transfer of Property Act applies when owners who hold estate as tenants in common transfer a part of the estate; the share of each co-owner is proportionately reduced equally. If the shares are unequal there is a greater reduction in the greater share, and a lesser reduction in the lesser share. In this case Wazuddin alone allegedly gifted 0.55 acre of land out of. his share and accordingly, it is section 44, not section 47 as contended by Mr Mahmudul Islam, which is applicable if the claim of gift by Hiba is found genuine. Under this provision, if one of the several co-owners transfers his share, the transferee stands in the shoes of the transferor. He acquires as against the other co-owners the same rights that of the transferee had, and is subject to any conditions affecting the share at the date of the transfer. The principle of this section is that of subrogation or substitution.</u>

22. The high Court Division fell in an error in interfering with the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge without reversing all the findings and also without assigning proper reasons. We find merit in this appeal. The judgment of the High Court Division is set aside. The appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.
